lessons.title: HR Strategy and the Business
lessons.objective: Learn basic words to talk about HR strategy and how HR helps the business grow.
lessons.intro:
Human Resources is about people. It is the part of the company that finds, supports and develops employees.

When a company grows, it needs the right people in the right roles. That is where HR comes in. HR creates a plan that connects people to the goals of the business.

At Czarnikow, the HR team works with offices in London, Brazil and around the world. They make sure every employee has what they need to do their best work.

grammarDeepDive.title: Simple Present — to be (am / is / are)
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The verb to be is the most basic and most important verb in English. In business, we use it hundreds of times a day to describe people, roles, facts and situations. At Czarnikow, you might say 'I am in HR', 'She is the director', or 'We are a global team'. Every one of these uses to be in the Simple Present.

The forms are simple: I am, you/we/they are, he/she/it is. In spoken English, we often use contractions: I'm, you're, she's, we're, they're. In business writing, the full forms are more common and sound more professional. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) agree that mastering to be is the first step to fluency, because it appears in almost every English sentence.

Use to be for: identity (She is the HR director), descriptions (The plan is clear), feelings (I am happy with the result), and locations (The office is in London). Remember: to be does not need do/does for questions — just move it to the front: Is she the manager? Are we ready?
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 1: Present Simple of 'be' — am, is, are.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 1 (am/is/are) and Unit 2 (am/is/are — questions).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on 'be' with usage notes and examples.

rolePlays.title: HR Director Meets the CEO
rolePlays.setup: It is Monday morning at Czarnikow's London office. Sophie, the HR director, is in a meeting with the CEO. They are discussing the HR plan for the next year. The company wants to grow, and HR needs to hire 15 new people.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Sophie. Explain the HR strategy: the team is ready, the plan is clear, and you need 15 new hires. Use 'to be' forms.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the CEO. Ask Sophie simple questions: Is the team ready? Are the goals clear? Is the budget enough?
sampleDialogue: A: Good morning. I am ready to present the HR plan for next year.
B: Good morning, Sophie. Is the plan ready?
A: Yes, it is. Our main goal is to hire fifteen new people.
B: Are the teams ready for new members?
A: Yes, they are. The managers are prepared and the structure is clear.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three forms of 'to be' correctly (am, is, are). Student B asks at least two 'is/are' questions.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run it once as Student A; swap and run it again as Student B. Focus on correct use of am/is/are. Do not interrupt during the role play.

qAndA.question: What does HR strategy mean, according to the lesson?

lessons.title: The Company and Its Roles
lessons.objective: Learn the names of common roles in a company and how to describe them in simple English.
lessons.intro:
Every company has many people with different jobs. We call these jobs roles.

At the top, there is the CEO, the chief executive officer. Then we have directors, managers, team leaders, and team members. Each role has a clear job to do.

When we understand the structure, we know who to talk to. We know who makes the decisions and who does the work. This is called the organisational structure.

grammarDeepDive.title: Simple Present — Positive Sentences
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The Simple Present is the tense we use most at work. It describes facts, routines and permanent situations. When we talk about what people do in their jobs — their responsibilities, their daily tasks, their roles — we use the Simple Present. At Czarnikow, you might say 'Sophie manages the HR team' or 'James reports to the CEO'.

The key rule is the third-person -s. With I, you, we, they, the verb stays in its base form: I work, we manage, they report. With he, she, it, the verb adds -s (or -es after s, sh, ch, x, o): She works, he manages, it takes. This small letter is very important — forgetting it is one of the most common mistakes in business English.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) highlight that the Simple Present for jobs and roles gives a sense of permanence — this is what a person does as part of their job, not just today, but as a regular responsibility. When you describe the company structure, every sentence uses Simple Present because the structure is stable and ongoing.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 2–3: Simple Present for facts and routines, third-person -s.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 5 (Present Simple positive) and Unit 6 (Present Simple with he/she/it).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on Present Simple with job descriptions and role examples.

lessons.title: Numbers That Matter: HR Metrics
lessons.objective: Learn basic numbers, percentages and the idea of HR metrics and KPIs.
lessons.intro:
HR uses numbers to understand people at work. These numbers are called metrics.

For example, how many people work in the company? How many new people start every month? How many people leave? These are all HR metrics.

A KPI is a key performance indicator. It is a number that is very important for the team. When the KPI is good, the team is doing well.

grammarDeepDive.title: There is / There are
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In business English, we constantly need to say how many things exist or how many items are in a report, a team, or a list. The structure there is / there are is the simplest way to do this. At Czarnikow, you might say 'There is one new hire this month' or 'There are five open vacancies in the London office'.

The rule is straightforward: use there is with singular nouns (one thing) and there are with plural nouns (more than one). In spoken English, there's is common for the singular form. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) note that this structure is especially useful for introducing new information — when your listener does not yet know about the thing you are mentioning.

For negatives, add not: There is not (there isn't) a meeting today. There are not (there aren't) any new reports. For questions, reverse the order: Is there a new KPI? Are there any changes? This structure appears in almost every HR report and presentation, so mastering it gives you a solid foundation for talking about data and numbers.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 34: There is and there are.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 37 (There is/are) and Unit 38 (There is/are — questions).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on 'there is/there are' with countable and uncountable examples.

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'There are five employees' and not 'There is five employees'?

lessons.intro:
A performance review is a meeting. The manager and the employee sit together and talk about work.

They talk about the good things and the things that can improve. It is a moment to say "Well done" and also a moment to plan for the future.

A good review is calm, clear and honest. Both people listen and both people speak.

grammarDeepDive.title: Simple Present — Questions with Do / Does
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Asking questions is essential in business, especially in performance reviews. In the Simple Present, we form questions using Do or Does before the subject. We use Do with I, you, we, they and Does with he, she, it. The main verb stays in its base form — no -s, even after does.

The structure is: Do/Does + subject + base verb + rest of sentence? For example: Do you enjoy your work? Does she meet her targets? This pattern works for all regular verbs. Note that to be does not follow this rule — we say Is she happy? not Does she be happy?

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) explain that the most common mistake with do/does questions is adding -s to the verb after does. Remember: does already carries the third-person meaning, so the verb stays plain. In a performance review, asking good questions shows you are engaged and thoughtful — it is a skill as important as giving answers.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 7: Present Simple questions and short answers.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 6 (Present Simple negative) and Unit 7 (Present Simple questions with do/does).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on question formation with 'do' and 'does'.

lessons.objective: Learn basic words for recruitment and how to describe what is happening now.
lessons.intro:
Recruitment is the process of finding new people to join the company.

First, HR writes a job description. Then, they post the job online. People send their CVs. The best candidates come for an interview. Finally, one person gets the offer and becomes a new employee.

It is a journey, step by step. The goal is simple: find the right person for the right role.

grammarDeepDive.title: Present Continuous — Actions Happening Now
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The Present Continuous describes what is happening right now, at this moment. In a busy HR department like Czarnikow's, there is always something in progress: 'Oliver is reading CVs', 'Sophie is interviewing a candidate', 'We are preparing the offer letter'. All of these use the Present Continuous because the action is happening as we speak.

The structure is: subject + am/is/are + verb-ing. With I, use am. With he/she/it, use is. With you/we/they, use are. The -ing form is made by adding -ing to the base verb: read → reading, interview → interviewing. Watch out for spelling: verbs ending in -e drop it (write → writing), and short verbs with one vowel + one consonant double the final consonant (sit → sitting).

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) explain that the Present Continuous is also used for temporary situations and plans in the near future: 'We are hiring two people this month' (temporary) or 'She is starting on Monday' (planned). In recruitment, this tense appears everywhere because the process is dynamic — things are always moving forward.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 4–5: Present Continuous for now and for temporary actions.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 3 (Present Continuous) and Unit 4 (Present Simple vs Present Continuous).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on Present Continuous with examples of actions in progress.

grammarDeepDive.title: Wh- Questions in Interviews
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Wh- questions are the questions that start with What, Where, When, Why, Who and How. They are the most important type of question in a job interview because they ask for real information — not just 'yes' or 'no'. A recruiter who uses Wh- questions can learn about a candidate's experience, motivation, and personality in just a few minutes.

The structure of a Wh- question in the Present Simple is: Wh- word + do/does + subject + base verb. For example: Where do you work? or What does your team do? In the Past Simple, we use did: Why did you leave your last job? With the verb be, we do not need do: What is your role? Who is your manager?

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) emphasise that the most common mistake is forgetting the auxiliary verb (do/does/did) or putting the subject before the verb. Remember: in English questions, the verb comes before the subject. Practise this pattern until it becomes automatic, and interviews will feel much easier.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 34–36 on Wh- questions, question words, and question formation.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 44 (Who/What/Which) and Unit 45 (How long/How far/How often).
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on question words with examples of interview contexts.

grammarDeepDive.title: Adjectives: Describing Your Workplace
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Adjectives are words that describe nouns. In business English, adjectives are essential when you talk about your company, your team, or your workplace. In employer branding, adjectives are your main tool — they paint the picture of the company for candidates and the outside world. A few well-chosen adjectives can make the difference between a boring job advert and one that attracts top talent.

In English, adjectives usually go before the noun (a friendly team) or after the verb 'be' (the team is friendly). Unlike Portuguese, English adjectives do not change for gender or number: we say a modern office and modern offices — the adjective stays the same. This makes them easier to use, but students sometimes confuse adjectives with adverbs or nouns.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) explain that the key test is simple: if the word describes a noun, it is an adjective. If it describes a verb, it is an adverb. For employer branding, focus on positive adjectives that are true: friendly, fair, modern, supportive, diverse, collaborative. Authenticity matters — the best employer brand is the honest one.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 44–46 on adjectives, adjective order, and adjective + noun patterns.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 98 (Adjectives ending in -ing and -ed) and Unit 99 (Adjectives: position and order).
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on common workplace adjectives with usage examples.

grammarDeepDive.title: Imperatives: Giving Simple Instructions
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The imperative is the simplest sentence structure in English. You take the base form of the verb and use it as a direct instruction: Come, Sit, Take, Sign, Read. There is no subject — the listener understands that the instruction is for them. In onboarding, imperatives are everywhere because the new employee needs clear, short instructions to navigate their first day.

To make an imperative polite, add please — either at the beginning or the end: Please sit here or Sit here, please. To make a negative imperative, add don't: Don't worry, Don't forget your badge. The structure never changes — no conjugation, no auxiliary verb, no subject. This makes imperatives one of the easiest grammar points in English.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) note that imperatives are not rude by default — context and tone matter. In a warm onboarding situation, imperatives like Come with me and Ask any question are friendly. The key is to use a warm tone of voice and add please when appropriate.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 37 on imperatives, instructions, and polite requests.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 35 (Imperative) and Unit 36 (Let's and Shall we).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on imperatives with workplace and instruction examples.

qAndA.question: What is onboarding?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Onboarding is the process of welcoming a new employee. It includes showing the office, introducing the team, and helping the person understand how things work.

qAndA.question: What are three things HR does on the first day?
qAndA.modelAnswer: HR says welcome, shows the office, and presents the team. They also help with documents, badges, and the onboarding schedule.

qAndA.question: Why do imperatives not have a subject?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because the instruction is always directed at the listener — 'you' is understood. Adding 'you' would make it sound like a statement, not an instruction.

qAndA.question: Why is a good first day so important for a new employee?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because first impressions last. If a new employee feels welcome and organised, they start with confidence. A bad first day can make someone regret joining.

qAndA.question: What could go wrong if onboarding is poorly organised?
qAndA.modelAnswer: The new employee might feel lost, confused, or unwelcome. They might not know who to ask for help, waste time, or even decide to leave the company early.

grammarDeepDive.title: Can and Cannot: Talking About Ability
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Can is a modal verb that we use to talk about ability — what we are able to do. In a work context, it is the most important word for describing skills: I can speak English, She can use Excel, We can offer training. The negative form is cannot (one word) or the contraction can't. The question form is simple: Can you...?

The grammar rule is straightforward: can + base verb (no 'to', no '-s', no '-ing'). It is the same for every subject: I can, you can, he can, she can, we can, they can. This makes 'can' one of the easiest verbs to use. The only tricky part is pronunciation: in positive sentences, 'can' is often pronounced weakly (/kən/), while 'can't' is pronounced with a clear, strong vowel (/kɑːnt/ in British English).

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) explain that 'can' describes present ability, not future plans. For future ability, we say will be able to: After this course, I will be able to write reports in English. For now, focus on present ability — what you can and cannot do today. Training is the bridge between 'cannot' and 'can'.

Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 26 (Can, could, be able to) and Unit 27 (Could and was able to).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on 'can' with examples of ability, permission, and requests.

lessons.objective: Learn simple words to describe a good leader and give simple advice.
lessons.intro:
A leader is a person who guides a team.

A good leader listens, explains, and helps. A leader does not need to shout. A real leader brings calm and direction.

Leadership is not only for the boss. Every person can be a leader in their own work — when they help, when they plan, when they teach others.

grammarDeepDive.title: Should: Giving Advice About Leadership
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Should is a modal verb used to give advice, recommendations, and opinions about what is right or good to do. In the context of leadership, 'should' is the perfect word: A leader should listen. A manager should give clear feedback. You should lead by example. It is softer than 'must' (which sounds like a rule) and stronger than 'could' (which sounds like just a possibility).

The structure is simple: subject + should + base verb. It never changes: I should, you should, he should, she should, we should, they should. The negative form is should not (or shouldn't): A leader should not shout. You shouldn't ignore your team's ideas. Questions use inversion: Should we meet today? Should the manager explain the decision?

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) emphasise that 'should' expresses the speaker's opinion about what is the right thing to do. It is not about obligation (that is 'must') or ability (that is 'can'). In leadership discussions, 'should' is your main tool for talking about qualities, behaviours, and standards that good leaders follow.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 20–21 on should, ought to, and giving advice.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 33 (Should) and Unit 34 (Should 2 — 'I think you should').
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on 'should' with examples of advice, recommendation, and opinion.

rolePlays.title: James's Leadership Workshop
rolePlays.setup: James is leading a workshop on leadership at Czarnikow. He shares his views on what good leaders should and should not do. A participant asks questions and shares their own opinion.

rolePlays.studentB: You are a participant. Ask three questions and share one opinion of your own about leadership.
sampleDialogue: A: Welcome to the workshop. Let's talk about leadership. I believe a leader should always listen first.
B: Why is listening so important?
A: Because when you listen, people feel respected. A leader should not make decisions without hearing the team.
B: I agree. Should a leader also admit mistakes?
A: Absolutely. A good leader should be honest — even about their own mistakes. It builds trust.
B: I think a leader should also celebrate the team's wins. Not just focus on problems.
A: That's a great point. We should always recognise good work.

If you want respect, you should give respect first. Leadership is about people, not power.

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, what is the difference between a boss and a leader?

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'should' and 'must'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'Should' gives advice — it is a recommendation. 'Must' expresses obligation — it is a rule. 'You should arrive on time' is friendly advice. 'You must arrive on time' is a strict rule.

qAndA.question: Why does James say 'leadership is about people, not power'?

lessons.intro:
A career is the path of your working life.

At the beginning, you start in a junior role. After a few years, you can become a senior. Later, maybe a manager, or a specialist in your area.

HR helps people to plan their career. It is called career pathing. When you know where you want to go, it is easier to arrive.

grammarDeepDive.title: Going to — Future Plans
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In business English, we often need to talk about plans and intentions — things we have already decided to do. The structure going to is perfect for this. When Sophie asks Mariana about her next career step, Mariana can say 'I am going to apply for a senior role' because she has already thought about it and made her decision.

The structure is: subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb. For example: I am going to take a course. She is going to lead the project. We are going to hire two new analysts. The key idea is that the plan exists before the moment of speaking — it is not a sudden decision.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) explain that going to signals a prior intention. This is different from will, which often signals a decision made at the moment of speaking. At Czarnikow, when you talk about career goals, development plans, or team objectives for next quarter, going to is almost always the right choice.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 28 on 'going to' for plans and intentions.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 19 ('going to' for future plans) and Unit 20 (will vs going to).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on 'going to' with examples of future plans and intentions.

qAndA.question: What is career pathing?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Career pathing is when HR helps people plan their career — knowing where they want to go and what steps they need to take.

qAndA.question: What are the two main ways to grow at a company, according to the lesson?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: You can become a manager or you can specialise in your area. Both paths are valuable.

qAndA.question: Why do we use 'going to' instead of 'will' when talking about career plans?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because career plans are things we have already decided. 'Going to' is for prior intentions, while 'will' is for spontaneous decisions.

qAndA.question: Why is it important for a company to have clear career paths?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because employees can see where they are going. They feel motivated, they stay longer, and they work harder when they know there is a future for them.

qAndA.question: What can happen if an employee does not have a development plan?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: They may feel lost or unmotivated. They may not know what skills to develop. Eventually, they may leave the company for a place with better opportunities.

lessons.title: Coaching and Good Feedback
lessons.objective: Learn how to give and receive simple, positive feedback at work.
lessons.intro:
Feedback is when we tell someone how they are doing.

Good feedback is clear, kind and honest. We say the good things — and also the things that can improve. We speak softly and we listen carefully.

Coaching is a type of feedback. A coach does not give answers; a coach asks questions that help the other person to think.

grammarDeepDive.title: Adverbs of Manner
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Adverbs of manner describe how we do something. In business, especially in feedback and coaching, they are essential. When Emily tells João 'You presented clearly', the adverb clearly tells us how he presented. Without the adverb, the sentence would just be 'You presented' — correct, but it gives no feedback at all.

Most adverbs of manner are formed by adding -ly to the adjective: clear → clearly, kind → kindly, honest → honestly, careful → carefully. They usually come after the verb or after the object: She speaks clearly. He finished the report quickly. Some common adverbs are irregular: good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) emphasise that adverbs of manner are one of the most practical tools for giving feedback. Instead of just saying 'good job', you can say 'You explained the numbers clearly and responded to questions calmly' — this is specific, helpful feedback that the person can learn from.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 73 on adverbs of manner: formation, position and common irregulars.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 100 (Adjectives and adverbs) and Unit 101 (well/fast/hard etc.).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on adverbs of manner with examples and position rules.

commonMistakes.wrong: She speaks clear in meetings.
commonMistakes.right: She speaks clearly in meetings.
commonMistakes.why: 'Clear' is the adjective. After a verb, use the adverb form: clearly.

commonMistakes.wrong: He works hardly every day.
commonMistakes.right: He works hard every day.
commonMistakes.why: 'Hard' is both adjective and adverb. 'Hardly' means 'almost not' — a very different meaning.

commonMistakes.wrong: She did good in the presentation.
commonMistakes.right: She did well in the presentation.
commonMistakes.why: 'Good' is the adjective; 'well' is the adverb. After verbs, use 'well'.

commonMistakes.wrong: He responded the question politely.
commonMistakes.right: He responded to the question politely.
commonMistakes.why: 'Respond' needs the preposition 'to'. The adverb 'politely' comes after.

commonMistakes.wrong: She careful listens to feedback.
commonMistakes.right: She carefully listens to feedback.
commonMistakes.why: The adverb form is 'carefully', and it goes before the verb or after the object.

rolePlays.studentB: You are João. Respond to the positive feedback, share one thing you think went well and one thing you want to improve.
sampleDialogue: A: Hi João. Thanks for coming. I want to talk about your presentation last week. You spoke very clearly — well done.
B: Thank you, Emily. I felt good about it, but I think I spoke too quickly at the end.
A: That's a good observation. Next time, try to slow down and explain each point more carefully.
B: I will. I am also going to practise more before the next one.
A: Great. You are improving steadily — keep going.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least two adverbs of manner when giving feedback. Student B uses at least one adverb to describe their own performance.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Emphasise the coaching style: asking questions before giving answers. Swap roles after the first round.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Emily gives feedback to a team member
additionalAudios.speaker: emily
additionalAudios.transcript: Hi João. I wanted to talk about your client call yesterday. First, you spoke very clearly — the client understood everything. That was excellent. One thing to work on: you answered some questions too quickly. Next time, try to pause and think carefully before you respond. Also, remember to listen patiently — sometimes the client needs a moment to finish. Overall, you did well. Keep going.
tasks: Listen once without reading. Was the feedback mostly positive or mostly negative? (Answer: mostly positive)
Listen again. Find three adverbs of manner in the feedback.
What specific advice does Emily give for next time? (Answer: pause and think carefully, listen patiently)
Pronunciation drill: repeat 'clearly', 'quickly', 'carefully', 'patiently' — focus on the -ly ending.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — A coaching question technique
additionalAudios.speaker: sophie
additionalAudios.transcript: In coaching, we don't give answers — we ask questions. For example, instead of saying 'You need to be more organised', you can ask: 'How could you organise your time more effectively?' Instead of 'You spoke too fast', try: 'What would happen if you spoke more slowly?' The person thinks honestly about the answer. That's the power of coaching.
tasks: What is the difference between feedback and coaching, according to Sophie? (Answer: feedback gives answers, coaching asks questions)
Find the two coaching questions Sophie suggests.
What adverbs does Sophie use? (Answer: effectively, slowly, honestly)
Rewrite one of your own feedback points as a coaching question.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between feedback and coaching?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Feedback tells someone how they are doing. Coaching asks questions that help the person think and find their own answers.

qAndA.question: What are the three qualities of good feedback, according to the lesson?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Good feedback is clear, kind and honest.

qAndA.question: How do we form most adverbs of manner in English?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: We add -ly to the adjective. For example: clear becomes clearly, kind becomes kindly, careful becomes carefully.

qAndA.question: Why is coaching sometimes more effective than simply giving feedback?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because when people find the answer themselves, they understand it better and are more likely to act on it. It builds thinking skills.

qAndA.question: Why should feedback be specific rather than general?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because specific feedback tells the person exactly what they did well or what to change. 'You spoke clearly' is more helpful than just 'good job'.

contextualization: Think of a recent situation at Czarnikow where you received feedback. Describe it in English: Who gave it? How did they give it? Was it helpful?
Imagine you need to give feedback to a colleague who presented too quickly. Use two adverbs to give your feedback aloud.
What is one thing you do well at work? Describe it using an adverb: 'I _____ (verb) _____ (adverb).'
Think of a coaching question you could ask a junior colleague instead of giving direct advice. Say it aloud.

lessons.title: Happy Teams: Engagement at Work
lessons.objective: Learn to talk about how people feel at work and what makes them happy.
lessons.intro:
Engagement is how connected people feel to their work.

When employees are engaged, they like their job, they like their team, and they feel proud of the company. They smile more. They help more.

HR wants to know how people feel. Sometimes HR sends a short survey: "How happy are you at work?" The answers help the company to improve.

grammarDeepDive.title: Like + Verb-ing
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
One of the most natural ways to talk about what makes you happy at work is the pattern like + verb-ing. When Emily asks the team 'What do you like about your job?', they can answer 'I like working with the sugar team' or 'I like solving problems with my colleagues'. The -ing form after like focuses on the experience — the feeling of doing the activity.

The structure is simple: subject + like(s) + verb-ing. For the negative, add do not / does not: I do not like sitting in long meetings. For questions: Do you like working here? Does she like helping new colleagues? In British English, like + verb-ing is the most common pattern for talking about activities you enjoy.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) note that like + verb-ing emphasises the enjoyment of the activity itself. This makes it perfect for engagement surveys and conversations about well-being at work. When HR asks 'Do you like working at Czarnikow?', they want to know about your daily experience — and like + verb-ing is the natural way to answer.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 56 on verb + -ing (like, enjoy, love + doing).
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 53 (like doing) and Unit 54 (like doing vs would like to do).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on 'like' + verb patterns with usage notes on -ing vs to-infinitive.

commonMistakes.wrong: I like work with my team.
commonMistakes.right: I like working with my team.
commonMistakes.why: After 'like', use the -ing form of the verb: like working, like helping, like solving.

commonMistakes.wrong: She likes help new people.
commonMistakes.right: She likes helping new people.
commonMistakes.why: With he/she/it, use 'likes' + verb-ing: likes helping.

commonMistakes.wrong: I am like working here.
commonMistakes.right: I like working here.
commonMistakes.why: 'Like' is a normal verb here, not continuous. Do not add 'am'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Do you like to working here?
commonMistakes.right: Do you like working here?
commonMistakes.why: After 'like', use either verb-ing or to + base verb — never 'to + verb-ing'.

commonMistakes.wrong: He doesn't likes playing football.
commonMistakes.right: He doesn't like playing football.
commonMistakes.why: After 'doesn't', the verb returns to base form: doesn't like.

rolePlays.title: Engagement Survey Discussion
rolePlays.setup: Emily (HR) is sharing the results of an engagement survey with a team leader. The results show the team is mostly happy but some people feel disconnected.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Emily. Share two positive results and one area of concern. Ask what the team leader thinks.

sampleDialogue: A: Hi. I have the engagement survey results. The good news is that 85% of your team likes working here.
B: That's great to hear!
A: Also, most people enjoy working with their colleagues. But 20% feel disconnected from the company's goals.
B: I see. My team likes having our Friday coffee chats. Maybe we can also do a monthly session about company news?
A: That's a great idea. People like feeling connected to the bigger picture.

qAndA.question: What is employee engagement?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Engagement is how connected people feel to their work. Engaged employees like their job, their team, and feel proud of the company.

qAndA.question: Why does HR send engagement surveys?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: To understand how people feel at work. The answers help the company improve well-being and team spirit.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'I like working here' and 'I would like to work abroad'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'I like working here' means I enjoy my current experience. 'I would like to work abroad' expresses a wish or desire for the future.

qAndA.sampleAnswer: The manager can have a one-to-one conversation, listen to what the person needs, and involve them more in team activities and decisions.

lessons.title: Company Culture and Values
lessons.objective: Learn how to describe a company's culture and its main values in simple words.
lessons.intro:
Culture is the way things are done in a company.

Every company has its own culture: how people talk, how they dress, how they work together. Culture is also about values — the ideas that are important for everyone.

At Czarnikow, trust, respect and long-term relationships are important values. They are part of who we are.

grammarDeepDive.title: Have / Has Got
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When we describe a company, its culture and its people, we often need to say what they have: values, traditions, experience, offices. The structure have got / has got is a natural and very common way to do this in British English. Sophie can say 'Czarnikow has got a long tradition in commodities' or 'We have got a strong culture of trust'.

The forms are: I/you/we/they + have got and he/she/it + has got. For negatives: haven't got / hasn't got. For questions: Have you got...? Has the company got...? Note that have got means the same as have (without 'got'), but have got is more common in spoken British English.

Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) explains that have got is used for possession, characteristics and relationships — exactly the things we describe when talking about company culture. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) adds that have got is present tense only — for past tense, we use had (without 'got'). At Czarnikow, this structure helps you describe the company's identity clearly and confidently.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 30 on 'have' and 'have got' for possession and characteristics.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 9 ('have got' and 'have') with usage notes on British vs American English.
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on 'have got' with examples of possession, relationships and characteristics.

lessons.title: Diversity, Equity and Inclusion
lessons.objective: Learn the basic language of diversity and inclusion in a simple and respectful way.
lessons.intro:
Diversity means people are different.

In a good company, everyone is welcome — women and men, young and older people, people from many countries and many backgrounds.

Inclusion means everyone has a place. Nobody feels alone. Everyone can speak, and everyone is heard. This is called DEI: diversity, equity and inclusion.

grammarDeepDive.title: Everyone / Nobody + Singular Verbs
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When we talk about diversity and inclusion, we often use the words everyone and nobody. These are indefinite pronouns — they refer to all people or no people in a group. The important grammar rule is that both everyone and nobody take a singular verb: Everyone is welcome. Nobody feels left behind.

This can be confusing because everyone refers to many people, so students often want to say 'Everyone are welcome'. But in English, everyone is grammatically singular — just like every person. The same rule applies to everybody, someone, somebody, anyone, anybody, no one and nobody. They all take singular verbs.

Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) both explain that these indefinite pronouns follow the 'every = each one' logic. At Czarnikow, when Sophie leads a DEI workshop and says 'Everyone is welcome here' and 'Nobody is left behind', she is using powerful, inclusive language — and the grammar is simple once you remember the singular verb rule.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 85 on indefinite pronouns: everyone, someone, nobody + singular verbs.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 82 (someone, everybody, nobody etc.) and Unit 83 (every and all).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on 'everyone' and 'nobody' with grammar notes on singular verb agreement.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between diversity and inclusion?

qAndA.sampleAnswer: Equity means giving people what they need to succeed. It recognises that not everyone starts from the same place.

qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because 'everyone' means 'every single person' and 'nobody' means 'no single person' — they are grammatically singular in English.

qAndA.question: Why is diversity good for a global company like Czarnikow?

qAndA.question: What is the difference between having a DEI policy and truly living it?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A policy is written on paper. Living it means people actually behave inclusively every day — listening, respecting, including. It is about actions, not just words.

lessons.title: Talking to the Whole Company
lessons.objective: Learn how to describe how we communicate at work — emails, meetings and announcements.
lessons.intro:

It can be by email, by video, by meeting or by a simple message on the intranet. Good communication is clear, short and friendly.

grammarDeepDive.title: Prepositions of Communication — by, on, in
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In English, when we talk about how we communicate, we use small but important words called prepositions. The three most common are by, on and in. Each one tells us something different about the channel or place of the communication.

We use by when we talk about the method or channel: by email, by phone, by video, by chat. We use on when we talk about a platform or surface: on the intranet, on the website, on the phone (when we mean currently using the phone). We use in when we talk about being inside an event or space: in a meeting, in a call, in a conversation.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) explain that these prepositions are largely fixed phrases — they must be memorised as chunks rather than learned by a single rule. The Cambridge Dictionary confirms the standard collocations. A useful tip: think of by as the tool, on as the surface, and in as the container.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units on prepositions of means and instrument.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 125–128 on prepositions (at/on/in).
Cambridge Dictionary — entries for 'by email', 'on the phone', 'in a meeting'.

grammarDeepDive.title: Must / Must Not — Obligation and Prohibition
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Must is one of the most important modal verbs in business and HR English. We use it to express obligation — something that is necessary or required. When a company says 'we must follow the law', it means there is no choice: the law requires it.

Must not (or mustn't) expresses prohibition — something that is not allowed. 'You must not share personal data' means it is forbidden. This is very different from 'don't have to', which means something is optional. Compare: 'You must not smoke in the office' (forbidden) vs 'You don't have to wear a tie' (your choice).

Both Oxford Practice Grammar and Cambridge Grammar in Use explain that must is common in formal rules, policies and legal language — exactly the kind of language HR professionals need. The Cambridge Dictionary notes that 'must' often appears in company handbooks, compliance documents and workplace regulations. At Czarnikow, where the team operates across multiple countries, knowing how to express rules clearly with 'must' and 'must not' is essential.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 17 on must and mustn't for obligation and prohibition.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 31 (must) and Unit 32 (must vs have to).

qAndA.question: What are labour laws designed to protect?

qAndA.question: What does 'compliance' mean in the context of HR?

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'must not' and 'don't have to'?

qAndA.question: Why is it important for a global company like Czarnikow to understand labour laws in different countries?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because each country has different rules. If the company does not follow them, it can face fines, legal problems and damage to its reputation.

qAndA.question: What can happen if a manager does not follow the labour rules?

lessons.objective: Learn simple words to talk about salary, benefits and basic money questions at work.
lessons.intro:
Compensation is the money you receive for your work.

It has two main parts: the salary and the benefits. The salary is the money. The benefits can be health insurance, meal vouchers, a pension plan and more.

Every month, HR sends a pay slip. The pay slip shows how much you earn and the taxes. It is important to read and understand your pay slip.

grammarDeepDive.title: How Much / How Many — Asking About Quantity
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In English, when we ask about quantity, we must choose between how much and how many. The rule is clear: use how many with things you can count (countable nouns) and how much with things you cannot count (uncountable nouns) or with money.

In HR and compensation, this distinction is very practical. We say 'How many benefits do we offer?' because benefits are countable — you can say one benefit, two benefits, three benefits. We say 'How much does health insurance cost?' because cost is about money, which is uncountable in this context. The key test: if you can put a number before the noun (5 days, 3 benefits, 10 employees), use how many. If not (money, time, tax, salary), use how much.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) explain this as one of the fundamental quantifier rules in English. The Cambridge Dictionary provides additional examples in business contexts. Mastering this distinction helps HR professionals ask precise questions about compensation — something that happens daily at companies like Czarnikow.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 85 on how much and how many with countable and uncountable nouns.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 67 (countable/uncountable) and Unit 68 (how much/how many).
Cambridge Dictionary — entries for 'how much' and 'how many' with workplace examples.

qAndA.question: What are the two main parts of compensation?
qAndA.modelAnswer: The salary and the benefits. The salary is the money, and benefits can include things like health insurance, meal vouchers and a pension plan.

qAndA.question: What does a pay slip show?
qAndA.modelAnswer: A pay slip shows how much you earn (gross salary), the deductions (taxes, pension), and your net salary — the money you actually receive.

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'how much tax' but 'how many deductions'?

qAndA.question: Why is it important for employees to understand their pay slip?

qAndA.question: If you had to explain the difference between gross and net salary to a colleague, what would you say?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Gross salary is the total amount before any deductions. Net salary is what you actually receive after taxes, pension and other deductions are taken out.

lessons.title: Conflicts at Work: Keep Calm
lessons.objective: Learn how to describe small conflicts at work and how to calm them.
lessons.intro:
Sometimes people do not agree. This is normal.

A small conflict can happen in any team — maybe about a project, a deadline, or a simple message. The important thing is to stay calm and to listen to the other person.

HR can help when the conflict is bigger. But often, a simple conversation is enough. Calm words solve many problems.

grammarDeepDive.title: Let's / Why Don't We — Making Friendly Suggestions
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When there is a conflict or disagreement at work, the words we choose matter a lot. Two of the most useful structures for making friendly, collaborative suggestions are Let's and Why don't we. Both invite the other person to do something together — they are inclusive, not bossy.

Let's is short for 'let us' and is followed by the base form of the verb: Let's talk, Let's find a solution, Let's stay calm. Why don't we works the same way but sounds like a question: Why don't we take a break? Why don't we ask HR for help? Both forms are softer than saying 'You should...' or 'You must...', which can sound like orders — especially in a conflict.

Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) classifies 'let's' as a suggestion form, and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) groups it with other ways to propose actions. The Cambridge Dictionary notes that 'why don't we' is a common spoken form used in business to make polite proposals. At Czarnikow, where teamwork and respect are core values, using these soft suggestion forms helps maintain a positive atmosphere even when people disagree.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit on suggestions with let's, shall we, and why don't we.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 36 on suggestions (let's, shall we, why don't we).
Cambridge Dictionary — entries for 'let's' and 'why don't we' with spoken examples.

lessons.objective: Learn the language of remote and hybrid work in simple, everyday English.
lessons.intro:
Many people today do not work only in the office.

Some people work from home. Others go to the office a few days a week. This is called hybrid work: part home, part office.

To work from home, we need a good laptop, a good internet connection, and a quiet place. We also need to stay in touch with the team — by email, by chat and by video calls.

grammarDeepDive.title: Prepositions of Place — at, from, on (Home and Office)
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When we talk about where we work, English uses specific prepositions that must be memorised as fixed phrases. The three most important for hybrid work are at, from and on. Each one creates a different meaning.

We say work from home — 'from' tells us the starting point or location of the work. We say work at the office — 'at' tells us we are at that location. We use on for days and times: on Monday, on Friday morning. These are fixed collocations in English. You cannot say 'work in home' or 'work from the office' (this last one means leaving the office, which is the opposite!).

Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) covers prepositions of place in detail, and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) has dedicated units on at/in/on for location and time. The Cambridge Dictionary confirms that 'work from home' and 'work at the office' are the standard collocations. In today's hybrid world, especially at Czarnikow where employees split their week between home and the London office, getting these prepositions right is essential for daily communication.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units on prepositions of place (at, in, on) and prepositions with home/office.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 118–121 on at/in/on for place and Unit 116–117 for time.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries for 'work from home', 'at the office', 'on Monday'.

qAndA.question: What is hybrid work?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Hybrid work means working part of the week at the office and part from home. For example, three days at the office and two days from home.

qAndA.modelAnswer: You need a good laptop, a stable internet connection, a quiet place, and video call software to stay connected with your team.

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'work from home' and not 'work in home'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because 'from home' is a fixed expression in English that means the location where you do your work. 'In home' is not correct — we say 'at home' for general location, but 'from home' for working.

qAndA.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of hybrid work?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Advantages: flexibility, no commute on home days, better focus. Disadvantages: harder to connect with colleagues, need for good internet, and the risk of working too much without clear boundaries.

qAndA.question: How can a company make sure remote employees feel connected to the team?
qAndA.modelAnswer: By having regular video calls, using chat tools, organising team events, and making sure remote employees are included in all important meetings and decisions.

lessons.title: Aligning HR with Business Strategy
lessons.objective: Talk about how HR supports business goals, using natural business English at intermediate level.
lessons.intro:
HR has changed a lot over the last twenty years. It used to be mostly about contracts, payroll and paperwork. Today, HR is a real partner to the business.

Strategic HR means that every HR decision is connected to the company's goals. If the business is growing fast, HR focuses on recruitment. If the business wants to retain talent, HR looks at engagement and development.

A good HR leader can read the business plan and translate it into people priorities — the right hires, the right training, the right culture to make the strategy work.

grammarDeepDive.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The Present Perfect and the Past Simple are two of the most important tenses in business English, and one of the hardest pairs for Portuguese speakers. At Czarnikow, you use both every day — in emails, reports and meetings — so mastering the difference is essential for sounding natural and professional.

The Past Simple describes a finished action at a specific time in the past: We launched the programme last March. She joined the company in 2019. The key word is finished — the action is over, and we know when it happened. The Present Perfect connects a past action or experience to the present moment: We have reduced turnover by 30%. She has worked here for five years. The action started in the past but still matters now. As Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar puts it, the Present Perfect is about 'time up to now'.

The classic signal words help: yesterday, last week, in 2021, ago point to Past Simple; since, for, already, yet, ever, never, recently, so far point to Present Perfect. Murphy's English Grammar in Use recommends testing with the question 'Is the time finished or does it include now?' If it includes now, use the Present Perfect. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary adds that in formal business writing, the Present Perfect is often preferred for results and achievements because it emphasises relevance to the present.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 14: Present Perfect (1) — experiences; Unit 15: Present Perfect (2) — for and since.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 7–8: Present Perfect and Past Simple; Unit 12: for and since.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on Present Perfect vs Past Simple in business contexts.

rolePlays.title: HR Presents the Strategic Plan to the Board
rolePlays.setup: It is January at Czarnikow's London headquarters. Sophie, the HR director, is presenting the annual HR strategy to the executive committee. She needs to show what HR has achieved this year and what the business did last year to set the context.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Sophie. Present the HR results: what you have achieved so far (Present Perfect) and what happened at key moments last year (Past Simple). Cover recruitment, engagement and retention.

sampleDialogue: A: Good morning, everyone. I'd like to share what we have achieved this year and outline our plan for the next twelve months.
B: Thank you, Sophie. What are the headline numbers?
A: We have reduced voluntary turnover by 30% since January. Last quarter, we launched a new leadership programme that reached forty managers.

lessons.title: Designing an Organisational Structure
lessons.objective: Describe reporting lines, team structures and organisational change at intermediate level.
lessons.intro:
An organisational structure is the framework that shows how a company is built. It defines who reports to whom, how teams work together, and where decisions are made.

Some companies use a traditional hierarchy — clear levels, from the CEO down to the entry roles. Others prefer flatter models, with fewer layers and more autonomy in each team.

There is no perfect structure. The right model depends on the size of the company, the type of business and the culture it wants to build. HR is often asked to redesign the structure when the company grows or changes direction.

grammarDeepDive.title: Passive Voice — present
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The passive voice is one of the most important structures in business English. In reports, policies, organisational charts and process descriptions, the passive appears everywhere — because we often care more about what happens than who does it. At Czarnikow, you might read 'Decisions are made at regional level' or 'The structure is reviewed every two years'. Both are passive.

The structure is simple: subject + be (am/is/are) + past participle. The 'doer' can be added with by, but is often omitted when it is obvious or unimportant. For actions happening right now, we use the present continuous passive: is/are being + past participle — as in 'A new reporting line is being created'. Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar explains that we choose the passive when the action or result is more important than the agent.

Murphy's English Grammar in Use highlights that the passive is especially common in formal registers — exactly the tone used in HR documents, board papers and restructuring communications. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that overusing the passive can make writing feel impersonal, so good business writers mix active and passive depending on what they want to emphasise.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 22: The passive (1) — present simple passive.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 42: Passive (present); Unit 43: Passive (present continuous).
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on passive voice in formal and business English.

qAndA.question: What is an organisational structure?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: It is the framework that shows how a company is built — who reports to whom, how teams work together, and where decisions are made.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between a hierarchy and a flat structure?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A hierarchy has clear levels from CEO to entry roles. A flat structure has fewer layers and gives more autonomy to each team.

qAndA.question: Why is the passive voice so common in business English?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because in reports, policies and processes we often care more about what happens than who does it. The passive puts the focus on the action or the result.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say 'structure follows strategy'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because the organisational design should support the business goals. If you redesign the structure without a clear strategy, you may create confusion instead of efficiency.

qAndA.question: What risks does a company face during a restructuring?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: People may feel insecure, productivity may drop, and good employees may leave. Clear communication and a fair process help reduce these risks.

lessons.title: Reading HR Metrics and KPIs
lessons.objective: Discuss HR data, trends and KPIs with confidence at intermediate level.
lessons.intro:
Good HR teams rely on data. Every month, they look at a dashboard with the main people metrics and decide what to do next.

Typical HR KPIs include voluntary turnover, time to hire, cost per hire, employee engagement score and internal promotion rate. Each number tells part of the story, and together they give a clearer picture of how the company treats its people.

The hardest part is not producing the numbers — it is explaining them. A good HR business partner knows how to turn a spreadsheet into a conversation with the leadership team.

grammarDeepDive.title: Comparatives and superlatives
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In business, almost everything is about comparison: this quarter versus last quarter, our costs versus the industry average, one team's performance versus another's. That is why comparatives and superlatives are essential tools in every HR professional's language toolkit. At Czarnikow, when Harry presents the dashboard, nearly every sentence uses a comparative or a superlative to tell the story behind the numbers.

The rules are straightforward. For short adjectives (one syllable), add -er for the comparative and -est for the superlative: low → lower → the lowest. For longer adjectives (three or more syllables), use more/most: important → more important → the most important. Two-syllable adjectives vary — some take -er/-est (e.g. simple → simpler), others take more/most (e.g. complex → more complex). Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar recommends checking a dictionary when in doubt. The key irregulars are good → better → best, bad → worse → worst, far → further → furthest.

Murphy's English Grammar in Use stresses that we use than after comparatives ('Turnover is lower than last year') and the before superlatives ('This is the highest score'). The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary adds useful patterns for business: significantly/slightly/considerably + comparative to show the size of the difference — 'Time to hire is significantly longer this quarter.' These adverbs of degree make your data commentary sound precise and professional.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 44: Comparison (1) — -er/-est and more/most; Unit 45: Comparison (2) — irregular forms.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 105–108: Comparatives and superlatives; as...as.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on comparative structures in formal and business English.

rolePlays.title: Presenting the Quarterly HR Dashboard
rolePlays.setup: It is the end of Q3 at Czarnikow. Harry is presenting the HR dashboard to the leadership team. Turnover is down, engagement is up, but time to hire is longer than ever. The CFO wants to understand the cost implications.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Harry. Present the dashboard using comparatives and superlatives: what is better, what is worse, what is the best and worst result. Explain the trends clearly.

sampleDialogue: A: Good afternoon. Let me walk you through the Q3 HR dashboard. Voluntary turnover is lower than last quarter — down to eight per cent, the lowest this year.
B: That's encouraging. But is the cost per hire getting more expensive?
A: Slightly. It's about twelve per cent higher than last year, mainly because we are using more headhunters for senior roles.
B: Which team has the worst time-to-hire?

lessons.title: Running a Fair Performance Review
lessons.objective: Lead a professional performance review and use reported speech to summarise what was said.
lessons.intro:
Performance reviews can be stressful — but they do not have to be. A good review is not a surprise. It is the natural conclusion of small conversations that happen during the year.

In the meeting, the manager shares honest feedback: what went well, what needs to improve, and what goals come next. The employee also speaks — about challenges, support needed, and career aspirations.

The real value comes later. HR often collects the main points and follows up: what was agreed, what will be measured, and when to check progress again.

Czarnikow aims to follow up across every market we serve.

grammarDeepDive.title: Reported speech
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In business, we constantly report what others have said — in emails, meeting notes, review summaries and feedback forms. At Czarnikow, after a performance review, Sophie writes notes like 'He said he was happy with his results' or 'She told me she would apply for the senior role next year'. This is reported speech, and it is essential for professional communication.

The main rule is the tense shift: when we report past conversations, we usually move the tense back one step. 'I am proud' becomes 'She said she was proud'. 'I will apply' becomes 'He said he would apply'. 'I can do it' becomes 'She said she could do it'. Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar provides a complete tense-shift table that students should memorise. However, if the statement is still true, some speakers keep the original tense: 'She said the project is going well' — though the shifted version is always acceptable.

Murphy's English Grammar in Use also covers reporting questions: 'Are you happy?' becomes 'She asked if I was happy' — note the change from question to statement word order. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary adds that in formal business writing, reported speech is preferred over direct quotes, because it sounds more professional and allows the writer to summarise efficiently.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 35: Reported speech (1) — tense changes; Unit 36: Reported speech (2) — reporting questions.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 47–48: Reported speech; Unit 49: Reported questions.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on reported speech in business and formal writing.

commonMistakes.why: In reported speech, 'is' shifts to 'was' when reporting a past conversation.

commonMistakes.why: 'Told' needs a person after it ('told me/him/the team'). 'Said' does not.

commonMistakes.wrong: He said me he was proud.
commonMistakes.right: He told me he was proud. / He said he was proud.
commonMistakes.why: 'Said' does not take an indirect object. Use 'told + person' or 'said' alone.

commonMistakes.right: She asked if I had finished the project.
commonMistakes.why: Reported questions use statement word order (not question order) and 'if/whether'.

commonMistakes.right: They said they would improve next quarter.
commonMistakes.why: 'Will' shifts to 'would' in reported speech.

rolePlays.setup: Sophie is conducting a mid-year performance review with a senior analyst at Czarnikow. The analyst has exceeded targets in client work but needs to improve internal collaboration. After the meeting, both must summarise what the other said.

qAndA.question: What makes a good performance review, according to the lesson?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A good review is not a surprise. It is honest, specific and constructive. Both the manager and the employee speak, and they agree on clear next steps.

qAndA.question: What does HR do after the performance review meeting?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: HR collects the main points and follows up: what was agreed, what will be measured, and when to check progress again.

qAndA.question: What is the tense-shift rule in reported speech?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: When reporting a past conversation, we shift the tense back: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, have → had.

qAndA.question: Why is it important to acknowledge positive results before giving critical feedback?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because it builds trust and shows the employee that their work is valued. They are then more open to hearing areas for improvement.

qAndA.question: What happens if there is no follow-up after a performance review?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: The agreements are forgotten, the employee feels the meeting was pointless, and the same issues come up again in the next review. Follow-up turns words into action.

lessons.title: Running a Professional Recruitment Process
lessons.objective: Describe a recruitment process step by step and give advice on best practices.
lessons.intro:
Recruitment is more than posting a job and reading CVs. It is a structured process — and every step affects the final result.

It usually starts with a clear job description. Then comes sourcing: where will we look for candidates? LinkedIn, referrals, headhunters, internal mobility. Next, the screening — a short call to check the basics. After that, one or two rounds of interviews, perhaps a technical test, and finally the offer.

A professional recruiter keeps the candidate informed at every stage. Even a rejected candidate should leave the process with respect for the company — because today they are candidates, and tomorrow they might be clients, partners or brand ambassadors.

grammarDeepDive.title: Modals of advice and obligation
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In recruitment — and in business generally — we constantly give advice, make recommendations and state obligations. The language of modals is what makes the difference between 'You check references' (flat statement) and 'You should always check references before the offer' (clear professional advice). At Czarnikow, Oliver uses modals every day when training new recruiters and advising hiring managers.

Should is for strong advice or best practice: 'You should send feedback within 48 hours.' Could and might are for softer suggestions: 'You could consider an internal candidate first.' Must and have to express obligation: 'Every offer must be approved by the business owner.' Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar clarifies the key difference: must often reflects the speaker's authority ('I say it is necessary'), while have to reflects external rules ('the policy says so'). In practice, they are often interchangeable in business English.

Murphy's English Grammar in Use adds that the negative forms differ importantly: mustn't means 'it is forbidden' ('You mustn't share the candidate's data'), while don't have to means 'it is not necessary' ('You don't have to use a headhunter'). The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that in professional contexts, should is the most common modal because it balances authority with politeness — perfect for training, coaching and HR communication.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 30: Should; Unit 31: Must and have to; Unit 32: Can, could, may and might.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 31–33: Should; must/have to; mustn't vs don't have to.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on modal verbs in professional and advisory contexts.

rolePlays.setup: Oliver is training a new recruiter at Czarnikow. The new recruiter has just joined and needs to understand the company's recruitment process, from briefing to offer. Oliver walks them through each step, giving advice and explaining the rules.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Oliver. Walk the new recruiter through the process step by step. Use 'should' for advice, 'must/have to' for rules, and 'could/might' for suggestions. Cover: job description, sourcing, screening, interviews and offer.

sampleDialogue: A: Welcome to the team. Let me walk you through our recruitment process. The first thing you must do is get the job description approved by the hiring manager.
B: Should I use a specific template for the job description?
A: Yes, you should use the Czarnikow template — it is on the intranet. You could also look at similar roles for inspiration.
B: Do I have to post the role externally, or could I try internal candidates first?

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'must' and 'should' in business English?

lessons.title: Behavioural and Competency-Based Interviews
lessons.objective: Ask and answer behavioural interview questions using the STAR method.
lessons.intro:
The most reliable way to predict future behaviour is to look at past behaviour. That is the idea behind behavioural interviews.

Instead of asking "Are you a team player?", a good interviewer asks "Tell me about a time when your team disagreed on a decision. What did you do?" The candidate cannot give a theoretical answer — they have to tell a real story.

A useful framework is STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. It helps candidates structure their answers and interviewers compare them fairly. Done well, behavioural interviews are the fairest way to hire, because everyone is assessed on the same competencies.

grammarDeepDive.title: Past Simple vs Past Continuous
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In behavioural interviews, you need to tell stories about the past. That means you need two tenses working together: the Past Simple for completed, finished actions (I called the client, She accepted the offer) and the Past Continuous for longer background actions that were in progress when something else happened (While the team was finalising the proposal, the deadline moved forward). Together, they create a vivid narrative — one thing was happening (continuous) and then another thing interrupted or happened at the same time (simple).

The Past Simple is formed with the verb's past form: regular verbs add -ed (worked, called, assessed), while irregular verbs have unique forms (went, took, gave). The Past Continuous is formed with was/were + verb + -ing (was working, were interviewing). In STAR answers, the Situation and background often use Past Continuous, while the Action and Result use Past Simple. As Eastwood explains in Oxford Practice Grammar, the continuous tense 'sets the scene' for the story, while Murphy's English Grammar in Use emphasises that the simple tense 'moves the story forward'.

A common pattern in professional storytelling is: While I was [doing X], [Y happened]. For example: While I was managing the recruitment process, the hiring manager changed the requirements. Notice that the longer action (managing) uses Past Continuous and the shorter, interrupting action (changed) uses Past Simple. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that this pattern is essential for clear, professional narration in meetings, interviews and presentations.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 10: Past Continuous; Unit 9: Past Simple — regular and irregular verbs.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 6 (Past Continuous) and Unit 5 (Past Simple) with contrast exercises.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on Past Simple vs Past Continuous in narrative contexts.

rolePlays.setup: It is Thursday afternoon at Czarnikow's London office. Oliver, the HR Business Partner, is interviewing a candidate for a Senior Commercial Analyst role. The interview focuses on the competency 'negotiation under pressure'. Oliver uses STAR questions.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Oliver (interviewer). Ask at least three STAR questions about negotiation. Probe for specifics: What exactly did you do? What was the measurable result? Use Past Simple for your questions.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the candidate. Answer using full STAR stories from your career. Use Past Continuous for background and Past Simple for actions and results.
sampleDialogue: A: Good afternoon. Thank you for coming in. I'd like to start with a specific example. Tell me about a time when you had to negotiate under real pressure.
B: Certainly. While I was managing a contract renewal with a key supplier, the market price suddenly dropped by 12 per cent.
A: What was your specific task in that situation?
B: I was responsible for securing better terms without damaging the relationship. I called the supplier, presented the new market data, and proposed a phased price adjustment.
A: And what was the outcome?
B: We agreed on a 9 per cent reduction over six months. The supplier stayed on board and we saved the company roughly £180,000.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Interviewer asks at least 3 STAR questions with probes. Candidate delivers at least 2 full STAR answers mixing Past Simple and Past Continuous.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run it once with the student as interviewer; swap and run again as candidate. Focus on tense accuracy in the stories. After each round, highlight one well-formed sentence and correct one tense error.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Oliver explains the STAR method to a new interviewer
additionalAudios.speaker: oliver
additionalAudios.transcript: Right, so when you're conducting a behavioural interview, you need a framework. We use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Let me give you an example. Last month, I was interviewing a candidate for the trading desk. I asked: 'Tell me about a time when a deal went wrong.' While she was explaining the situation, I noticed she skipped the action completely. She jumped from the problem to the result. So I probed: 'What exactly did you do?' That's when the real story came out. She called the counterparty, renegotiated the terms, and saved the contract. Without the probe, I would have missed that entirely.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — A candidate gives a STAR answer about teamwork
additionalAudios.speaker: emily
additionalAudios.transcript: Sure, I can give you a specific example. While I was working at Czarnikow's São Paulo office, the team was struggling with a tight deadline on a compliance project. My task was to coordinate three departments. I organised daily stand-ups, created a shared tracker, and escalated blockers to senior management. The result was that we delivered two days early and the audit passed with zero findings. I learned that clear communication under pressure makes all the difference.

qAndA.question: What is the main idea behind behavioural interviews?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: The idea is that past behaviour predicts future behaviour. Instead of asking theoretical questions, interviewers ask for real examples of what the candidate did.

qAndA.question: What does STAR stand for and why is it useful?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result. It helps candidates structure their answers and allows interviewers to compare answers fairly.

qAndA.question: When do we use Past Simple and when Past Continuous in a STAR answer?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: We use Past Continuous for the background or ongoing situation (While I was managing...) and Past Simple for the specific completed actions and results (I called the client, we saved £180,000).

qAndA.question: Why are structured interviews considered fairer than unstructured ones?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because every candidate is assessed on the same competencies with the same questions. This reduces bias, since the interviewer cannot just go with a 'gut feeling'.

qAndA.question: What should an interviewer do when a candidate gives a vague or theoretical answer?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: The interviewer should probe further by asking 'What exactly did you do?' or 'Can you give me a specific example?' to get below the surface and assess the real competency.

lessons.title: Building a Strong Employer Brand
lessons.objective: Talk about employer branding campaigns, reputation and how companies attract talent.
lessons.intro:
Employer branding has been one of the biggest shifts in HR over the last decade. In the past, companies only cared about how they looked to customers. Today, the way you look to candidates is just as important.

A strong employer brand is not a marketing trick. It is a truthful story about what it is really like to work at the company — supported by the experiences of current employees on platforms like Glassdoor, LinkedIn and social media.

Companies have been investing heavily in employee stories, career pages, and transparent communication about culture and values. When reality matches the story, the brand grows. When it doesn't, candidates quickly notice.

commonChallenges: Students confuse Present Perfect Simple (have done) with Present Perfect Continuous (have been doing). Clarify: Continuous emphasises the duration and ongoing nature; Simple emphasises the result or completion.

Brazilian students often avoid the continuous form entirely because Portuguese does not have a direct equivalent. Encourage them to think of 'tem estado fazendo' or 'vem fazendo' as rough equivalents.
Some students struggle with when to use 'for' vs 'since'. Reinforce: 'for' + duration (for six months), 'since' + point in time (since January).
