rolePlays.title: Board Presentation — Defending the People Strategy
rolePlays.setup: Sophie is presenting Czarnikow's multi-year people strategy to the main board. The CFO is openly sceptical about the ROI of leadership investments. The CEO is supportive but expects hard evidence.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Sophie. Present three strategic HR priorities using inversion for emphasis. Defend each with evidence. Anticipate the CFO's objections.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the CFO. Challenge every claim with 'Where is the evidence?' and 'What is the ROI?'. Use formal, probing language.
sampleDialogue: A: Good afternoon. Rarely has the people agenda been more central to our commercial success.
B: Rarely, you say. Can you quantify that centrality?
A: I can. Not only have we reduced attrition by 14 percent — we have saved £2.3 million in replacement costs.
B: That is retention. What about leadership capability?
A: Only by investing in senior talent development can we build the pipeline the board has asked for.
B: And the return on that investment?
A: We project a 3:1 return over three years. The data is in appendix four.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three inverted structures naturally. Student B asks at least three probing questions. Both maintain board-level register throughout.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run once, then swap roles. After each round give one positive observation and one refinement. Focus on whether inversion sounds natural, not forced.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Sophie addresses the board on strategic HR

Only by partnering with finance have we been able to isolate the true cost of attrition, which last year exceeded two million pounds. Never before have we had this level of analytical rigour. The evidence is clear: strategic HR is not a cost centre. It is, without question, a source of competitive advantage.

I respect the ambition, but rarely have I approved an investment without a rigorous counterfactual. Show me the evidence, and I will be your strongest advocate.

qAndA.question: What three things do the best HR leaders do relentlessly, according to the lesson?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: They connect the talent agenda to concrete business outcomes, make bold trade-offs about where to invest, and build coalitions with finance, strategy and operations.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say the HR function has 'rarely been under more scrutiny'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because HR directors now have to demonstrate, with evidence, how the people agenda moves commercial, operational and financial outcomes — rhetoric alone is no longer enough.

qAndA.question: When and why do we use inversion in formal English?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: We use inversion after negative or restrictive adverbs (Rarely, Never, Not only, Only by) to add emphasis and rhetorical weight. It is mainly used in formal writing and speeches.

qAndA.question: Is it possible for HR to be truly strategic without strong analytical capability? Why or why not?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: It is very difficult, because without analytical rigour HR cannot isolate the impact of its interventions or speak the language of the business with credibility.

qAndA.question: What risks does an HR leader face when making 'bold, sometimes unpopular' trade-offs?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: They risk losing political support, alienating parts of the organisation, and being held accountable if the trade-off does not deliver. However, avoiding bold decisions may be even riskier in the long term.

contextualization: Think about Czarnikow's HR function. In your view, is it seen as a strategic partner by the business? Why or why not?
Describe one bold trade-off that HR at Czarnikow could make this year. Use at least one inverted sentence.
How does your own team demonstrate the impact of people initiatives? What evidence do you use?
If you were presenting to Czarnikow's board, what would be your opening sentence? Try using inversion.

productionTasks.task: Present to your teacher, in 90 seconds, boardroom speech positioning HR as a strategic partner at Czarnikow. Include at least four inverted sentences. Reference at least two pieces of evidence or data. Maintain a formal, executive register throughout.
productionTasks.successCriteria: Your presentation contains at least four correct inverted structures. The student speaks for at least 75 seconds without breaking register. At least two evidence-based arguments are presented.

pairWork.title: Board Challenge — HR vs Finance
pairWork.instructions: One student is the HR director presenting strategic priorities using inversion for emphasis. The other is the CFO, challenging every claim and asking for evidence. After 4 minutes, swap roles. At the end, each student shares the strongest argument the other made.

lessons.title: Designing Adaptive Organisational Structures
lessons.objective: Discuss complex organisational design trade-offs using precise, senior-level business language.
lessons.intro:
Organisational design is one of the most underestimated disciplines in modern management. Most companies overhaul their structure every few years, rarely acknowledging that a new org chart alone changes very little. Structure is only one lever among several: authority, information flows, accountability, incentives and culture must all move together, or not at all.

Adaptive structures aim to balance two opposing pressures. On one side, the need for integration — alignment, scale, shared systems. On the other, the need for local responsiveness — speed, context, empowerment. Managed well, this tension is productive; managed poorly, it produces matrices where nothing gets decided.

The best structural decisions are made with a clear hypothesis about what the company must get radically better at in the next three to five years. Structure follows that hypothesis — not the other way around. Designing for yesterday's challenges is how companies end up reorganising every eighteen months, exhausting their leaders and losing institutional memory in the process.

vocab.example: Czarnikow values a strong org design in the HR team at Czarnikow.

lessons.situation: James is advising a business unit undergoing its third reorganisation in four years. He pushes the leadership to articulate what they must be radically better at.
lessons.grammarDetail: Participle clauses. Reduce subordinate clauses to sound more concise and formal: Having reviewed three previous reorganisations, the team concluded structure was never the real issue. Faced with mounting complexity, leaders must resist the temptation of yet another redesign.

exercises.title: 1. Read aloud
exercises.instruction: Practise these design phrases:
sentences: Having reviewed three previous reorganisations, we concluded structure was never the real constraint.
Faced with a matrix of shared accountabilities, decisions were quietly escalated upwards.
Designed for yesterday's model, the structure is already eroding responsiveness.

exercises.title: 2. Pratique: Participle clauses — reducing subordinate clauses
exercises.instruction: Complete cada lacuna e clique em “Corrigir”. A dica entre parênteses é a forma base.

___ (face) with a matrix that slowed decisions, the team proposed a flatter design.

exercises.title: 4. Reading comprehension
exercises.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
exercises.passage:
Organisational design is one of the most underestimated disciplines in modern management. Most companies overhaul their structure every few years, rarely acknowledging that a new org chart alone changes very little. Structure is only one lever among several: authority, information flows, accountability, incentives and culture must all move together, or not at all.

Adaptive structures aim to balance two opposing pressures. On one side, the need for integration — alignment, scale, shared systems. On the other, the need for local responsiveness — speed, context, empowerment. Managed well, this tension is productive; managed poorly, it produces matrices where nothing gets decided.

The best structural decisions are made with a clear hypothesis about what the company must get radically better at in the next three to five years. Structure follows that hypothesis — not the other way around. Designing for yesterday's challenges is how companies end up reorganising every eighteen months, exhausting their leaders and losing institutional memory in the process.

items.q: According to the text, what does a new org chart achieve on its own?
items.why: "a new org chart alone changes very little" — o gráfico sozinho é apenas um dos vários fatores.

items.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a lever that must move together with structure?
items.why: O texto lista authority, information flows, accountability, incentives e culture. "Remuneration bands" não aparece.

items.q: Which two pressures must an adaptive structure balance?
items.why: "balance two opposing pressures… integration… local responsiveness".

items.q: What is the consequence of managing that tension poorly?
options: Matrices in which nothing gets decided
items.why: "managed poorly, it produces matrices where nothing gets decided".

items.q: According to the text, structure should follow…
options: the preferences of the leadership team
a clear hypothesis about what the company must get better at
items.why: "Structure follows that hypothesis — not the other way around."

items.q: What two costs does the text attach to reorganising every eighteen months?
options: Exhausted leaders and lost institutional memory
items.why: "exhausting their leaders and losing institutional memory in the process".

items.q: Calling org design "underestimated" implies that managers…
options: treat it as less consequential than it really is
spend too much money on consultants
understand it better than they admit
items.why: Inferência: "underestimated" = subestimado — dão a ela menos peso do que ela merece.

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: Structure should be designed backwards from strategy.
Redrawing the org chart is the fastest way to change behaviour.
Frequent restructuring carries a hidden cost.
Empowerment and alignment pull in different directions.
items.why: Inferência: o texto inteiro é um argumento contra a ideia de que o organograma, sozinho, muda comportamento.

items.q: A leadership team is about to start a reorganisation. What would the author advise first?
options: Benchmark the structure against three competitors
Reduce the number of management layers
Articulate what the company must be radically better at
items.why: Inferência: a hipótese vem primeiro, e só então a estrutura segue.

items.q: What does "or not at all" at the end of the first paragraph suggest?
options: Some levers matter more than others
Moving only part of the system is worse than moving nothing
Culture is the only lever that counts
items.why: Inferência: os fatores movem-se juntos — mexer só em alguns é meia-mudança, que não entrega o resultado.

exercises.title: 5. Listening comprehension
exercises.instruction: Ouça James aconselhando a liderança da unidade. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right — before we look at any boxes and lines, I want the leadership to answer one question: what must this business be radically better at in three years' time? Not what is broken today. Three years.

This is the third reorganisation in four years, and every one of them started with a chart. Having watched two of them from the outside, I would say the pattern is fairly clear. Authority was redrawn, but incentives were never touched, and the information the regional teams needed still sat in London. So decisions kept drifting upwards.

If we go again without agreeing the hypothesis first, we will simply reshuffle the same constraint. My recommendation is that we hold off on the structure for a fortnight. Spend that time writing down the two or three capabilities that will decide whether we win — then design backwards from those.

And whatever we land on, we live with it for five years. Every reorganisation costs you institutional memory, and this business has spent a great deal of it already.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What does James want the leadership to answer BEFORE looking at the structure?
options: What is broken in the business today
What the business must be radically better at in three years
How many layers the structure should have
items.why: "what must this business be radically better at in three years' time? Not what is broken today."

items.q: How many reorganisations has this unit been through?
items.why: "This is the third reorganisation in four years."

items.q: According to James, what was changed in the past reorganisations — and what was not?
options: Incentives were changed; authority was not
Authority was redrawn; incentives were never touched
Culture was changed; systems were not
Headcount was cut; authority was not
items.why: "Authority was redrawn, but incentives were never touched."

items.q: Why did decisions keep drifting upwards?
options: The regional teams lacked the information they needed
The matrix had too many layers
items.why: "the information the regional teams needed still sat in London. So decisions kept drifting upwards."

items.q: What does James recommend they do for a fortnight?
options: Pause the structure and write down the deciding capabilities
Run a pilot in one region
items.why: "hold off on the structure for a fortnight… writing down the two or three capabilities that will decide whether we win".

items.q: How long does James want the new structure to last?
items.why: "whatever we land on, we live with it for five years."

items.q: What cost does James attach to repeated reorganisation?
items.why: "Every reorganisation costs you institutional memory."

items.q: What does James mean by "we will simply reshuffle the same constraint"?
options: The new structure will hit the same limitation as the old one
The same people will be moved between roles
The reorganisation will take longer than planned
items.why: Inferência: sem tratar a causa (informação e incentivos), a nova estrutura reproduz o mesmo gargalo.

items.q: How would you best describe James's tone?
options: Constructive, but sceptical about repeating the pattern
items.why: Inferência: ele critica o padrão, mas propõe um caminho concreto — não descarta a liderança.

items.q: What would James consider a successful outcome of the fortnight?
options: A new org chart approved by the board
An agreed, written hypothesis before any boxes and lines
A decision to cancel the reorganisation
A list of roles to be made redundant
items.why: Inferência: ele quer a hipótese acordada e escrita primeiro; a estrutura é desenhada a partir dela.

exercises.title: 6. Vocabulary in context
exercises.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Structure is only one lever among several." A lever is…
options: a means of producing an effect
items.why: Lever = alavanca: aquilo em que você age para produzir um efeito.

items.q: "Her span of control widened from six to fourteen." This refers to…
options: the number of people reporting directly to her
the regions she is responsible for
items.why: Span of control = amplitude de controle: quantos reportam diretamente.

items.q: The board decided to overhaul the reporting lines. To overhaul means to…
items.why: To overhaul = reformular profundamente — não é um ajuste pequeno.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Empowerment without clear ___ creates confusion, not agility."
items.why: Accountability = responsabilização: quem responde pelo resultado.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "The ___ between London and São Paulo broke down, so the desk priced on stale data."
items.why: Information flow = fluxo de informação, o que falhou entre os dois escritórios.

items.q: In a matrix organisation, a manager typically…
options: reports to two lines at once
items.why: Matriz = dupla linha de reporte (funcional e de negócio).

items.q: Institutional memory is best described as…
options: what the organisation retains about why things were done
the length of service of the leadership team
items.why: É o conhecimento acumulado sobre as razões das decisões — o que se perde a cada reorganização.

items.q: Choose the correct verb: "We need to ___ the regional heads to sign off deals under two million."
items.why: To empower = empoderar, dar autoridade para decidir.

items.q: Which pair of benefits sits on the integration side of the trade-off?
items.why: Integração traz alinhamento, escala e sistemas compartilhados; velocidade e contexto ficam do lado da responsividade.

items.q: Org design covers…
options: the chart plus authority, information flows and incentives
items.why: É a tese central da lição: o organograma é só um dos elementos do desenho.

exercises.title: 7. Expressions & phrasal verbs
exercises.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em reuniões de reestruturação. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The CFO still has to sign off on the new structure." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "We will roll out the new model region by region." To roll out means to…
items.why: Roll out = implementar de forma progressiva.

items.q: "Two regional heads pushed back on the proposal." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "There are a few details to iron out before Friday." To iron out means to…
items.why: Iron out = aparar arestas, resolver pontos menores.

items.q: "He will hand over the desk in March." To hand over means to…
items.why: Hand over = passar a responsabilidade a outra pessoa.

items.q: "Given the margin pressure, we had to scale back the programme." To scale back means to…
items.why: Scale back = reduzir escopo ou tamanho.

items.q: "The team agreed the plan but never followed through." They…
options: failed to carry it to completion
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado.

items.q: "Give the new structure six months to bed in." To bed in means to…
items.why: Bed in (BrE) = assentar, começar a funcionar como esperado.

items.q: "The review was carried out by an external team." To carry out means to…
items.why: Carry out = executar, realizar.

items.q: "None of that will move the needle on decision speed." This means it will…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, fazer diferença perceptível.

lessons.wrapup: Structure is a promise about what the company must be great at next.
takeaways: Structure alone changes nothing.
Balance integration and local responsiveness.
Design for the next five years, not the last five.
An org chart is only one lever among several.
Authority, information flows and culture must move together.
Adaptive structures balance opposing pressures productively.
Designing for yesterday's challenges causes perpetual reorganisation.
Institutional memory is lost when restructuring is too frequent.
The best structural decisions follow a clear hypothesis.
Empowerment without accountability creates confusion, not agility.

teacherGuide.overview: Lesson 42 addresses adaptive organisational design at C1–C2 level. Grammar focus: participle clauses to reduce subordinate clauses. By the end, the student should discuss complex org-design trade-offs using concise, formal structures.

lessonFlow.instructions: Ask: Has your company ever gone through a reorganisation? What worked? What didn't? Let the student share freely.
Read the intro aloud. Work through the 10 vocab items. Student repeats each and creates a sentence linking it to Czarnikow's context.
Explain participle clauses (present, past, perfect). Walk through the 12 examples aloud. Do the 5 quickPractice items together. Review common mistakes, especially dangling participles.
Read the situation. Do Read Aloud and Reduce the Clause exercises. Play Audio A once without transcript, then with it. Check tasks.
Run the role play (James advising on a reorganisation). Swap roles after one round. Then discuss 3 Q&A questions orally, encouraging participle clauses.
Ask the 4 contextualisation prompts. Do the speaking production task. Close by reading the 10 takeaways aloud together.

commonChallenges: Dangling participles are the most common error (e.g. 'Having reviewed the data, the structure was changed' — who reviewed?). Drill: the subject of the participle must match the subject of the main clause.
Students may confuse present participles (active) with past participles (passive). Use clear pairs: 'Having reviewed' (we reviewed) vs 'Reviewed by the team' (the plan was reviewed).
Brazilian students sometimes avoid participle clauses entirely because they feel unnatural. Encourage practice by converting familiar sentences step by step.

items.q: Because they were given real authority, the regional teams responded quickly.

extraPractice.title: Error correction (editing) — ache e corrija o erro sutil
extraPractice.note: Um erro de C1/C2 por frase. Corrija e diga por quê.

items.q: Having reviewed the data, the redesign was abandoned by us.
items.a: Having reviewed the data, we abandoned the redesign. (sujeito da participial deve ser o agente: we, não 'the redesign')

items.q: Faced of mounting complexity, leaders hesitate.
items.a: Faced with mounting complexity, leaders hesitate. (a colocação correta é 'faced with')

items.q: Empowering to decide locally, teams moved faster.
items.a: Empowered to decide locally, teams moved faster. (sentido passivo exige particípio passado: empowered)

items.q: After overhauled twice, the structure still failed.
items.a: Having been overhauled twice, the structure still failed. (cláusula passiva perfeita: 'having been + particípio')

items.q: Recognising that span of control had widened, so we delayered.
items.a: Recognising that span of control had widened, we delayered. ('so' redundante após a participial inicial)

items.q: Stripping of its memory, the function underperformed.
items.a: Stripped of its memory, the function underperformed. (sentido passivo: stripped, não stripping)

items.q: How do you decide whether a structural change is genuinely warranted?
items.a: Having seen reorganisations repeatedly fail to fix behavioural problems, I now treat structure as a last resort rather than a first instinct.

items.q: What is the central tension in your current operating model?
items.a: Caught between the pull of global integration and the need for local responsiveness, we have deliberately favoured the latter.

items.q: Describe a redesign that did not deliver what was promised.
items.a: Overhauled twice in three years, the function gained little but lost considerable institutional memory in the process.

items.q: How do you protect accountability in a matrix structure?
items.a: Designed without explicit decision rights, a matrix invariably blurs accountability, so we now define them before the chart is drawn.

items.q: What did empowering your regional teams actually change?
items.a: Granted real decision rights, our regional heads moved with a speed the central model had never permitted.

items.q: If you could change one thing about how your firm is structured, what would it be?
items.a: Forced to choose a single lever, I would clarify accountability long before I touched a single reporting line.

grammarDeepDive.title: Participle Clauses — Reducing Subordinate Clauses
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Participle clauses are a hallmark of concise, formal English. They replace longer subordinate clauses introduced by because, when, after, although with a more economical structure built around a participle (-ing or -ed form). In executive writing at Czarnikow, you might write 'Having reviewed three previous reorganisations, we concluded that structure was never the real constraint' instead of 'Because we had reviewed three previous reorganisations, we concluded...'. The participle version is shorter, more elegant, and signals advanced command of the language.

There are three main types. Present participle clauses use the -ing form for simultaneous or causal actions: 'Facing mounting complexity, leaders must resist the temptation of yet another redesign.' Past participle clauses use the -ed/-en form for passive meaning: 'Designed for yesterday's model, the structure eroded responsiveness.' Perfect participle clauses use having + past participle for completed prior actions: 'Having consulted all stakeholders, the team proposed a new design.' Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar covers these in the unit on participle clauses; Murphy's English Grammar in Use addresses them in Unit 67; and the Cambridge Grammar of English describes them as characteristic of formal written registers.

The most important rule is that the implied subject of the participle clause must be the same as the subject of the main clause. A mismatch creates a dangling participle, which is both grammatically incorrect and often unintentionally comic: 'Having reviewed the data, the reorganisation was approved' implies the reorganisation reviewed the data. Correct: 'Having reviewed the data, the board approved the reorganisation.'
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Unit on participle clauses and reduced relative clauses.
English Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 67: -ing and -ed clauses.
Cambridge Grammar of English (Carter & McCarthy) — Section on non-finite clauses in formal written registers.

examples.en: Managed poorly, the tension between integration and responsiveness produces paralysis.
examples.pt: Mal gerida, a tensão entre integração e responsividade produz paralisia.

commonMistakes.wrong: Having reviewed the data, the reorganisation was approved.
commonMistakes.right: Having reviewed the data, the board approved the reorganisation.
commonMistakes.why: The subject of the participle clause must match the main clause subject. The reorganisation did not review the data.

commonMistakes.wrong: Facing with complexity, leaders retreated.
commonMistakes.right: Faced with complexity, leaders retreated.
commonMistakes.why: 'Faced with' (past participle, passive) is the correct collocation. 'Facing' works without 'with': 'Facing complexity, leaders retreated.'

commonMistakes.wrong: Designed for the future, we launched the new structure.
commonMistakes.right: Designed for the future, the new structure was launched.
commonMistakes.why: 'We' were not designed — the structure was. Match the participle to the correct subject.

commonMistakes.wrong: Having been overhauling the structure, the team felt exhausted.
commonMistakes.right: Having overhauled the structure, the team felt exhausted.
commonMistakes.why: Use the perfect participle (having + past participle) for a completed action, not the continuous form.

commonMistakes.wrong: Reorganised the department, results improved.
commonMistakes.right: Having reorganised the department, the team saw improved results.
commonMistakes.why: A participle clause needs a participle form (having reorganised), not a bare past tense.

rolePlays.title: Advising on Organisational Redesign
rolePlays.setup: James is meeting the leadership of a business unit at Czarnikow that has been reorganised three times in four years. Morale is low and institutional memory has been lost. James must convince them to start with a hypothesis, not a new org chart.
rolePlays.studentA: You are James. Push the leadership to articulate what the company must be radically better at. Use participle clauses to sound concise and authoritative.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the business unit leader. You are frustrated and want a quick restructuring. Push back on James's slower approach.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say organisational design is 'underestimated'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because most companies overhaul their structure every few years without acknowledging that a new org chart alone changes very little — authority, information flows, accountability, incentives and culture must all move together.

qAndA.question: What are the two opposing pressures that adaptive structures must balance?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Integration (alignment, scale, shared systems) on one side, and local responsiveness (speed, context, empowerment) on the other.

qAndA.question: What is a dangling participle, and why does it matter?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A dangling participle is when the implied subject of the participle clause does not match the subject of the main clause, creating ambiguity or unintended meaning. It matters because it undermines clarity and credibility in formal writing.

qAndA.question: Why is 'designing for yesterday's challenges' dangerous for an organisation?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because it leads to structures that solve old problems rather than building capability for the future, resulting in perpetual reorganisations that exhaust leaders and erode institutional memory.

qAndA.question: Should Czarnikow favour integration or local responsiveness in its current structure? Defend your view.
qAndA.sampleAnswer: There is no single answer — it depends on Czarnikow's strategic priorities. If speed and market responsiveness matter most, lean towards local empowerment; if scale and consistency are critical, lean towards integration. The best answer is a deliberate, evidence-based balance.

lessons.title: People Analytics and Evidence-Based HR
lessons.objective: Interpret complex HR data with academic and commercial precision, avoiding overclaim.
lessons.intro:
People analytics has matured from novelty into a legitimate discipline. A decade ago, HR functions produced descriptive dashboards — how many employees, how many leavers, how many hires. Today, leading teams run predictive models, conduct controlled experiments and partner with data scientists to test causal hypotheses.

With that maturity comes greater responsibility. Correlation is not causation, and even the most elegant model can mislead if the underlying data is biased or incomplete. A good people analyst is, above all, intellectually honest: willing to say "the evidence suggests, but does not prove", rather than dressing up opinion in the language of science.

The strategic value lies in the questions, not the tools. The right question — "Which managers retain talent significantly above the organisational average, and what do they actually do differently?" — often produces more insight than a twenty-tab dashboard that answers none of the questions that leaders truly care about.

items.q: How do you present an uncertain finding to executives who want a clear answer?
items.a: I tend to say that the data points in a particular direction while being explicit about the caveats, since overclaiming would only erode the credibility of the analysis.

items.q: When has a correlation in your data turned out to be misleading?

items.q: How do you guard against overclaiming in people analytics?
items.a: I make a discipline of stating only what the evidence supports, no more and no less, and of flagging confounders before anyone else can.

items.q: Why does intellectual honesty matter in HR reporting?
items.a: Because a single overstated claim that later collapses tends to discredit the entire function, whereas measured language compounds trust over time.

grammarDeepDive.title: Hedging and Cautious Language
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Hedging is the use of linguistic devices to express uncertainty, caution or tentativeness. In people analytics and evidence-based HR, it is not a weakness — it is a mark of intellectual honesty and analytical rigour. At Czarnikow, when Harry reviews a study claiming a new engagement programme increased productivity by 18 percent, he does not say 'The programme increased productivity' — he says 'The data suggests a meaningful relationship between the programme and productivity gains, though we should be cautious about claiming direct causation.' This precision distinguishes reliable analysis from opinion dressed in the language of science.

Common hedging devices include modal verbs (may, might, could, would), adverbs (possibly, apparently, seemingly, arguably), reporting verbs (suggests, indicates, implies, appears), phrases (it is plausible that, on balance, there is some evidence that, the data is consistent with), and qualifiers (to some extent, in certain contexts, under specific conditions). Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar treats hedging in the unit on modal verbs for possibility and probability; Murphy's English Grammar in Use covers it in units on may/might and appears to; and the Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary provides extensive usage notes on hedging markers in academic and professional contexts.

The key skill is calibrating the strength of the hedge to the strength of the evidence. Strong evidence warrants mild hedging ('The data strongly suggests...'); weak evidence demands more caution ('It is conceivable that...'). Overclaiming damages credibility; overhedging obscures the message. The best analysts master a middle register that is precise, honest and still actionable.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Unit on modal verbs: may, might, could for possibility and probability.
English Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Units on may/might, appears to, and reporting with caution.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on hedging language in academic and professional English.

commonMistakes.wrong: The programme proved that engagement increased.
commonMistakes.right: The data suggests that engagement may have increased following the programme.
commonMistakes.why: 'Proved' implies absolute certainty. In analytics, 'suggests' or 'indicates' is almost always more appropriate.

commonMistakes.wrong: Remote work causes higher productivity.
commonMistakes.right: There is some evidence that remote work is associated with higher productivity.
commonMistakes.why: 'Causes' implies proven causation. 'Is associated with' correctly signals correlation without overclaiming.

commonMistakes.wrong: The survey shows employees are happy.
commonMistakes.right: The survey results are consistent with an improvement in employee satisfaction.
commonMistakes.why: 'Shows' can be too strong. 'Are consistent with' acknowledges the data while leaving room for alternative interpretations.

commonMistakes.wrong: Obviously, the leadership programme works.
commonMistakes.right: On the available evidence, the leadership programme appears to have a positive effect.
commonMistakes.why: 'Obviously' dismisses the need for evidence. Hedging with 'appears to' maintains intellectual honesty.

commonMistakes.wrong: The data is clear: attrition fell because of the new policy.
commonMistakes.right: The data is suggestive: attrition fell during the period in which the new policy was implemented.
commonMistakes.why: Saying 'because of' assumes causation. Noting the temporal overlap ('during the period') is more rigorous.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'the data proves' and 'the data suggests'? When should you use each?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'Proves' implies absolute certainty and is rarely appropriate in analytics. 'Suggests' indicates the evidence points in a direction without claiming certainty. Use 'proves' only when evidence is overwhelming; use 'suggests' in most other cases.

qAndA.sampleAnswer: I would use a controlled experiment with a treatment group and a control group, measure productivity before and after the programme, control for confounding variables such as market conditions and team composition, and use a sufficient sample size to detect a meaningful effect.

lessons.title: Rethinking Performance Management
lessons.objective: Critically evaluate performance management systems at executive level.
lessons.intro:
Few HR practices have been as fiercely debated in the last decade as performance management. The traditional annual review — ratings, forced distributions, individual bonuses — has been criticised as demotivating, backward-looking and statistically unreliable. Several well-known companies have dismantled theirs, only to quietly reintroduce elements a few years later.

The underlying tension is honest. On one hand, organisations need differentiation: to reward contribution, make investment decisions and hold people accountable. On the other, most employees experience formal ratings as reductive and anxiety-inducing, particularly when tied to compensation.

The most thoughtful systems today are hybrid. They separate development conversations, which are frequent and genuinely forward-looking, from compensation decisions, which are deliberate and transparent but less central to daily life. They also invest heavily in manager capability, recognising that no system, however elegant, can compensate for a manager who avoids honest conversations.

grammarDeepDive.title: Complex Sentence Structures — Subordination
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Complex subordination is the backbone of executive-level argumentation. It allows a speaker or writer to express multiple ideas — conditions, concessions, contrasts, causes — within a single, elegant sentence. At Czarnikow, Sophie might write: 'Although the annual review has been widely criticised — with some justification — few organisations that have abandoned it entirely have found a superior alternative.' This sentence contains a concessive clause, a parenthetical aside, and a relative clause, yet it reads clearly because each subordinate element is precisely placed.

The main conjunctions for subordination are: although / even though (concession), whereas / while (contrast), provided that / on condition that (condition), given that / in view of the fact that (reason), and whether or not (alternative). Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar covers complex sentences in the units on clauses; Murphy's English Grammar in Use addresses subordination in Units 111–114; and the Cambridge Grammar of English discusses the role of subordination in creating cohesive, authoritative prose in professional contexts.

The skill lies in balance. Too many subordinate clauses in one sentence produce opacity; too few produce a staccato style that lacks nuance. The best executive writers aim for one or two subordinate elements per sentence, varying sentence length to maintain rhythm. The goal is not complexity for its own sake, but the precise expression of complex ideas.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Units on complex sentences and subordinate clauses.
English Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Units 111–114: although/in spite of, whereas/while, provided that.
Cambridge Grammar of English (Carter & McCarthy) — Section on subordination in professional and academic registers.

commonMistakes.wrong: Although the review was criticised. Few companies found an alternative.
commonMistakes.right: Although the review was criticised, few companies found an alternative.
commonMistakes.why: 'Although' introduces a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone. It must be joined to the main clause with a comma, not a full stop.

commonMistakes.wrong: The system works provided that the managers is capable.
commonMistakes.right: The system works provided that the managers are capable.
commonMistakes.why: Subject-verb agreement: 'managers' is plural and requires 'are', not 'is'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Whereas the board wants differentiation, but employees resist ratings.
commonMistakes.right: Whereas the board wants differentiation, employees resist ratings.
commonMistakes.why: 'Whereas' already signals contrast. Adding 'but' creates a double conjunction — remove one.

commonMistakes.wrong: Even though they dismantled the system, however, they reintroduced it later.
commonMistakes.right: Even though they dismantled the system, they reintroduced it later.
commonMistakes.why: 'Even though' and 'however' serve similar functions. Using both is redundant.

commonMistakes.wrong: Given that most employees experience ratings as reductive so organisations should change.
commonMistakes.right: Given that most employees experience ratings as reductive, organisations should consider changing their approach.
commonMistakes.why: 'Given that' introduces a subordinate clause. Use a comma before the main clause, not 'so'.

rolePlays.title: Redesigning Performance Management at Czarnikow
rolePlays.setup: Sophie is presenting a proposal to redesign Czarnikow's performance management system. The board demands differentiation; employees have pushed back strongly against ratings. Sophie must find a middle ground.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Sophie. Propose a hybrid system that separates development from compensation. Use complex subordination to present nuanced arguments.
rolePlays.studentB: You are a board member. You believe differentiation is essential and are wary of removing ratings. Challenge Sophie's proposal.
sampleDialogue: A: Although the current system has served us well in some respects, the evidence suggests that tying ratings directly to bonuses is undermining development conversations.
B: But without differentiation, how do we reward top performers?

A: Provided that we separate the development conversation from the compensation review, we can achieve both. Development discussions would be quarterly and genuinely forward-looking, whereas compensation calibration would happen annually.
B: What guarantees that managers will have honest conversations if there is no rating to anchor them?
A: Given that the quality of the conversation depends on the manager, not the form, we propose investing heavily in manager coaching.
B: Even though I see the logic, I am not convinced we can remove ratings entirely.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three complex subordinated sentences. Student B raises at least two substantive objections. Both maintain board-level register.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run once, swap roles. After each round, identify one well-constructed subordinated sentence and one opportunity for improvement.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Sophie proposes the hybrid system
additionalAudios.speaker: sophie
additionalAudios.transcript: Although the annual review has been a cornerstone of our performance management for over a decade, the evidence from our own data — and from the broader HR literature — suggests it is no longer fit for purpose in its current form. Whereas forced distributions were designed to ensure differentiation, what they have actually produced is anxiety and, in some cases, a reluctance to have honest conversations. What I am proposing is a hybrid: development conversations that are quarterly, genuine and forward-looking, combined with an annual compensation calibration that is transparent and evidence-based. Provided that we invest in manager capability, I believe this system can deliver both differentiation and development.
tasks: Listen once without reading. What is Sophie proposing? (Answer: a hybrid system separating development from compensation)
Listen again. How many subordinate clauses can you count? (Answer: at least 5)
What does Sophie identify as the main problem with forced distributions? (Answer: anxiety and reluctance to have honest conversations)
Repeat 'Provided that we invest in manager capability, I believe this system can deliver both differentiation and development' with confidence.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — A board member challenges the proposal
additionalAudios.speaker: james
additionalAudios.transcript: Sophie, even though I find your analysis compelling, I have a concern. Whether or not we retain a formal rating, the board needs a mechanism for differentiation. Given that compensation budgets are finite, we must make choices. In view of the fact that some managers already avoid difficult conversations, I am not confident that removing the rating anchor will improve things. Convince me that the coaching investment will be sufficient.

Repeat 'Given that compensation budgets are finite, we must make choices' with appropriate gravitas.

lessons.title: Talent Acquisition as Competitive Advantage
lessons.objective: Position talent acquisition strategically and debate trade-offs with executive stakeholders.
lessons.intro:
In industries where talent is scarce and highly mobile, the quality of talent acquisition is no longer a back-office concern — it is a genuine source of competitive advantage. Companies that consistently hire better than their competitors compound that advantage over years, sometimes decades.

What separates the best from the rest is not the sophistication of their tools, but the discipline of their choices. They invest in deep understanding of the roles that matter most. They build long-term relationships with candidates they are not yet ready to hire. They refuse to compromise on the few characteristics that predict success, while remaining genuinely open on those that do not.

The weakest acquisition functions behave reactively — filling vacancies as they appear, with little strategic view. The strongest build a proactive pipeline, often bringing in talent before there is an open role. The return on that investment is not always visible in quarterly KPIs, but it shows up unmistakably in the quality of leadership five years later.

grammarDeepDive.title: Nominalisation for Formal Register
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Nominalisation is the process of converting verbs (and sometimes adjectives) into nouns, creating a more formal, impersonal and authoritative register. In executive communication at Czarnikow, Oliver might write 'The identification of critical roles precedes the development of targeted pipelines' rather than 'We identify critical roles before we develop targeted pipelines.' The nominalised version is more detached, more strategic, and more typical of board papers, strategy documents and formal proposals.

Common nominalisation patterns include: identify → identification, assess → assessment, develop → development, acquire → acquisition, invest → investment, recognise → recognition, evaluate → evaluation, approve → approval, prioritise → prioritisation, implement → implementation. Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar covers nominalisation in the unit on formal style and word formation; Murphy's English Grammar in Use addresses it in the context of formal writing patterns; and the Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary provides extensive guidance on nominal forms and their register implications.

The key is balance. Overuse of nominalisation produces 'zombie prose' — dense, impersonal text where the actors and actions disappear behind abstract nouns. The best executive writers use nominalisation strategically: to foreground a concept, to create a formal tone for a specific purpose, or to compress complex ideas. They then return to active, verb-based sentences for clarity and energy. The goal is controlled formality, not gratuitous abstraction.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Unit on formal style and nominalisation / word formation.
English Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Sections on formal writing patterns and noun phrases.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on nominal forms with register guidance and usage notes.

commonMistakes.wrong: The identify of critical roles is important.
commonMistakes.right: The identification of critical roles is important.
commonMistakes.why: 'Identify' is a verb. The nominal form is 'identification'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The assessment of candidates assessment was rigorous.
commonMistakes.right: The assessment of candidates was rigorous.
commonMistakes.why: Do not repeat the noun. One 'assessment' is sufficient.

commonMistakes.wrong: The development of developing a pipeline takes time.
commonMistakes.right: The development of a pipeline takes time.
commonMistakes.why: Do not mix the nominal form with the gerund. Choose one: 'The development of a pipeline' or 'Developing a pipeline'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The facilitation of the implementation of the restructuring of the department was complex.
commonMistakes.right: The restructuring of the department was facilitated through a carefully managed implementation.
commonMistakes.why: Stacking multiple nominalisations creates unreadable prose. Unpack and use verbs where possible.

commonMistakes.wrong: We made the identification of three candidates.
commonMistakes.right: We identified three candidates. / The identification of three candidates was completed.
commonMistakes.why: 'Made the identification' is an awkward hybrid. Either use the verb directly or the full nominal form.

rolePlays.title: Defending the Talent Acquisition Budget
rolePlays.setup: Oliver is presenting a proposal to increase Czarnikow's talent acquisition budget by 40 percent. The CFO is sceptical and wants to see ROI projections. Oliver must argue that proactive sourcing will pay off in two to three years.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Oliver. Defend the budget increase using nominalised, executive-level language. Present evidence that proactive pipelines outperform reactive hiring.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the CFO. Challenge every claim with financial discipline. Ask for ROI, payback period, and evidence from comparable companies.
sampleDialogue: A: The identification of critical roles — and the development of targeted pipelines — is not a cost. It is an investment with compounding returns.
B: What is the projected return?
A: Our assessment of comparable companies suggests a 3:1 return over three years. The acquisition of senior talent proactively reduces replacement costs by an estimated 35 percent.
B: Estimated? I need more than estimates.
A: The evaluation of our own data confirms the pattern. The deterioration of our pipeline last year led directly to two failed senior hires — at a combined cost of over £400,000.
B: That is a retrospective argument. What about going forward?
A: The prioritisation of proactive sourcing will compound our talent advantage year on year. The recognition of this by the board is, in my view, overdue.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least four nominalised structures naturally. Student B asks at least three financially rigorous questions. Both maintain executive register.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run once, swap roles. After each round, identify one effective use of nominalisation and one place where a verbal form would have been clearer.

lessons.title: Mastering Executive-Level Interviewing
lessons.objective: Conduct and critique executive interviews with sophistication and diagnostic precision.
lessons.intro:
Interviewing a senior executive has remarkably little in common with interviewing a junior candidate. At the top of the organisation, almost every candidate has the technical credentials. The real challenge is diagnostic: can you, in ninety minutes, form a credible view of how this person thinks, leads and makes difficult decisions under pressure?

The best executive interviewers resist the temptation of the polished narrative. They probe repeatedly. They ask about failures as rigorously as successes. They pay close attention to the question behind the answer — the pattern of thinking, not the specific episode. If a candidate had handled their last transformation differently, what would have changed? What do they now wish they had done sooner?

The interview is also a two-way assessment. Senior candidates are interviewing the company at the same time. They watch how decisions are made in the process itself, how consistent the messages are across stakeholders, and whether the interviewers ask anything beyond surface-level questions. A weak process is one of the most visible signals a company can send.

grammarDeepDive.title: Mixed Conditionals
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Mixed conditionals are among the most sophisticated structures in English, and mastering them is a hallmark of a truly advanced speaker. They combine elements of the second conditional (hypothetical present) and the third conditional (hypothetical past) to express how a past event affects the present, or how a present condition would have changed a past outcome. In executive-level business English, mixed conditionals appear constantly in strategic reviews, post-mortems, and forward-looking analysis.

There are two main patterns. Type 1 (past → present): If + past perfect, ... would + base verb. Example: If we had restructured in 2021, we would be market leaders today. This asks: what if the past had been different — where would we be now? Type 2 (present → past): If + past simple, ... would have + past participle. Example: If I were more risk-averse, I would not have taken that role. This asks: if my character were different, how would my past actions have changed? Both Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's English Grammar in Use treat mixed conditionals as the final stage of conditional mastery, and the Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes their high frequency in formal argumentation.

In practice, mixed conditionals are the language of strategic reflection. They allow speakers to connect cause and consequence across time — exactly the kind of thinking that executive interviews are designed to test. At Czarnikow, where decisions about sugar markets, trade routes, and personnel can have multi-year consequences, the ability to articulate 'If we had acted then, where would we be now?' is not merely grammatical — it is a core leadership competence.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar Advanced (John Eastwood) — Unit 38: Mixed conditionals — combining past and present hypothetical meaning.
English Grammar in Use Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 40: Mixed conditionals — if + past perfect with would + infinitive; if + past simple with would have + past participle.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — 'conditional' entry: mixed forms with usage notes and register guidance.

examples.pt: Se eu fosse mais paciente, não teria descartado aquele candidato tão rapidamente no mês passado.

commonMistakes.wrong: If he would have listened, the company would be stronger.
commonMistakes.right: If he had listened, the company would be stronger.
commonMistakes.why: Never use 'would have' in the if-clause of a mixed conditional. Use the past perfect (had + past participle).

commonMistakes.wrong: If we invested earlier, we would lead the market today.
commonMistakes.right: If we had invested earlier, we would lead the market today.
commonMistakes.why: When referring to a specific past action, use the past perfect (had invested), not the simple past.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I was more decisive, I would have acted.
commonMistakes.right: If I were more decisive, I would have acted.
commonMistakes.why: In formal/written English, use 'were' (not 'was') for hypothetical present states — even with 'I' and third person singular.

commonMistakes.wrong: If she had took the role, she would be abroad now.
commonMistakes.right: If she had taken the role, she would be abroad now.
commonMistakes.why: Use the past participle 'taken' (not the simple past 'took') after 'had'.

commonMistakes.wrong: If the board acted sooner, we wouldn't be facing this now.
commonMistakes.right: If the board had acted sooner, we wouldn't be facing this now.
commonMistakes.why: A specific past action that didn't happen requires 'had acted' (past perfect), not 'acted' (simple past).

rolePlays.title: Executive Interview: Country Director Candidate
rolePlays.setup: Oliver is conducting a final-round interview for a new country director at Czarnikow. The candidate led a major restructuring at a competitor firm two years ago. Oliver wants to understand how the candidate thinks under pressure and whether past decisions reveal the right leadership pattern.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Oliver, the interviewer. Probe the candidate's past decisions using mixed conditionals: 'If you had done X differently, where would the business be today?' Push beyond polished narratives. Ask about failures, not just successes.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the candidate. Answer honestly, using mixed conditionals to reflect: 'If I had acted sooner, the outcome would be different today.' Show self-awareness and diagnostic thinking.
sampleDialogue: A: Thank you for coming. Let me start with your restructuring at Global Trade Corp. If you had approached it differently, where would the business be today?
B: That is a fair question. If I had started the listening tour earlier, I would have identified the real resistance sooner. The business would probably be six months ahead of where it is now.
A: Interesting. If you were less consensus-driven, would you have made those cuts faster?
B: Honestly, yes. If I were more decisive by nature, I would have acted in the first quarter rather than the third. But I also believe the coalitions I built made the change more durable.
A: And if the board had not supported you, what would have happened?
B: If the board had blocked the plan, I would not be sitting here today — I would have resigned.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A asks at least three probing questions using mixed conditionals. Student B responds with at least two mixed conditional reflections showing self-awareness.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run the role play once, then swap roles. Focus on the quality of diagnostic probing, not just grammatical accuracy. After each round, highlight one strong moment and one area for improvement.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Oliver probes a candidate's transformation experience
additionalAudios.speaker: oliver
additionalAudios.transcript: Let us go back to the restructuring you led in twenty twenty-two. I am interested in the decisions you made under pressure. If you had started the process six months earlier, where would the business be today? And more importantly, if you were less risk-averse by nature, would you have made the difficult cuts sooner? I ask because the role here at Czarnikow demands someone who can make consequential decisions quickly and live with the uncertainty. Credentials are rarely the issue at this level. What matters is how you think when the answers are not clear.
tasks: Listen once without reading. What is Oliver most interested in? (Answer: how the candidate thinks under pressure)
Listen again. Find two mixed conditional questions Oliver asks.
Listen a third time. What does Oliver say is rarely the issue at this level? (Answer: credentials)
Pronunciation drill: repeat 'consequential decisions' and 'live with the uncertainty' three times with natural stress.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — A candidate reflects on a past decision
additionalAudios.speaker: emily
additionalAudios.transcript: If I had listened more carefully to the middle managers in the first month, I would not have lost three key people in the transition. That is something I reflect on regularly. And if I were more naturally confrontational, I would have challenged the CEO's timeline much earlier. But I believe the coalition I built made the outcome more sustainable. If the board had not backed me, the entire transformation would have collapsed. That experience taught me that credibility is earned in the first sixty days, not the first six months.
tasks: How many mixed conditionals does the candidate use? (Answer: 3)
What would the candidate have done differently? (Answer: listened more carefully to middle managers)
What does the candidate say credibility depends on? (Answer: the first sixty days)
Repeat the sentence 'Credibility is earned in the first sixty days' with conviction.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say that executive interviewing is 'diagnostic' rather than conversational?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because at the executive level, almost every candidate has the technical credentials. The interviewer must diagnose how the person thinks, leads, and handles pressure — not just confirm their CV.

qAndA.question: What does the lesson mean by 'the question behind the answer'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: It means the interviewer should focus on the candidate's pattern of thinking — how they reason, what they prioritise — rather than the specific story or episode they describe.

qAndA.question: When do we use a past→present mixed conditional versus a present→past mixed conditional?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Past→present (If + past perfect, would + base) is used when a past action affects the present. Present→past (If + past simple, would have + past participle) is used when a present trait would have changed a past action.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say a weak interview process is 'one of the most visible signals a company can send'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because senior candidates are evaluating the company as much as the company is evaluating them. A poorly structured process suggests poor decision-making and a lack of organisational rigour.

qAndA.question: How would you redesign Czarnikow's executive interview process based on the principles in this lesson?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: I would include diagnostic probing questions, structured around past decisions and counterfactual thinking. I would ensure consistency across interviewers and include a two-way element where the candidate can assess the company.

contextualization: Think about the most senior hire you have been involved with at Czarnikow. What diagnostic question would you now ask differently?
If Czarnikow had hired differently for a key role in the past, where would the business be today? Use a mixed conditional.
Describe a time when an interview process revealed something unexpected about a candidate. What was the 'question behind the answer'?
If you were redesigning Czarnikow's executive interview process, what would be the first thing you would change?

productionTasks.task: Present to your teacher, in 90-second in which you play an executive interviewer at Czarnikow. Ask at least three diagnostic questions using mixed conditionals. Focus on probing past decisions and patterns of thinking, not surface-level achievements.
productionTasks.successCriteria: Your presentation contains at least three correctly formed mixed conditionals and demonstrates a diagnostic probing style rather than a simple Q&A format.

pairWork.title: Executive Interview Simulation
pairWork.instructions: In pairs, one student is the interviewer and the other is the candidate for a senior role at Czarnikow. The interviewer must ask at least three mixed conditional questions probing past decisions. The candidate must answer reflectively using mixed conditionals. After 4 minutes, swap roles. At the end, each person shares the most insightful question or answer from their partner.

lessons.title: Employer Brand and the Battle for Reputation
lessons.objective: Analyse employer brand positioning and discuss reputation risks with nuance.
lessons.intro:
The employer brand of a modern company is shaped by countless signals the company barely controls: Glassdoor reviews, LinkedIn posts from former employees, leaked internal memos, interview experiences shared on Reddit, and, increasingly, the public positions the company takes on contested social issues.

That reality has forced a redefinition of what employer branding actually is. It cannot, realistically, be a carefully curated story delivered through owned channels. It has to be managed as reputation — an ongoing dialogue, where authenticity is the only defensible strategy. The moment the internal reality and the external story diverge, the market notices within weeks.

For HR leaders, this creates an uncomfortable but necessary alliance with communications, legal and the executive office. A bad first month experience for a new hire is no longer only an HR problem; it is a reputation risk. Conversely, a strong, honest culture is perhaps the most durable competitive moat a company can build.

vocab.example: Sophie explained the reputation to the team in the HR team at Czarnikow.
The manager asked us to curate the new trading plan.
The owned channel is a key part of our work in the HR team at Czarnikow.
The contested issue is a key part of our work in the HR team at Czarnikow.
Sophie explained the authenticity to the team in the HR team at Czarnikow.
The manager asked us to diverge the new trading plan.
A clear reputational risk helps us succeed in the HR team at Czarnikow.
The competitive moat is a key part of our work in the HR team at Czarnikow.
The leaked memo is a key part of our work in the HR team at Czarnikow.
We discussed the alignment during the meeting in the HR team at Czarnikow.

lessons.situation: Emily is managing a reputational crisis after a former employee published a critical article. She coordinates with communications and legal.
lessons.grammarDetail: Discourse markers. Sophisticated writing uses markers to guide the reader: notwithstanding, to be clear, that said, more fundamentally, by contrast, indeed.

exercises.instruction: Practise these reputation phrases:
sentences: Notwithstanding our best communication efforts, the internal reality ultimately shapes the brand.

exercises.title: 2. Add a marker
exercises.instruction: Insert a discourse marker. Digite a resposta em cada lacuna e clique em “Corrigir”.

___ , reputation is earned, not designed.
___ , culture determines the employer brand more than any campaign.

takeaways: Reputation is managed, not controlled.
Authenticity is the only defensible strategy.
Culture is the longest-lived competitive moat.
Employer brand is shaped by signals the company barely controls.
Internal reality and external story must align — divergence is spotted within weeks.
Discourse markers signal sophistication and guide the reader through complex arguments.

HR must build an alliance with communications, legal, and the executive office.

teacherGuide.overview: Lesson 47 — Apex HR. Employer Brand and the Battle for Reputation. Explores how employer brand is shaped by uncontrollable signals and the grammar of advanced discourse markers. By the end, the student should be able to discuss reputational risk with nuance and deploy discourse markers to structure sophisticated arguments.

lessonFlow.instructions: Ask: what do people say about Czarnikow as an employer on Glassdoor or LinkedIn? What shapes the employer brand most — the careers page or what employees actually experience? Let the student share freely.
Read the intro aloud. Go through the 10 vocab words: student repeats each one and uses it in a sentence about employer branding at Czarnikow or a competitor.
Explain discourse markers using the grammarDeepDive section. Read the 12 examples aloud. Do the 5 quick-practice items together. Review common mistakes, especially overuse and misplacement.
Read the situation. Do the Read Aloud and Add a Marker exercises. Play Audio A once without reading, then again with the transcript. Check answers.
Run the role play: student manages a reputational crisis. After each round, give one positive note and one correction on marker usage. Then do 2-3 of the Q&A questions orally.

lessonFlow.what: Make It Your Own + production + wrap-up
lessonFlow.instructions: Ask the 4 contextualisation prompts. Do the speaking production task (record and play back). Finish by reading the 10 takeaway phrases aloud together.

commonChallenges: Students tend to overuse 'however' and 'on the other hand' while neglecting more sophisticated markers like 'notwithstanding', 'that said', and 'more fundamentally'. Encourage variety by asking them to use a different marker each time.
Some students place discourse markers in unnatural positions, especially mid-sentence when they should be at the start. Drill sentence-initial placement first before exploring mid-sentence options.
The concept of employer brand as 'reputation management' rather than 'marketing' may be new. Use real examples from Glassdoor or LinkedIn to make it concrete.
