grammarDeepDive.title: Modal Verbs — 'can' and 'could' for Polite Requests
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In English, the two most common modals for asking for something at work are 'can' and 'could'. They look similar, but they carry very different levels of politeness — and choosing the wrong one can make a simple request sound either rude or pushy.

'Can' is the everyday, neutral form. We use it with people we know well and in informal situations: 'Can you help me with this?'. It is not rude, but in a formal or hierarchical situation (asking a manager, a client, a new colleague) it can sound a little abrupt.

'Could' is the polite, softer form. It is the past form of 'can', but in requests it does not mean the past — it means 'would you be willing'. Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) explains that 'could' is used for 'hypothetical politeness': we are not sure if the person will agree, so we soften the request. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) notes that 'could you...?' and 'could I...?' are the safest polite request forms in everyday business English.

A useful rule: in any Czarnikow request to a manager, a client, or a new colleague, default to 'could'. With 'please', you get the softest common form: 'Could I please have two more days on the report?'. With close colleagues, 'can' is perfectly fine.

For negotiation specifically, there is a third level: 'Would it be possible...'. This is even softer than 'could' and is the right form for a slightly bigger ask: 'Would it be possible to move the deadline to Wednesday?'. Use it when you are asking for something you know is not trivial.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units on modal verbs, especially 'can, could, would' for polite requests.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 37 (can, could, may) and Unit 38 (polite requests and offers).
Oxford Business English Handbook — chapter on negotiation language.

commonMistakes.wrong: I want two more days on the report.
commonMistakes.right: Could I have two more days on the report, please?
commonMistakes.why: 'I want' sounds direct in English. In any negotiation, start with 'Could I have...' or 'Would it be possible...'.

commonMistakes.wrong: You can give me more time?
commonMistakes.right: Could you give me more time, please?
commonMistakes.why: In a polite request, English inverts the subject: 'Could you...' — not 'You could...?'. Also, 'could' is softer than 'can'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Is possible to move the deadline?
commonMistakes.right: Would it be possible to move the deadline?
commonMistakes.why: English adds 'Would it' at the start — 'Is possible' is a direct translation from Portuguese ('É possível').

commonMistakes.wrong: I need you help me.
commonMistakes.right: Could you help me, please?
commonMistakes.why: 'I need you' is an imperative in English. Polite negotiation uses 'Could you' + question mark.

commonMistakes.wrong: Could I to have more time?
commonMistakes.right: Could I have more time?
commonMistakes.why: After 'could', never use 'to'. The structure is 'Could + subject + verb (base form)'.

B: Yes, of course. What's the situation?

B: Thursday is important because I need the numbers for the Friday meeting.
A: I see. Would it be possible to send a short summary on Thursday morning, and the full report by Monday?
B: That could work. Yes, let's do that.

qAndA.question: What is a negotiation, according to the lesson?
qAndA.modelAnswer: A polite conversation to find a good answer for everyone. It is about asking, listening, and finding a middle point — not about winning.

qAndA.question: What are three polite words Oliver uses in his request?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'Could', 'would it be possible', and 'please'. He also uses 'I completely understand' to show respect for the other side.

qAndA.question: Why is 'Could I have more time?' more polite than 'I want more time'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'Could I have' is a soft, hypothetical form — it shows the speaker accepts the other person might say no. 'I want' is an imperative and sounds like a demand.

qAndA.question: Why is it important to offer a middle point in a negotiation?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because it shows the other side that you respect their constraints, not just your own. A middle point is almost always easier to accept than a full win or full loss.

qAndA.question: What is the role of listening in a small negotiation?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Listening tells you what the other person actually cares about. Without listening, you cannot find the middle point — you are only asking for your own side.

lessons.title: Making Decisions at Work
lessons.objective: Learn basic phrases to share opinions and make simple decisions.
lessons.intro:
Every day, we make decisions at work. Some are small — "Which meeting first?". Some are big — "Which project do we choose?"

To make a good decision, we look at the options, we ask for opinions, and we think about the result. It is important to listen to different people before we choose.

A good decision is not always the fastest one. Sometimes we need time to think. Sometimes we need to ask one more question before we say yes or no.

grammarDeepDive.title: Simple Present — 'I think' and 'I believe' for Opinions
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When we share an opinion in English, we use Simple Present, not Present Continuous. We say 'I think option A is better' — never 'I am thinking option A is better'. This is one of the most common mistakes Portuguese speakers make in English meetings, because in Portuguese we sometimes say 'Estou pensando que...'.

Why Simple Present? Because 'think' and 'believe' are what grammar books call state verbs — they describe a mental state, not an action in progress. Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) lists 'think, believe, know, feel, understand, agree' as the most common state verbs in English. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) makes the same point: these verbs almost always use Simple Present, even when you are expressing an opinion right now in this exact moment.

There is one small exception: 'I am thinking about' (not 'that'). This means 'I am considering' and is perfectly fine: 'I am thinking about moving to a new supplier'. But when you share an opinion, stay with Simple Present: 'I think the new supplier is better'.

Other useful opinion openers that work the same way:

  • I believe — slightly stronger than 'I think'.
  • In my opinion — more formal, good for meetings.
  • From my point of view — makes it clear it is your perspective.
  • It seems to me — softer, leaves room for other views.

A practical rule: in a Czarnikow meeting, start your opinion with one of these five phrases. It sounds natural, polite, and confident — even when you are not sure of your English grammar.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — chapter on state verbs and Simple Present for opinions.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 4 (state verbs) and Unit 5 (Simple Present vs Present Continuous).
Oxford Business English Handbook — section on meeting and decision language.

commonMistakes.wrong: I am thinking that option A is better.
commonMistakes.right: I think option A is better.
commonMistakes.why: 'Think' is a state verb — it uses Simple Present, not Present Continuous, when you share an opinion.

commonMistakes.wrong: I am believing we need more time.
commonMistakes.right: I believe we need more time.
commonMistakes.why: 'Believe' is also a state verb — always Simple Present for opinions and beliefs.

commonMistakes.wrong: In my opinion is better to wait.
commonMistakes.right: In my opinion, it is better to wait.
commonMistakes.why: After 'In my opinion', English needs a subject (usually 'it') before the verb — not just the verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: I think that yes.
commonMistakes.right: I think so.
commonMistakes.why: The fixed English answer to a 'do you agree' question is 'I think so', not 'I think that yes'.

commonMistakes.wrong: For me, option A is better.
commonMistakes.right: In my opinion, option A is better.
commonMistakes.why: 'For me' exists in English but is informal. For a Czarnikow meeting, use 'In my opinion' or 'I think'.

rolePlays.title: Choosing between two sugar suppliers
rolePlays.setup: At a Czarnikow meeting, the sugar desk is choosing between two new suppliers: Supplier A is cheaper but new in the market. Supplier B is slightly more expensive but has 10 years of reliable delivery.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Sophie. Share your opinion clearly using 'I think' or 'I believe'. Give one reason. Then listen to the other side and decide whether to agree or propose a middle point.
rolePlays.studentB: You are Harry. Share a different opinion using 'In my opinion' or 'From my point of view'. Give one reason that is different from A's.
sampleDialogue: A: I think we should go with Supplier B. I believe the 10 years of reliable delivery is more important than the price difference.
B: In my opinion, we should try Supplier A. From my point of view, the cheaper price gives us a better margin, and we can start with a small order to test them.
A: That's a fair point. But I'm still worried about delivery risk. Could we try a small order first, and only grow it if Supplier A delivers on time?
B: I think that's a good compromise. Let's agree on a small trial order, and review after 3 months.
A: Perfect. Decision made — small trial order with Supplier A, review in 3 months.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least two opinion phrases ('I think', 'I believe'). Student B uses at least two different ones ('In my opinion', 'From my point of view'). Both listen, find a middle point, and close with a clear decision.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run once, swap roles. Focus on the listening moment — students must show they heard the other side before proposing a middle point.

But I'm happy to hear other views.

qAndA.question: What are three phrases from the lesson to share an opinion?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'I think', 'I believe', and 'In my opinion'. Other useful ones are 'From my point of view' and 'It seems to me'.

qAndA.question: What should you do before you make a decision, according to the lesson?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Look at the options, ask for different opinions, and think about the result. Sometimes also ask for more information before you say yes or no.

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'I think option A is better' and not 'I am thinking option A is better'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because 'think' is a state verb. State verbs use Simple Present, even when you are expressing the opinion right now.

qAndA.question: Why is it important to listen to other people before you decide at work?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because other people often see things you don't. Listening makes your own decision stronger — you find risks and opportunities you would have missed alone.

qAndA.question: When is a fast decision worse than a slow one?
qAndA.modelAnswer: When the cost of being wrong is high. If the decision is easy to reverse, fast is fine. If the decision is hard to reverse, taking an extra day to think is usually worth it.

lessons.title: Problems and Solutions
lessons.objective: Describe small work problems and propose simple solutions.
lessons.intro:
At work, problems are normal. Every day, something does not work perfectly — a late delivery, a missing file, a small mistake.

When we find a problem, we stop for a moment and ask: what is the real problem? Then we think: what can we do? We look for a simple solution — not the perfect one, just a good one for today.

A calm mind solves problems faster than a stressed one. Big breath, small steps.

grammarDeepDive.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In English, some nouns can be counted (one meeting, two meetings) and some cannot (information, advice, work). The ones that cannot be counted are called uncountable — and Portuguese speakers often get them wrong because in Portuguese, many of them can be counted: duas informações, dois conselhos.

In English, you never say 'an information', 'two informations', or 'an advice'. These are always uncountable. Instead, you use 'some information', 'a piece of information', 'a lot of information'.

Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) gives a clear list of common uncountable nouns in business English: information, advice, news, work, research, progress, equipment, furniture, feedback, luggage, money. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) agrees and adds that these words only take a singular verb: 'The information is useful', not 'The information are useful'.

A useful trick: when you want to talk about one specific piece of something uncountable, use 'a piece of' or 'a bit of'. A piece of advice. A piece of information. A bit of advice. These phrases let you sound natural without breaking the rule.

For problem-solving conversations, this matters a lot. You will often need to say things like 'I need some information', 'Could I ask for a piece of advice?', 'We have a lot of work to do'. Getting these right makes you sound instantly more fluent.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — chapter on countable and uncountable nouns.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 69 (countable and uncountable) and Unit 70 (a/an, some).
Oxford Learner's Dictionaries — 'information' and 'advice' entries with uncountable markers.

lessons.objective: Learn the basic language of simple projects — tasks, people and deadlines.
lessons.intro:
A project is a group of tasks with a clear goal and a deadline.

Every project needs three things: who does what, and when it must be ready. The person in charge is the project manager. Their job is to organise, to follow up, and to remove problems.

A small project can be just a list on paper. A big project needs a spreadsheet or a tool. But the idea is always the same: clear tasks, clear owners, clear deadlines.

grammarDeepDive.title: Prepositions of Time — 'by', 'on' and 'in'
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When we talk about when something happens or must be finished, English uses three main prepositions: by, on, and in. Each one has its own job, and mixing them up is one of the most common Portuguese-speaker mistakes.

By is used for deadlines — the latest moment something must be done. 'Please finish the report by Friday' means Friday at the latest; it can be Wednesday, it can be Thursday, but it cannot be Saturday. Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) explains that 'by' answers the question 'no later than when?'.

On is used for days and specific dates: 'on Monday', 'on 15 March', 'on my birthday'. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) confirms that 'on' is the only correct preposition for days of the week and specific calendar dates.

In is used for longer periods — months, years, seasons, parts of the day (except 'at night'): 'in March', 'in 2025', 'in the morning', 'in summer'.

A quick test: if you can answer 'on what day?', use on. If you can answer 'in what month/year?', use in. If you mean 'no later than this moment', use by.

One trap: 'until' is not the same as 'by'. 'Work until Friday' means you keep working all the way to Friday. 'Finish by Friday' means the work must be done no later than Friday. For deadlines, always use by.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — chapter on prepositions of time (at, in, on, by).
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 121-123 on time prepositions.
Oxford Learner's Dictionaries — entries on 'by', 'on', 'in' with time examples.

lessons.title: Time Management: One Day at Work
lessons.objective: Describe a typical working day and talk about priorities and time.
lessons.intro:
A working day has many tasks. Some are urgent, some are important, some are small. Good time management is about choosing the right task at the right moment.

Many people start the day with the hardest task, when the mind is fresh. They leave emails for later. They put meetings together, so the rest of the day is for real work.

A calendar is your best friend at work. It helps you see the day, protect time for important things, and say "Sorry, I am busy" when needed.

grammarDeepDive.title: Daily Routine Verbs and Frequency Adverbs
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When we describe our working day, we use Simple Present — just like with schedules. The structure is: I + verb + (object) + (time). 'I start work at nine.' 'I check my emails in the morning.' 'I take a break at three.'

To say how often we do something, we add a frequency adverb: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never. The position of the adverb is very specific in English: it goes between the subject and the main verb.

'I always start with my hardest task.' (not 'I start always') — Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) explains this rule clearly: adverbs of frequency sit just before the main verb, not after.

The one exception is the verb 'to be': with 'to be', the adverb goes after the verb. 'I am always busy in the morning', not 'I always am busy'. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) points out that this is one of the most common mistakes Portuguese speakers make, because the pattern feels backwards.

For describing a workday, the most useful frequency adverbs are:

  • Always = 100% of the time
  • Usually = most of the time
  • Often = many times
  • Sometimes = occasionally
  • Rarely = almost never
  • Never = 0%

A simple rule: when describing your Czarnikow day, start each sentence with 'I + frequency adverb + verb'. This single pattern covers 80% of what you will ever need to say about your routine.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — chapter on Simple Present and adverbs of frequency.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 5 (Simple Present) and Unit 106 (word order, adverbs of frequency).
Oxford Learner's Dictionaries — entries on 'always', 'usually', 'often' with position examples.

qAndA.question: What three pieces of advice does the lesson give about time management?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Start the day with the hardest task when the mind is fresh. Leave emails for later. Put meetings together so the rest of the day is for real work.

qAndA.question: Where do frequency adverbs go in an English sentence?
qAndA.modelAnswer: They go BEFORE the main verb: 'I always start', 'I usually check'. The only exception is the verb 'to be', where the adverb goes AFTER: 'I am always busy'.

qAndA.question: Why is it better to do the hardest task first?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because your mind is freshest in the morning. The hardest task is also usually the one you don't want to do, so doing it first removes the mental weight from the whole day.

lessons.intro:
Small talk is the short, friendly conversation before the real work starts.

At events, coffee breaks or in the corridor, people talk about simple things — the weather, travel, food, the weekend. It is not deep — and that is the point. It helps us feel comfortable with each other.

In British English, small talk is very important. People often start with "How are you?" and "Have you been here before?" Answer briefly and return the question. That is the magic trick.

grammarDeepDive.title: Question Forms — 'how', 'what', and 'where'
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In English, most questions start with a question word plus an auxiliary verb. The three most useful question words for small talk are how, what and where. Each one opens a different kind of conversation.

How asks about a state or a way: 'How are you?', 'How was your weekend?', 'How do you find London?'. It is the warmest, friendliest opener — the British classic.

What asks for specific information: 'What do you do at Czarnikow?', 'What did you think of the speaker?', 'What's new with you?'. It is more direct than 'how' but still perfectly polite.

Where asks about place: 'Where are you from?', 'Where do you live?', 'Where did you work before Czarnikow?'. Good for learning someone's background without sounding nosy.

The grammar rule: in Present Simple questions with you/we/they, you need 'do' as an auxiliary. Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) explains this clearly: the structure is question word + do + subject + main verb. 'What do you do?' — never 'What you do?'. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) agrees and lists dropping the 'do' as one of the top three Present Simple mistakes.

With he/she/it, use 'does' instead: 'What does Oliver do?', 'Where does Sophie live?'. And with the verb 'to be', no auxiliary at all: 'How are you?', 'Where is the meeting?'.

A simple rule for small talk: start with 'How', move to 'What do you', and close with 'Where are you from?'. Three questions, fifteen seconds — that is a complete, polite British small-talk opening.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — chapters on question forms and auxiliary verbs.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 49 (question forms) and Unit 50 (auxiliary 'do').
Oxford Business English Handbook — chapter on networking and small talk.

qAndA.question: What topics are safe for small talk, according to the lesson?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Simple, light topics: the weather, travel, food, the weekend, and the event itself. Avoid politics, religion, or strong personal opinions.

qAndA.question: What is the 'magic trick' of British small talk?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Answer briefly and return the question. For example: 'Fine, thanks — and you?'. It keeps the conversation balanced and friendly.

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'What do you do?' and not 'What you do?'
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because English Present Simple questions with 'you/we/they' need the auxiliary 'do' before the subject. The structure is 'question word + do + subject + main verb'.

qAndA.question: Why is small talk important in business, even though it is 'not deep'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because it builds comfort and trust before the real conversation. People who never do small talk feel cold to others, and that makes real business harder later.

qAndA.question: Why is it a good idea to close the small talk with 'Let's keep in touch' and offer a card?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because it turns a pleasant 2-minute chat into a real professional connection. Without that small gesture, the conversation disappears the moment you walk away.

lessons.title: Giving and Getting Feedback
lessons.objective: Learn simple phrases to give and receive daily feedback at work.
lessons.intro:
Feedback is information. It helps us know what is working well, and what we can do better.

Good feedback is short, clear and kind. We say something positive, and then, if needed, we mention one thing to improve. We do not give a long list of problems — just one or two useful points.

Getting feedback is also a skill. Listen calmly, say thank you, and ask a question if you need to understand better. Do not defend yourself right away.

grammarDeepDive.title: Positive and Neutral Adjectives at Work
grammarDeepDive.explanation: Adjectives describe people, things and situations. In business English, choosing the right adjective makes your feedback sound professional and kind. We use positive adjectives (clear, strong, helpful, honest, friendly, calm, kind, professional) to recognise good work, and neutral adjectives (short, long, quick, slow, simple, detailed) to describe something without judging it. In English, adjectives go before the noun (‘a clear report’) or after the verb be (‘the report is clear’). They do not change form for singular or plural: ‘a helpful colleague / helpful colleagues’. This is different from Portuguese, where adjectives agree in number and gender. To make feedback softer, we often add ‘very’, ‘really’ or ‘quite’: ‘That was a really clear presentation.’ To give a small suggestion, use a neutral adjective with a verb: ‘Next time, try a shorter introduction.’ This keeps your tone kind and professional — exactly what Czarnikow expects in daily conversations between trading desks, operations and clients.

Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 98: Adjectives and adverbs.

lessons.title: Reporting and Status Updates
lessons.objective: Share simple status updates at work in a clear and organised way.
lessons.intro:
A status update is a short report: what is done, what is in progress, and what is next.

Managers love clear updates. They do not need a long story — just the facts. "I have finished the report. I am working on the slides. Next, I will talk to the client."

Good updates save time and build trust. When your manager knows what you are doing, they stop asking — and you can focus on the work.

grammarDeepDive.title: Present Perfect with ‘just’, ‘already’ and ‘yet’
grammarDeepDive.explanation: The Present Perfect connects the past with the present. We use it to talk about recent actions that are important now — like finishing a task a few minutes ago or not having done something you were expected to do. The structure is have/has + past participle: I have finished. She has sent. With this tense, we often use three small words: just = a very short time ago. ‘I have just finished the report.’ already = earlier than expected (positive idea). ‘I have already sent the email.’ yet = up to now (used in negatives and questions). ‘I haven’t called the client yet.’ / ‘Have you called them yet?’ The position matters: just and already go between ‘have’ and the main verb, while yet goes at the end of the sentence. This is different from Portuguese, where ‘já’ and ‘ainda’ are more flexible. Using these three words correctly makes your status updates sound professional and natural — exactly how a Czarnikow trader or analyst reports to London or São Paulo.

lessons.intro:
A short business report has three parts: situation, facts, and recommendation.

First, describe the situation in one or two sentences. Then, share the main facts or numbers. Finally, say what you think we should do next.

A good report is short and clear. Use simple words, short sentences, and small numbers. If the reader finishes in two minutes with the right information, your report is a success.

grammarDeepDive.title: Linkers: and, but, so
grammarDeepDive.explanation: Linkers are small words that join ideas together. In business writing, they are very important because they show the reader how two sentences are connected. Without linkers, a report sounds like a list; with linkers, it sounds like a clear story. The three most useful linkers at Confidence level are: and — to add another idea of the same kind: ‘The report is short and clear.’ but — to show a contrast or a problem: ‘Sales are up, but costs are also higher.’ so — to show a result or next step: ‘Freight is expensive, so we must review the forecast.’ In written English, we usually put a comma before ‘but’ and ‘so’ when they join two full sentences. ‘And’ often has no comma in short sentences. In Portuguese you can sometimes leave the linker out, but in English the reader expects it — otherwise the connection is not clear. Using these three words well makes your Czarnikow reports feel organised, professional and easy to read for both London and Brazil colleagues.

Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 116: Conjunctions: and / but / or / so.

lessons.grammar: I feel / I think — opening phrases
lessons.objective: Use soft, calm phrases for small difficult conversations.
lessons.intro:
Some conversations at work are not easy. Maybe you need to say no, to share a concern, or to ask a colleague to change something.

The best way is to stay calm, speak slowly, and start with I instead of you. "I feel worried about the deadline" is much better than "You are always late".

A difficult conversation is a gift of honesty. It is short, respectful, and focused on a solution.

grammarDeepDive.title: Soft Opening Phrases: ‘I feel’ and ‘I think’
grammarDeepDive.explanation: In English, the way you open a difficult conversation changes everything. If you start with ‘You’, it often sounds like an attack, even when you don't mean it that way: ‘You are always late.’ If you start with ‘I’, the same idea sounds calm and professional: ‘I feel worried when we start late.’ Two phrases are especially useful at Confidence level: I feel + adjective — to share an emotion: ‘I feel a little worried about this deadline.’ I think + clause — to share an opinion: ‘I think we should speak to the supplier today.’ You can also soften the tone with small words like a little, a bit, maybe, or perhaps: ‘I feel a bit concerned about the freight costs.’ In Portuguese, we often use a direct ‘você’ with a calm tone, but in English the words themselves do the softening — tone alone is not enough. Using ‘I feel / I think’ is a key professional skill at Czarnikow, where colleagues come from very different cultures and styles of communication.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 135: Verbs of opinion and feeling.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 50: I think / I believe.
Cambridge Dictionary — ‘I think, I feel, I believe’ entry.

lessons.objective: Learn simple phrases to share ideas, problems and plans with a manager.
lessons.intro:
Your manager is a busy person. When you talk to them, be short and clear.

Start with the goal of the conversation. "I would like to share a problem", or "I have an idea about the new project". Then, in three or four sentences, give the key points.

Managers appreciate people who come with a short problem and a possible solution. They do not like surprises, and they do not like long stories with no clear point.

grammarDeepDive.title: ‘Would like’ vs ‘want’ — Polite Requests at Work
grammarDeepDive.explanation: In English, want and would like have almost the same meaning, but they sound very different. Want is direct and sometimes childish: ‘I want more time.’ Would like is polite and professional: ‘I would like a little more time.’ At work — and especially with a manager — we almost always use would like. The structure is: I would like + noun: ‘I would like your advice.’ I would like + to + verb: ‘I would like to share a quick idea.’ In spoken English, would like is often contracted to I'd like: ‘I'd like to talk about Q2.’ This is natural and friendly, not too formal. In Portuguese, the difference between ‘quero’ and ‘gostaria’ is similar but often optional; in English, the polite form is expected at work. At Czarnikow, using ‘would like’ with your manager, your clients and the London office shows professionalism and respect — without sounding stiff.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 145: Would like, want.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 36: Would like / Do you want?
Cambridge Dictionary — ‘would like’ entry.

lessons.objective: Learn simple phrases to work with colleagues from different cultures.
lessons.intro:
Business is international. Every day, we work with people from different countries.

Different cultures have different habits. Some people speak directly, others more softly. Some start meetings on time, others chat first. None of them are wrong — they are just different.

The best tool is curiosity. Ask questions with respect. "How do you usually start meetings in your country?" is a great way to learn and build a friendly relationship.

grammarDeepDive.title: Comparatives with ‘more’ and ‘less’
grammarDeepDive.explanation: When we compare two things in English, we use a comparative form. There are two main patterns: 1. Short adjectives (1 syllable) usually add -er: fast → faster, old → older, short → shorter. 2. Long adjectives (2+ syllables) use more before them: formal → more formal, direct → more direct, professional → more professional. To say something is less, we usually use less before the adjective, for both short and long: less formal, less long, less friendly. A very natural alternative is not as ... as: ‘London lunches are not as long as Spanish lunches.’ We connect the two things with than: ‘Brazilian emails are more friendly than British ones.’ Never say ‘more directer’ or ‘more friendlier’ — choose one form. In Portuguese, we use ‘mais ... (do) que’, so ‘more ... than’ is easy to remember. At Czarnikow, using comparatives well helps you describe real differences between the London, São Paulo and other offices — with respect and without judging.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 86: Comparative and superlative forms.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 105: Comparatives (older / more expensive).
Cambridge Dictionary — ‘comparison: comparisons of equality (as tall as)’ entry.

lessons.title: Numbers, Data and Simple Charts
lessons.objective: Learn to read and say numbers, percentages and simple charts in English.
lessons.intro:
Numbers are the language of business. Sales, costs, hours, people — everything is measured.

In English, big numbers can feel tricky at first. 1,000 is "a thousand". 1,000,000 is "a million". Percentages use the word percent, as in "ten percent".

Simple charts tell a story. A line going up means growth. A line going down means decline. A big piece of the pie means a big part. Numbers, then a story — that is the way.

grammarDeepDive.title: Big Numbers, Percentages and Decimals in English
grammarDeepDive.explanation: Numbers in English follow a clear pattern once you learn the blocks. Thousands are grouped with commas: 1,500 = one thousand five hundred. Millions follow the same idea: 1,200,000 = one million, two hundred thousand. We often say ‘one point two million’ as a shortcut. For percentages, we use the word ‘percent’ after the number: ‘ten percent’, ‘twenty-five percent’. Note that ‘percent’ is singular, and we never say ‘twenty-five percents’. For decimals, English uses a point (not a comma): 3.5 = ‘three point five’. Each digit after the point is said separately: 3.25 = ‘three point two five’. To describe movement in a report, we commonly use: go up by / increase by + percentage: ‘Sales went up by 8 percent.’ go down by / decrease by + percentage: ‘Costs went down by 3.5 percent.’ stay the same / remain stable: ‘Prices remained stable in March.’ In Portuguese, the comma and point are inverted (1,5 / 1.500), so always double-check when writing or speaking with international colleagues. At Czarnikow, clear numbers and clear trends are the foundation of every market report and client call.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Appendix: Numbers and dates.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Appendix 7: Numbers.
Cambridge Dictionary — ‘numbers: ordinal and cardinal’ and ‘percent, percentage’ entries.

lessons.title: Change at Work: Adapting to New Things
lessons.objective: Talk about small changes at work and how we adapt to them.
lessons.intro:
Change is normal in business. A new tool, a new process, a new manager, a new team — change happens all the time.

At the beginning, change can feel uncomfortable. We know the old way. The new way feels slower. But after a few weeks, the new way becomes the normal way.

A positive attitude helps. Ask questions, try the new tool, share what works. A small smile goes a long way during change.

grammarDeepDive.title: ‘Be going to’ for Future Plans
grammarDeepDive.explanation: In English, we use be going to + base verb to talk about plans we have already decided, and about things we can see will happen soon. The structure is: subject + am/is/are + going to + verb. For example: ‘I am going to try the new tool this week.’ / ‘We are going to meet on Monday.’ ‘Going to’ is very common at work because it shows a clear, decided plan. It is different from: - will, which we use for spontaneous decisions or promises: ‘OK, I will send it now.’ - Present Continuous, which we use for fixed arrangements with a date/time: ‘I'm meeting Sophie at 3pm.’ In spoken English, ‘going to’ is often pronounced ‘gonna’, but in writing and formal speech we keep the full form. Negatives use not: ‘I am not going to attend the call.’ Questions move the verb to the front: ‘Are you going to join the training?’ In Portuguese, ‘vou fazer’ maps very well to ‘I am going to do’, so the meaning is intuitive. The main trap is forgetting am / is / are — English always needs the auxiliary. At Czarnikow, this is the best tense to talk about process changes, new tools, team reorganisations and upcoming training.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 23: Be going to.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 20: I am going to do.
Cambridge Dictionary — ‘future: be going to (I am going to work)’ entry.

lessons.grammar: Helping verbs — let me / can I
lessons.objective: Learn basic phrases to welcome and help clients in a friendly way.
lessons.intro:
Clients are the people who pay for our products or services. Without them, there is no business.

Good customer service is simple: be friendly, listen carefully, and solve the problem. Smile, even on the phone — the client can hear it in your voice.

When a client is unhappy, do not argue. Say "I understand", apologise if needed, and look for a solution. A happy client tells two friends. An unhappy client tells ten.

grammarDeepDive.title: ‘Let me’ and ‘Can I’ — Polite Offers of Help
grammarDeepDive.explanation: Two simple structures make your customer service sound warm and professional in English: Let me + base verb — you take the action. ‘Let me check that for you.’ / ‘Let me put you on hold for a moment.’ This sounds friendly and proactive. Can I + base verb — you ask the client if you can help. ‘Can I help you with anything else?’ / ‘Can I confirm your order number?’ This sounds polite and respectful. Both are informal-to-neutral and work perfectly on the phone, by email and in meetings. In more formal situations, you can upgrade ‘can I’ to ‘may I’: ‘May I ask for your reference number?’ Notice: after let me and can I, we always use the base form of the verb, never ‘to + verb’ or ‘-ing’. Don't say ‘Let me to check’ or ‘Can I helping’. In Portuguese, we often use ‘Deixa eu...’ and ‘Posso...’, which map very well. At Czarnikow, these phrases are especially useful with clients from the sugar trading, freight and logistics side, where calm, clear offers of help make the difference between a stressful call and a loyal client.

lessons.title: Ethics and Doing the Right Thing
lessons.objective: Learn simple words to talk about honesty, ethics and doing the right thing at work.
lessons.intro:
Ethics is about doing the right thing, even when nobody is watching.

At work, there are many small ethical choices every day. Do you share a secret? Do you take the credit for someone else's idea? Do you tell a small lie to save time? Each small choice builds who you are as a professional.

A good rule is simple: if you would feel uncomfortable telling your family what you did at work, think twice. Honesty is not old-fashioned. It is the base of long-term trust.

grammarDeepDive.title: ‘Should’ and ‘Shouldn't’ — Advice and Moral Rules
grammarDeepDive.explanation: Should is a modal verb used to give advice, suggestions and soft rules. It is very common when we talk about ethics, good practice and what is the right thing to do. The structure is simple: subject + should + base verb: ‘We should tell the truth.’ subject + shouldn't + base verb (negative): ‘You shouldn't hide a mistake.’ Key features of modal verbs: - They never change form. It is ‘he should’, not ‘he shoulds’. - They are followed by the base verb, not ‘to + verb’. Say ‘you should tell’, never ‘you should to tell’. - They make questions by inverting: ‘Should I report this?’ ‘Should’ is softer than must (strong obligation, like a law or policy) and stronger than could (a possibility). Use ‘must’ for company rules: ‘You must follow the compliance policy.’ Use ‘should’ for ethical advice: ‘You should speak up if you see something wrong.’ In Portuguese, ‘deveria / deve’ is very close, so the idea is intuitive. At Czarnikow, ‘should’ is the right verb to talk about the Code of Conduct, data protection, honest reporting and long-term trust with clients and suppliers.

lessons.title: Leading Effective Meetings
lessons.grammar: Present Perfect vs Past Simple in updates
lessons.objective: Chair a professional meeting, manage time and keep people focused.
lessons.intro:
Meetings, done well, are one of the most useful tools in business. Done badly, they are where time goes to die. The difference is not the topic — it is the chair.

A good chairperson does three things consistently. They share a clear agenda in advance, so everyone arrives prepared. They protect the time, gently interrupting when a topic drifts too far. And, crucially, they close with decisions and owners — never "let's think about it" without naming who is going to think, by when, and bring what back.

The test of a meeting is not how many people spoke or how long it lasted. It is whether anyone, one week later, can describe what was decided and who is doing what.

grammarDeepDive.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple in Meeting Updates
grammarDeepDive.explanation: In meetings, you constantly report what has happened and what was done. English gives you two tenses that both talk about the past, but with different focus: Present Perfect (have/has + past participle) — the result matters now. We don't say when exactly: 'We have finished the proposal — we can move forward.' The listener thinks: 'Great, it's done, what's next?' Past Simple (verb + -ed / irregular) — we state when it happened: 'We finished the proposal last Friday.' The listener thinks: 'OK, Friday, noted.' Key signals: - already, just, yet, this week, so far → Present Perfect - yesterday, last Monday, two hours ago, in March → Past Simple A common meeting pattern is to combine both: 'I sent the report yesterday (Past Simple — says when) and the client has already confirmed the numbers' (Present Perfect — result matters now). In Portuguese, 'fiz' and 'tenho feito' are used differently, so this distinction can feel confusing. The simplest rule for Czarnikow meetings: if you mention a specific time, use Past Simple; if you want to show the current impact, use Present Perfect.

Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 13: Present Perfect and Past Simple (1).
Cambridge Dictionary — 'present perfect or past simple?' entry.

lessons.title: Writing Effective Business Emails
lessons.objective: Write clear, professional emails with structure, tone and appropriate formality.
lessons.intro:
Most professionals write more emails in a year than anything else they will ever write. Yet very few have ever been trained in how to write them well. The result is the inbox many of us live in — long, vague, hard to answer.

A good email does three things quickly: it tells the reader what it is about, what is expected of them, and by when. The first line should answer the question "Why am I reading this?" The last line should answer the question "What do I do now?"

Tone also matters. Emails are read faster than they are written, and subtle things — word choice, length, punctuation — shape the reader's reaction more than we realise. When in doubt, shorter, calmer and clearer always wins.

grammarDeepDive.title: Passive Voice for Formal Business Emails
grammarDeepDive.explanation: The passive voice switches the focus from who did the action to what was done. This is very useful in professional emails because it sounds neutral, polite and objective. Active: We have updated the report. (focus on 'we') Passive: The report has been updated. (focus on 'the report') The structure is: subject + be (in the right tense) + past participle. Common tenses in business emails: - Present Simple passive: 'Invoices are sent on the first of each month.' - Present Perfect passive: 'The report has been updated.' - Future passive: 'Your request will be reviewed by Friday.' - Present Continuous passive: 'Your order is being processed.' Use the passive when: 1. The doer is obvious or unimportant: 'The invoice has been sent.' (everyone knows who sends invoices) 2. You want a formal tone with clients: 'Your request will be handled promptly.' 3. You want to soften a negative message: 'The deadline was not met.' (avoids naming blame) Do not overuse it — if every sentence is passive, the email feels robotic. A good rule for Czarnikow emails: 1–2 passive sentences per email, the rest in active voice.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 47: The passive (1) — forms.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 42: Passive (1) — is done / was done.

lessons.title: Mastering Calls and Video Meetings
lessons.objective: Handle phone and video calls professionally, including turn-taking in larger meetings.
lessons.intro:
Remote communication has its own grammar. On a video call, you cannot simply start speaking when you feel ready — you might cut across someone else because of a delay, or miss your moment entirely because everyone is being too polite.

Good video participants signal before they speak. A small wave, a short "can I add something?", or simply using the chat for quick points. They also use people's names more than in person, because eye contact doesn't travel through a screen.

Audio quality matters more than people think. A cheap headset makes you harder to follow, which quietly undermines everything you say. Investing in a decent microphone is one of the smallest, most effective professional moves you can make.

grammarDeepDive.title: Polite Interrupting and Turn-Taking on Calls
grammarDeepDive.explanation: Interrupting is not rude in English — it is necessary, especially on calls with many people. What matters is how you interrupt. English has a clear set of softening phrases that signal 'I want to speak' without cutting someone off. To enter a conversation: - 'Sorry to jump in — ...' (most common, friendly) - 'If I may, ...' (slightly more formal) - 'Can I add something quickly?' (asks permission) - 'Just a quick point on that.' (short, direct) To hand the turn to someone else: - 'Over to you, Harry.' - 'I think Sophie wanted to say something.' - 'Shall we hear from the Brazil desk?' To politely disagree during a turn: - 'I see your point, but could I offer a different perspective?' - 'That is interesting — I would add that ...' These phrases are not grammar rules in the traditional sense — they are discourse markers, formulaic phrases that manage conversation flow. In Portuguese, we often use tone of voice and timing; in English, the words themselves carry the politeness. On a Czarnikow video call with London, São Paulo and other offices, these phrases prevent the awkward silence-then-everyone-speaks-at-once problem.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 266: Discourse markers in conversation.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 50: Verbs of speaking and thinking.
Cambridge Dictionary — 'interrupting politely' and 'turn-taking' entries.

lessons.title: Delivering Business Presentations
lessons.grammar: Linking and contrast — however, on the other hand
lessons.objective: Structure and deliver a persuasive business presentation at intermediate level.
lessons.intro:
A good business presentation is not a report read out loud. It is a guided journey, built around a clear message that the audience should remember one week later.

Start by deciding that message — the one sentence the audience must walk away with. Everything else supports it. If a slide does not support the message, it should not be in the deck, however pretty it looks.

Delivery matters as much as content. Pause more than you think you should. Look at individuals, not at the screen. And remember: you already know the material better than anyone in the room. Your job is not to prove you are smart — it is to make the audience smarter about this topic.

grammarDeepDive.title: Linking and Contrast: however, on the other hand, nevertheless, that said
grammarDeepDive.explanation: In presentations, you often need to move from one argument to a contrasting one. English uses special linking words for this. They make your speaking and writing sound structured and professional. however — the most common formal contrast word. It replaces 'but' in a more polished way: 'The market is tough; however, our position is strong.' on the other hand — used to present a second, contrasting perspective: 'Raw sugar is more profitable. On the other hand, refined sugar offers long-term stability.' nevertheless / nonetheless — stronger than 'however', signals 'even so': 'The deadline is tight. Nevertheless, the team has delivered before under pressure.' that said — a softer, slightly informal contrast: 'Results are positive. That said, we should keep watching costs.' Punctuation matters: in writing, however usually comes after a semicolon or full stop, and is followed by a comma: 'Sales are strong; however, costs are up.' In spoken English, a short pause before and after does the same job. Do not confuse however (contrast) with moreover/furthermore (addition). At Czarnikow, these contrast words are essential for presenting two sides of a market, comparing raw vs refined sugar, or balancing risk and opportunity in a pitch.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 253: Linking words — contrast.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 110: Although / though / even though; in spite of / despite.

lessons.title: Negotiation: Finding the Win-Win
lessons.objective: Negotiate professionally using structured conditionals and value-trading phrases.
lessons.intro:
Good negotiation is not about winning against the other side. It is about building an agreement that both sides actually want to honour after the handshake. The difference is enormous, both in outcome and in the relationship afterwards.

Skilled negotiators rarely give anything for free. They trade: "If you can commit to a larger volume, we could look at a better price". Each concession is linked to something they receive in return. That keeps the process fair and visible to everyone.

Equally important is understanding what the other side actually wants — not what they say first. Their opening position is usually less important than the interests behind it. Ask questions, listen for clues, and be patient. The best deals come from understanding, not from pressure.

grammarDeepDive.title: Conditionals for Negotiation: 'if you… we could…'
grammarDeepDive.explanation: Conditionals are the grammar of negotiation. They let you propose a trade without committing to it: 'If you can commit to a two-year contract, we could offer a better rate.' The if-clause sets the condition; the main clause shows the reward. This structure keeps both sides flexible. At Rise level, we use two conditional patterns: Type 1 (realistic offers): if + present simple, will/can/could + base verb. 'If you increase the volume, we can reduce the price.' This sounds confident and practical — the deal is realistic. Type 2 (diplomatic/hypothetical offers): if + past simple, would/could + base verb. 'If you increased the volume, we would be able to reduce the price.' This sounds softer and more tentative — useful when you want to test the water. Other useful negotiation structures: - provided (that) = if (more formal): 'We could match that, provided the volume doubles.' - as long as = if (condition): 'We can offer free shipping as long as you order quarterly.' In Portuguese, 'se você puder... nós poderíamos...' works similarly, but English has a clearer grammatical distinction between real (Type 1) and hypothetical (Type 2). At Czarnikow, using the right conditional signals professionalism: Type 1 for live offers, Type 2 for early-stage exploration.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 144: Conditionals (1) — real situations.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 25: If I do / If I did.
Cambridge Dictionary — 'conditionals: types' and 'provided/as long as' entries.

lessons.title: Making Better Decisions
lessons.grammar: Modals of possibility — might, could, may
lessons.objective: Discuss decisions, weigh options and express uncertainty professionally.
lessons.intro:
Most business decisions are made with incomplete information. Waiting for perfect data is often a decision in itself — a decision to do nothing while the world moves on.

Good decision-makers develop a few useful habits. They separate the important decisions from the merely urgent. They write down the real question before exploring options. And they explicitly consider what they would do if their favourite option turned out to be wrong — a simple stress test that catches most bad choices early.

Language matters too. In group decisions, the words you use shape what feels acceptable. "What might happen if…" opens discussion. "That's a bad idea" closes it. The same observation delivered two different ways produces two very different rooms.

grammarDeepDive.title: Modals of Possibility: might, could, may
grammarDeepDive.explanation: When we talk about future outcomes, risks or options at work, we rarely say things with 100% certainty. English has three modal verbs that let you express possibility without overclaiming: might — something is possible but not certain: 'Freight costs might rise next quarter.' could — something is possible, often with a condition: 'This could work if we adjust the timeline.' may — similar to 'might', slightly more formal: 'The client may prefer a shorter contract.' All three are followed by the base verb (no 'to', no '-s'): 'It might work. She could help. They may agree.' Negatives: might not, could not (couldn't), may not. Note: 'may not' does not contract to 'mayn't' in modern English. These modals are essential in decision discussions because they open the room instead of closing it. Compare: - 'This is a bad idea.' (closes the discussion) - 'This might not be the best option.' (invites other views) In Portuguese, 'pode ser que...', 'talvez' and 'é possível que...' cover similar ground. At Czarnikow, using might/could/may makes you sound thoughtful and professional — you are showing you have considered multiple outcomes, not just your favourite one.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 109: May, might (possibility).
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 29: May and might (1).
Cambridge Dictionary — 'may, might or could?' entry.

lessons.title: Problem Solving in Practice
lessons.objective: Diagnose business problems systematically and explain root causes.
lessons.intro:
The most common mistake in problem solving is rushing to the solution before understanding the problem. We see a symptom, grab the first explanation that feels right, and start fixing — only to discover, weeks later, that the real cause was somewhere else entirely.

A useful discipline is five whys: ask "why?" five times in a row, going deeper each time. The surface problem is rarely the real one. A late delivery might be due to a missed container, which was due to a supplier change, which was due to a sourcing decision taken six months ago for an entirely different reason.

Root causes are almost always less dramatic and more systemic than the symptom suggests. Good problem solvers stay patient, resist blame, and look for the quiet structural issues that allowed the visible problem to happen in the first place.

grammarDeepDive.title: Reason Connectors: because, due to, since
grammarDeepDive.explanation: When explaining problems and root causes, you need to connect a result with a reason. English offers three main connectors, each with a slightly different use: because + clause (subject + verb): the most common and versatile. 'The report was late because the data file was not shared on time.' due to / owing to + noun phrase: more formal, common in written reports. 'The delay was due to a missing approval.' Note: due to is often interchangeable with owing to, though due to is more common in modern business English. since + clause: used when the reason is already known by both speakers. 'Since we know the root cause, we can now plan the fix.' This is different from 'since' meaning 'from that time' — context makes it clear. In written reports and emails, mixing these three connectors makes your writing more varied and professional. At Czarnikow, you often need to explain why a shipment was late, why costs changed, or why a process broke — and choosing the right connector helps the reader follow your logic quickly.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 251: Reason: because, as, since, due to.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 112: Because / since / as.
Cambridge Dictionary — 'because, since, as, due to, owing to' entry.

roles.name: Harry (investigator)
lines: The report was late again. Let me walk you through the five whys.

additionalAudios.title: Audio 1 — Harry explains the five whys
additionalAudios.speaker: Harry (neutral British)
additionalAudios.transcript: So, the monthly report has been late three times in a row. I decided to use the five whys method. First: why was it late? Because the data file arrived after the deadline. Second: why did the file arrive late? Because the approval step took five extra days. Third: why did the approval take so long? Due to the fact that there is no set deadline for it. The root cause is structural, not personal. Since the approval process has no deadline, it drifts every month.
additionalAudios.task: Listen and write the chain of five whys Harry describes.

additionalAudios.title: Audio 2 — Harry proposes a fix
additionalAudios.speaker: Harry (neutral British)
additionalAudios.transcript: Since we now know the root cause, I would like to propose a simple fix. We should add a three-day deadline to the approval step. Because the current process has no deadline, people treat it as low priority. If we set a clear cut-off, the file should arrive on time, and the report will be ready by Monday morning. This is a systemic fix, not a quick patch.
additionalAudios.task: Listen and note: the root cause, the proposed fix, and the connector words Harry uses.

qAndA.q: What is the difference between a symptom and a root cause?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A symptom is what you see on the surface (the report is late); a root cause is the deeper reason it happens (no deadline in the process).

qAndA.q: When do we use 'due to' instead of 'because'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'Due to' is followed by a noun phrase and sounds more formal; 'because' is followed by a clause.

qAndA.q: Why is 'five whys' a useful problem-solving technique?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because it forces you to go deeper than the first obvious answer and find the structural issue.

qAndA.q: What is a recurring problem you see at Czarnikow?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Data files arriving late for the monthly report — I think the root cause is a lack of clear deadlines in the handover process.

qAndA.q: Do you prefer quick fixes or systemic fixes?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: I prefer systemic fixes because they prevent the problem from coming back, even though they take longer to implement.

lessons.title: Project Management Fundamentals
lessons.objective: Plan, track and report on a project using professional project-management language.
lessons.intro:
Project management is, at its heart, a promise to the business: "This will be ready, at this cost, with this quality, by this date." Every element of the discipline — planning, tracking, risk management, communication — is about protecting that promise.

Most projects do not fail because of technical issues. They fail because scope creeps quietly, risks are tracked but not managed, and stakeholders discover bad news too late. Good project managers make the invisible visible: they surface issues early, escalate without drama, and keep the business honestly informed about the state of the promise.

By the end of the month, a skilled PM will already have adjusted the plan twice, flagged one risk to the sponsor, and rewritten the status update in plain English. By the end of the quarter, they will have kept the promise — or renegotiated it in time.

grammarDeepDive.title: Future Continuous and Future Perfect for Project Updates
grammarDeepDive.explanation: In project management, you often need to describe what will be happening at a future point or what will be completed by a deadline. English gives you two precise tenses for this: Future continuous (will be + -ing) — an action in progress at a future point: 'Next week, we will be running user tests every day.' 'At 3 pm tomorrow, I will be meeting the sponsor.' Future perfect (will have + past participle) — an action completed before a future point: 'By the end of Q2, we will have delivered three milestones.' 'By Friday, the team will have finalised the design.' Key time markers: - Future continuous: this time next week, at 3 pm, next Monday, during Q3 - Future perfect: by Friday, by the end of the month, by Q3, before the deadline These tenses are extremely common in status updates, planning meetings and sponsor reports. They sound more precise and professional than simple 'will + verb'. In Portuguese, we sometimes use the present progressive ('estaremos testando') or the compound future ('teremos entregue'), which map well. At Czarnikow, mastering these tenses means your project updates give the sponsor exactly what they need: a clear picture of what is happening when, and what will be done by when.
references: Eastwood, J. — Oxford Practice Grammar, Unit 26: Future continuous; Unit 28: Future perfect.
Murphy, R. — English Grammar in Use (Cambridge), Unit 24: Will be doing / will have done.
Cambridge Dictionary — 'future continuous' and 'future perfect' entries.

lessons.title: Productivity and Focused Work
lessons.objective: Discuss productivity habits, focus and the economics of deep work.
lessons.intro:
We live in an age of constant interruption. Notifications, messages, emails and meetings compete for our attention every few minutes. Research consistently shows that, after an interruption, it takes several minutes to return to the same depth of focus — and most of us are interrupted long before those minutes pass.

The most productive professionals protect their attention like a scarce resource. They block time for deep work. They turn off notifications during that time. They make themselves genuinely unavailable for two or three hours a day — not because they don't care about their colleagues, but because they care about doing good work.

It is worth being honest: you cannot be everywhere, all the time, and still produce your best thinking. Choosing what not to do is often more valuable than doing more. Every hour protected for focus is an hour multiplied by its quality.

grammarDeepDive.title: Gerunds after Prepositions
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In English, when a verb comes immediately after a preposition, it must take the -ing form (the gerund). This rule has no exceptions. We say 'good at focusing', 'tired of waiting', 'interested in learning'. The preposition demands a noun or a noun-like form — and the gerund is the verb acting as a noun.

This is one of the most common grammar patterns in professional English. In meetings, emails and reports, we constantly use phrases like 'instead of sending', 'before starting', 'after finishing', 'responsible for managing'. The pattern is always the same: preposition + verb-ing. Many students make the mistake of using the infinitive ('interested in to learn'), but this is always wrong in English.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood, Unit 60) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy, Unit 65) explain this rule clearly. Eastwood notes that the gerund after a preposition works exactly like a noun: 'good at maths' and 'good at focusing' follow the same pattern. Murphy adds that certain verb + preposition combinations (such as succeed in, apologise for, insist on) always require the gerund. Learning these combinations is the fastest way to sound natural.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 60: Verb/Adjective + preposition + -ing form.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 65: Verb + preposition + -ing.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on gerunds after prepositions with business examples.

rolePlays.title: Coaching a Colleague on Productivity
rolePlays.setup: It is Wednesday afternoon at Czarnikow's London office. Emily has noticed that a colleague on the sugar desk is struggling with constant interruptions and wants to help them set up a deep work routine.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Emily. Suggest blocking two hours every morning for deep work. Explain the benefits using gerunds: 'instead of multitasking...', 'by focusing on one thing...'.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the colleague. You are sceptical at first — you worry about missing urgent messages. Ask questions and gradually agree to try it for one week.
sampleDialogue: A: I've been thinking about your workload. Have you considered blocking two hours every morning for deep work?
B: I'm worried about missing urgent messages from the Brazil office.
A: I understand. But instead of checking your inbox every five minutes, you could set a rule — only check at 10 and at 12.
B: I'm not great at ignoring notifications, to be honest.
A: That's normal. By turning them off completely, you'll be surprised how much you get done.
B: OK, I'll try it for a week. I'm interested in seeing if it really works.

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'interested in improving' and not 'interested in improve'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because 'in' is a preposition, and after a preposition the verb must take the -ing form (gerund). The infinitive is not allowed after prepositions in English.

lessons.title: Networking with Confidence
lessons.objective: Navigate professional networking events with confidence and natural conversation.
lessons.intro:
Networking has a bad reputation, largely because most people confuse it with collecting business cards or handing out CVs. Real networking is the opposite: it is the slow, honest cultivation of relationships with people whose work interests you, before you ever need anything from them.

At events, the best approach is usually the simplest. Introduce yourself with one sentence. Ask a curious question. Listen properly, rather than waiting to speak. Follow up afterwards with a short, specific note — "It was really interesting to hear about your work on X" — and leave the rest to time.

The people you will genuinely benefit from knowing are usually not the ones in a hurry to meet everyone in the room. They are the ones in small, interesting conversations near the side. Find them, lower your voice, and enjoy a proper chat.

grammarDeepDive.title: Question Tags in Professional Conversation
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Question tags are short questions added to the end of a statement. They are extremely common in British English, especially in small talk, networking and informal professional conversation. The pattern is simple: if the main clause is positive, the tag is negative; if the main clause is negative, the tag is positive. For example: 'You work in sugar, don't you?' and 'You don't work in freight, do you?'

The tag always uses the same auxiliary verb as the main clause. If the main clause uses is, the tag uses isn't. If it uses have (as a perfect auxiliary), the tag uses haven't. If there is no auxiliary, we use do/does/did. This is the part students find trickiest — but with practice, it becomes automatic. The key is to listen for the auxiliary in the statement and simply mirror it in the tag.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood, Unit 35) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy, Unit 51) explain that question tags serve two purposes: checking information ('You're Emily, aren't you?' — rising intonation, genuine question) and making conversation ('It's a lovely day, isn't it?' — falling intonation, expecting agreement). In networking situations, most tags are the second type — they are social lubricant, not real questions.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 35: Question tags.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 51: Question tags.
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on question tags with intonation guidance.

I thought I recognised you from the panel discussion earlier. The talk on Brazilian sugar exports was fascinating, wasn't it? I'd love to hear more about your work. Listen again. Write down all four question tags you hear.
Listen a third time. Which tag sounds like a genuine question and which sounds like small talk? (Hint: pay attention to intonation.)

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — Oliver describes a networking mistake
additionalAudios.speaker: oliver
additionalAudios.transcript: I made a classic networking mistake last year. I went to a conference and spent the whole evening trying to meet as many people as possible. I handed out about thirty business cards, but I didn't have a single proper conversation. The people I met didn't remember me, did they? Not at all. This year, I'm doing it differently. I'm going to find two or three interesting people and have real conversations. That's better, isn't it?
tasks: Listen once. What was Oliver's mistake? (Answer: He tried to meet too many people instead of having proper conversations.)
Listen again. Find two question tags in the audio. (Expected: 'did they?', 'isn't it?')
Do you agree with Oliver's new approach? Answer in 3–4 sentences.
Repeat the phrase 'I'm going to find two or three interesting people and have real conversations' aloud. Focus on natural rhythm.

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, what is real networking?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Real networking is the slow, honest cultivation of relationships with people whose work interests you, before you ever need anything from them.

qAndA.question: What does the lesson suggest you do after meeting someone at an event?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Follow up with a short, specific note — for example, 'It was really interesting to hear about your work on X' — and leave the rest to time.

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'You work in sugar, don't you?' and not 'You work in sugar, isn't it?'
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because the main clause uses 'you work' with no auxiliary verb. In the tag, we need the auxiliary 'do' for Present Simple, and since the clause is positive, the tag is negative: 'don't you?'.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say 'find the small conversations on the side'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because the most interesting and genuine people are usually not trying to network with everyone in the room. They are having real conversations in small groups, which are more valuable than superficial introductions.

qAndA.question: How could Czarnikow employees use networking at a sugar industry conference?
qAndA.modelAnswer: They could meet buyers from Brazilian mills, learn about new freight routes, build relationships with potential clients, and stay updated on industry trends — all through genuine conversations, not just exchanging cards.

contextualization: Think about the last professional event you attended. Describe it in 3 sentences, using at least one question tag (e.g., 'It was interesting, wasn't it?').
Imagine you are at a Czarnikow networking dinner. How would you introduce yourself? Practise a 15-second introduction aloud.
What is the hardest part of networking for you? Say it using a question tag: 'Starting conversations is the hardest part, isn't it?' or your own version.
Think of a colleague you admire. How would you describe their networking style? Use 2–3 sentences with at least one question tag.

productionTasks.successCriteria: Your presentation contains at least three question tags with appropriate intonation, a brief self-introduction, and a follow-up suggestion. The student speaks for at least 30 seconds.

pairWork.title: Conference mingling simulation
pairWork.description: In pairs, both students are at a Czarnikow industry event. Student A starts a conversation with a question tag ('It's a great event, isn't it?'). They must keep the conversation going for 3 minutes using at least 4 question tags between them. Then swap who initiates. After both rounds, each student identifies the most natural-sounding tag the other person used.

lessons.title: The Art of Useful Feedback
lessons.objective: Give and receive feedback with clarity, kindness and specificity.
lessons.intro:
Most feedback at work is either too vague to be useful or too harsh to be heard. Vague feedback — "you did a great job" — feels nice but does not help anyone grow. Harsh feedback — "that was terrible" — closes the conversation before it even starts.

Useful feedback is specific and behavioural. Instead of "you were unclear in the meeting", try "when you moved from the budget numbers to the forecast, I lost the connection — can you tell me how you saw the link?" That is something you can actually respond to.

Receiving feedback is also a skill. Good professionals learn to resist their first reaction — usually defensive — and stay curious for a few seconds longer. Ask for the example behind the comment. Say thank you, even when it stings. Decide later what to do with it.

teacherGuide.overview: This lesson explores giving and receiving professional feedback, with a grammar focus on reported speech. By the end, the student should be able to report what others have said in meetings and feedback conversations with correct tense shifts.

lessonFlow.instructions: Ask: when was the last time someone gave you feedback at work? Was it useful? What made it useful or not? Let them talk freely; note any reported speech they use naturally.
Read the intro aloud. Go through the 10 vocab words: student repeats each one and uses it in a sentence about feedback situations at Czarnikow.
Explain reported speech with tense shifts. Read the 12 examples aloud. Do the 5 gap-fills together. Review the common mistakes — especially forgetting to shift 'will' to 'would' and 'can' to 'could'.
Read the situation. Do the Read Aloud and Report It exercises. Play Audio A once without reading, then again with the transcript. Check answers.
Run the role play twice, swapping roles. After each round, give one positive note and one reported speech correction. Then do 2–3 of the Q&A questions orally.

lessonFlow.what: Make It Your Own + production + wrap-up

commonChallenges: Students often forget the tense shift: 'He said he will send it' instead of 'He said he would send it'. Drill the pattern: Present → Past, will → would, can → could.
Some students use 'say' and 'tell' interchangeably. Remind them: 'say' does not take a person object directly ('She said that...'), but 'tell' does ('She told me that...').
Students may struggle with reported questions. Emphasise that the word order changes to statement order: 'She asked whether we could...' not 'She asked could we...'.
