grammarDeepDive.title: Reported Speech in Professional Contexts
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Reported speech (also called indirect speech) is how we tell someone what another person said, without quoting their exact words. In professional English, we use it constantly — in meetings, emails, and feedback conversations. Instead of saying 'The client said: "The proposal is too long"', we say 'The client said the proposal was too long'. The meaning is the same, but reported speech sounds more professional and is easier to weave into discussion.

The main rule is the tense shift: when the reporting verb (said, told, mentioned, explained) is in the past, the tenses inside the reported clause shift back one step. Present Simple becomes Past Simple (is → was), Present Perfect becomes Past Perfect (has reviewed → had reviewed), will becomes would, and can becomes could. For reported questions, we also change the word order from question form to statement form: 'Can you simplify it?' becomes 'She asked whether we could simplify it'.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood, Units 46–48) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy, Units 47–48) explain that in professional contexts, the tense shift is not always obligatory — if the information is still true, some speakers keep the original tense. However, shifting the tense is always grammatically correct and sounds more polished. In a Czarnikow context, reported speech is essential for summarising client feedback, relaying instructions from managers, and reporting what was discussed in meetings you attended.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 46–48: Reported speech, reported questions, and reporting verbs.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 47–48: Reported speech and reported questions.
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on reported speech with tense shift tables and business examples.

examples.en: The client said they found the sugar proposal too technical.
examples.pt: O cliente disse que achou a proposta de açúcar muito técnica.

examples.en: Sophie told me she would revise the freight report by Thursday.
examples.pt: Sophie me disse que revisaria o relatório de frete até quinta.

examples.en: He mentioned that the shipping costs had increased by fifteen per cent.
examples.pt: Ele mencionou que os custos de envio haviam aumentado quinze por cento.

examples.en: They explained that the deadline had been moved to next Friday.
examples.pt: Eles explicaram que o prazo havia sido movido para a próxima sexta.

examples.en: The manager said she wanted more clarity in the quarterly review.
examples.pt: A gerente disse que queria mais clareza na revisão trimestral.

examples.en: Oliver told the team he could not attend the Monday meeting.
examples.pt: Oliver disse à equipe que não poderia participar da reunião de segunda.

examples.en: She asked whether we could simplify the risk assessment.
examples.pt: Ela perguntou se poderíamos simplificar a avaliação de risco.

examples.en: The Brazil office reported that sugar exports had reached a new high.
examples.pt: O escritório do Brasil informou que as exportações de açúcar haviam atingido um novo recorde.

examples.en: James said he had already reviewed the client's feedback.
examples.pt: James disse que já havia revisado o feedback do cliente.

examples.en: She mentioned that the São Paulo team was working on a new proposal.
examples.pt: Ela mencionou que a equipe de São Paulo estava trabalhando em uma nova proposta.

examples.en: They told us they would schedule a follow-up meeting for the next week.
examples.pt: Eles nos disseram que agendariam uma reunião de acompanhamento para a semana seguinte.

examples.en: The analyst said the sugar market had been unusually quiet that month.
examples.pt: O analista disse que o mercado de açúcar havia estado incomumente calmo naquele mês.

commonMistakes.wrong: He said he will send the report tomorrow.
commonMistakes.right: He said he would send the report the next day.
commonMistakes.why: When the reporting verb is past ('said'), 'will' shifts to 'would' and 'tomorrow' shifts to 'the next day'.

commonMistakes.wrong: She told that the proposal was ready.
commonMistakes.right: She said that the proposal was ready. / She told me that the proposal was ready.
commonMistakes.why: 'Tell' needs a person object (told me, told us, told the team). 'Say' does not take a person object directly.

commonMistakes.wrong: He asked could we finish earlier.
commonMistakes.right: He asked whether we could finish earlier.
commonMistakes.why: In reported questions, we use statement word order (subject + verb), not question word order. Use 'whether' or 'if' to introduce the question.

commonMistakes.wrong: The client said the costs are too high.
commonMistakes.right: The client said the costs were too high.
commonMistakes.why: When the reporting verb is past, the tense inside the clause shifts back: 'are' becomes 'were'. (Keeping 'are' is sometimes acceptable if still true, but 'were' is always correct.)

commonMistakes.wrong: She said me that she agreed.
commonMistakes.right: She told me that she agreed. / She said that she agreed.
commonMistakes.why: 'Said me' is never correct in English. Use 'told me' or 'said (that)'.

rolePlays.title: Giving Feedback After a Client Meeting
rolePlays.setup: It is Thursday afternoon at Czarnikow's London office. Sophie is giving feedback to a senior analyst after a difficult client meeting about a sugar supply proposal. The client had concerns about the proposal's length and technical language.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Sophie. Give specific, kind feedback about the presentation. Use reported speech to relay what the client said: 'The client said they found...', 'They mentioned that...'.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the senior analyst. Listen to the feedback, resist being defensive, ask for specific examples, and suggest improvements.
sampleDialogue: A: Thanks for making time. I wanted to share some feedback from the client meeting.
B: Of course. I'd like to hear it.
A: Overall, the client said they found the proposal very thorough — that was positive. However, they mentioned that some sections were too technical for their team.
B: Could you give me an example of what they meant?
A: Yes. They said the risk analysis section used too much jargon. They asked whether we could simplify it.
B: That's helpful. I'll rewrite that section in plainer language. Thank you for telling me.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three reported speech structures ('said that', 'told me that', 'mentioned that', 'asked whether'). Student B responds non-defensively and asks clarifying questions.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run it once, then swap roles. After each round, highlight one well-used reported speech structure and correct one tense shift error.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Sophie summarises client feedback

One more thing: the client said they had been very impressed by our market analysis. So it's not all bad — we just need to make the technical parts more accessible.

Listen again. Write down all the reported speech phrases you hear (e.g., 'they said...', 'they mentioned that...').

He mentioned that several new mills had expressed interest in working with us. Sophie told the team she would prepare a new client proposal by next Wednesday. I asked whether we could also review our freight costs, and James said that was a good idea. So we have clear next steps.

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, what makes feedback vague?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Feedback is vague when it does not include specific examples or behaviours — for instance, just saying 'you did a great job' or 'that was terrible' without explaining what exactly was good or bad.

qAndA.question: What does the lesson suggest you do when you receive feedback that stings?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Resist your first reaction (usually defensive), stay curious for a few seconds longer, ask for the example behind the comment, say thank you, and decide later what to do with it.

qAndA.question: Why do we change 'will' to 'would' in reported speech?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because when the reporting verb is in the past (e.g., 'said', 'told'), the tenses inside the reported clause shift back one step. 'Will' (present/future) shifts to 'would' (past). This is called backshift.

qAndA.question: Why is reported speech especially useful in a business like Czarnikow?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because professionals constantly need to relay information from meetings, client calls, and feedback sessions. Reported speech lets you summarise what others said without quoting them directly, which sounds more professional and is clearer.

qAndA.question: How could a Czarnikow employee use the SBI feedback model (Situation, Behaviour, Impact)?
qAndA.modelAnswer: They could say: 'In the client meeting yesterday (situation), when you used very technical language in the risk section (behaviour), the client looked confused and asked for a simpler version (impact).' This is specific, not personal, and gives the person something concrete to change.

contextualization: Think of feedback you received recently at Czarnikow. Report it using 'My manager said that...' or 'My colleague told me that...'. Use correct tense shifts.
Imagine a client told you: 'The report is too long and I need it by Friday.' Report this to a colleague using reported speech.
Describe a time you gave someone feedback at work. How did they react? Tell the story in 30 seconds, using at least two reported speech structures.
Think about the difference between 'Your report was bad' and 'The client said the risk section was too technical for their board.' Which is more useful? Explain why in 2–3 sentences.

Include at least four reported speech structures ('The client said...', 'They mentioned that...', 'They asked whether...', 'They told us...'). Cover both positive and constructive feedback.

pairWork.title: Feedback relay chain
pairWork.description: Student A reads a piece of direct feedback aloud (e.g., 'The sugar report is excellent but too long'). After all rounds, discuss which tense shifts were trickiest.

lessons.title: Status Reports and Escalation
lessons.objective: Write structured status reports and escalate issues professionally.
lessons.intro:
A good status report answers three questions in under a minute: what is going well, what is at risk, and what decision the reader needs to make. Everything else is background noise that busy people will skim past.

Colour coding helps. Green for on track, amber for needs attention, red for blocked. Honest colour coding is more valuable than optimistic one. A senior leader who reads five reports a week can spot amber-that-should-have-been-red within moments, and quickly stops trusting the author.

Escalation is the uncomfortable cousin of status reporting. It means saying, in writing, that something is not okay and you need help. Good escalations are factual, short and respectful. Bad escalations are either apologetic to the point of hiding the problem, or aggressive enough to burn bridges for the future.

vocab.example: The RAG status shaped our approach to the risk committee this quarter.
In sugar trading, on track often decides the outcome of a harvest report.
The team discussed at risk during the cargo review.
The team discussed blocker during the cargo review.
Sophie asked the analyst to flag the cargo carefully.
We need to escalate the board paper this week.
The mitigation shaped our approach to the risk committee this quarter.
Sophie asked the analyst to highlight the sugar contract carefully.
Her feedback on the cargo was factual and well received.
The team discussed summary during the cargo review.

lessons.situation: Harry is writing a weekly status report for a programme with three workstreams — one green, one amber, one red.
lessons.grammarDetail: Reporting verbs. Build a small bank: to confirm, to highlight, to flag, to note, to raise, to escalate. Example: I'd like to flag a risk on the delivery side. I can confirm the milestone has been met.

lessons.wrapup: An honest red beats an optimistic amber every time.

grammarDeepDive.title: Reporting Verbs — confirm, highlight, flag
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Reporting verbs are the tools you use to present information in a professional, structured way. Instead of saying 'I want to tell you something', you say 'I'd like to flag a risk' or 'I can confirm the result'. Each verb carries a slightly different meaning and sets the reader's expectations before they even finish the sentence.

The most common reporting verbs in business are confirm (yes, it happened), highlight (look at this — it matters), flag (warning — there is a risk), note (for the record), raise (bring up for discussion), and escalate (pass upward because it needs a bigger decision). Using the right verb saves the reader time and shows you understand the weight of your own message.

In status reports, these verbs often appear with 'I'd like to…' or 'I can…' at the start of a sentence. This pattern is polite and professional. Notice that in English, these verbs are followed directly by a noun or a that-clause: I can confirm that…, I'd like to flag a risk.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 53 on verb + that-clause structures for reporting.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 48 (Reported speech) and Unit 53 (Verb + object + to-infinitive).
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on 'confirm', 'highlight', 'flag', 'escalate' with business usage examples.

examples.pt: Podemos levantar isso no próximo comitê diretivo?

examples.pt: Harry escalou o problema para a mesa de negociação de Londres.

examples.pt: Posso confirmar que o contrato foi assinado por ambas as partes.

examples.en: She highlighted the improvement in delivery times from Brazil.
examples.pt: Ela destacou a melhora nos prazos de entrega do Brasil.

examples.en: The team flagged a risk with the new supplier in India.
examples.pt: A equipe sinalizou um risco com o novo fornecedor na Índia.

rolePlays.setup: It is Friday morning at Czarnikow's London office. Harry is presenting the weekly programme status to the Head of Operations. There are three workstreams: logistics (green), commercial (amber), and IT migration (red).

qAndA.question: What do the colours green, amber and red mean in a status report?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Green means on track, amber means at risk or needs attention, and red means blocked or in serious trouble.

qAndA.question: Why does Harry say honest colour coding is more valuable than optimistic coding?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because senior leaders read many reports and can quickly spot when amber should have been red. If you hide problems, people stop trusting your updates.

qAndA.question: Imagine a Czarnikow freight booking is two days late. How would you flag this in a status report?
qAndA.modelAnswer: I'd like to flag a delay on the freight booking for the March shipment. The vessel is two days behind schedule and we may need to adjust the delivery window.

qAndA.question: Do you think it is harder to escalate an issue to a senior leader or to a colleague at the same level? Why?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Open answer. Most students say escalating to seniors is harder because of hierarchy and fear of blame. The key is to keep it factual and short.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'flag' and 'highlight'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Flag usually signals a risk or a problem. Highlight draws attention to something important — often positive, but not always. Both are reporting verbs used in professional updates.

lessons.title: Business Writing That Gets Read
lessons.objective: Write business documents that respect the reader's time and effort.
lessons.intro:
Busy readers do not read. They skim. They catch the first line, the headings, and whatever is in bold. If your message is hidden in the third paragraph, half your readers will never reach it.

That is why good business writing front-loads the main point. The headline answers the question. The first line explains why it matters. Everything after is detail for the readers who want more.

Cutting words is another underrated skill. "It should be noted that" means nothing. "In order to" is just "to". "At this moment in time" is "now". Every unnecessary phrase you remove makes the important ones land harder. Good writing is not about adding more — it is about taking away.

grammarDeepDive.title: Concise Constructions — Cutting Fillers
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In business English, shorter is almost always better. Readers are busy. They skim emails, reports and memos looking for the key point. If your message is buried under filler phrases, half your audience will never find it. Concise writing means removing words that add no meaning.

The most common fillers in business writing are: in order to (just use 'to'), at this moment in time (just use 'now'), it should be noted that (delete it entirely), due to the fact that (use 'because'), and we are writing to inform you that (just say the thing). Each one adds five to ten words without changing the meaning. Over a full document, they can double the length.

The trick is to write your first draft freely, then go back and cut. Look for any phrase you can remove without losing meaning. If the sentence still works without it, it was filler. Professional writers at places like Czarnikow edit their own emails before sending — that extra minute saves the reader five.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 3 on sentence structure and Unit 100 on formal vs informal writing.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 99 (Conjunctions: because, although) and Appendix 7 on formal/informal register.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on 'concise', 'filler', 'front-load' with examples of plain English.

examples.en: 'In order to meet the deadline' → 'To meet the deadline'.
examples.pt: 'A fim de cumprir o prazo' → 'Para cumprir o prazo'.

examples.en: 'At this moment in time, the vessel is delayed' → 'The vessel is delayed now'.
examples.pt: 'Neste momento, o navio está atrasado' → 'O navio está atrasado agora'.

examples.en: 'It should be noted that costs have risen' → 'Costs have risen'.
examples.pt: 'Deve-se notar que os custos subiram' → 'Os custos subiram'.

examples.en: 'Due to the fact that the buyer cancelled' → 'Because the buyer cancelled'.
examples.pt: 'Devido ao fato de o comprador ter cancelado' → 'Porque o comprador cancelou'.

examples.en: Charlotte's original memo was three pages. The edited version is one page.
examples.pt: O memorando original da Charlotte tinha três páginas. A versão editada tem uma.

examples.pt: 'Estamos escrevendo para informar que o contrato está pronto' → 'O contrato está pronto'.

examples.en: Front-load the headline: 'Freight costs up 8% — action needed by Friday'.
examples.pt: Comece pelo título: 'Custos de frete subiram 8% — ação necessária até sexta'.

examples.en: 'The purpose of this email is to update you' → just give the update.
examples.pt: 'O objetivo deste e-mail é atualizá-lo' → simplesmente dê a atualização.

examples.en: A punchy subject line saves the reader thirty seconds.

rolePlays.title: Editing the Executive Memo
rolePlays.setup: Charlotte has written a three-page memo for the Czarnikow executive committee about rising freight costs between Brazil and London. Her manager asks her to cut it to one page. She must present the edited version and explain what she removed and why.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Charlotte. Present your one-page edited memo. Explain three things you cut and why they were fillers.
rolePlays.studentB: You are Charlotte's manager. Listen to the edited version. Ask: 'Did we lose any important information?' and 'Is the headline clear enough?'
sampleDialogue: A: I've edited the memo down to one page. The headline now reads: 'Freight costs up 8% — decision needed by Friday'.
B: Good. What did you cut?

A: Three things. First, I removed two paragraphs of background that the committee already knows. Second, I replaced 'in order to reduce exposure' with 'to reduce exposure'. Third, I deleted 'it should be noted that' in four places — it added nothing.
B: Did we lose any important information?
A: No. Everything essential is still there, just in fewer words.
B: Is the headline clear enough for someone who has sixty seconds?
A: Yes — it tells them the problem and the deadline in one line.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A identifies at least three fillers that were removed. Student B asks relevant follow-up questions about clarity.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run once each way. Encourage students to bring a real email they wrote recently and try to cut it in half.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say busy readers 'do not read — they skim'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because people in business receive many emails and documents. They look at headings, bold text and the first line. If the key message is buried, they miss it.

qAndA.question: What does 'front-load the main point' mean and why is it important?
qAndA.modelAnswer: It means putting the most important information first — in the headline or opening sentence. It is important because many readers only read the beginning.

qAndA.question: Rewrite this Czarnikow sentence concisely: 'We would like to take this opportunity to inform you that the sugar contract for Q3 has been finalised.'
qAndA.modelAnswer: The Q3 sugar contract has been finalised.

qAndA.question: Do you think short emails can sometimes feel rude? How do you balance conciseness with politeness?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Open answer. Good discussion point: a short email with a polite opening ('Hi Charlotte, thanks for your note') and a clear sign-off is both concise and warm.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'concise' and 'short'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Short means few words. Concise means every word earns its place — nothing is wasted. A concise text can still be detailed, but it has no filler.

contextualization: Find an email you sent this week. Can you cut it by 30% without losing meaning?
Think about a report you receive regularly at Czarnikow. Is the main point in the first paragraph or buried later?
How do you decide what goes in a subject line? Do you front-load the key information?
In Portuguese business writing, longer phrases are sometimes considered more polite. How does English differ?

pairWork.title: Filler-spotting race
pairWork.description: Both students receive the same wordy paragraph (use the Audio A transcript). They have 3 minutes to independently rewrite it as concisely as possible. Then they compare versions: who used fewer words? Did either version lose important information? Together, they agree on the best combined version.

lessons.title: Leading Difficult Conversations
lessons.objective: Run a difficult conversation at work with calm, structure and outcome focus.
lessons.intro:
Difficult conversations are difficult precisely because they matter. The instinct is to avoid them, hoping the situation will resolve itself. In practice, avoided conversations almost always get worse, and the longer they wait, the higher the cost of finally having them.

A useful structure is to prepare three things. First, the facts — what actually happened, in neutral language. Second, the impact — how it affected others, without blame. Third, the ask — what you would like to be different, going forward. Those three together give the other person something real to work with.

Tone during the conversation is as important as content. Speak slowly. Pause after the difficult sentence. Give the other person space to react, even if that reaction is uncomfortable. Resist the temptation to soften the message so much that it disappears. Kindness is not the same as vagueness.

grammarDeepDive.title: Softeners and Reformulation
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Softeners are phrases that make a difficult message easier to hear without removing the message itself. In English, we use them constantly in professional life: I may have misread this, but…, I wonder whether…, I'd like to share something…. They signal to the listener that you are being thoughtful, not attacking. The message still lands — it just arrives more gently.

Reformulation is the skill of saying the same thing in a different way when the first attempt did not land well. Phrases like let me put that differently, what I mean is, and to be clearer allow you to correct course mid-conversation without losing face. In difficult conversations, you will often need to reformulate two or three times before the other person truly hears the point.

The structure for a difficult conversation is: facts (what happened, neutrally), impact (how it affected others, without blame), and the ask (what you want to be different). Softeners wrap around this structure. They do not replace it. A conversation that is all softener and no substance is worse than no conversation at all.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 40 on modal verbs for politeness (would, could, might) and Unit 51 on indirect questions.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 36 (Would) and Unit 37 (Could and was able to) for polite softening.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on 'soften', 'reformulate', 'de-escalate' with examples of workplace diplomacy.

rolePlays.title: The Difficult Feedback Conversation
rolePlays.setup: James is a senior trader at Czarnikow's London office. He has noticed that a colleague on the trading desk tends to interrupt junior analysts during the weekly calls, causing them to stop contributing. James needs to address this directly but respectfully.
rolePlays.studentA: You are James. Use the facts-impact-ask structure. Start with a softener, state the facts neutrally, explain the impact, and make a clear ask for change.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the senior colleague. You are surprised by the feedback. React naturally — you may be defensive at first, then start to listen. Ask: 'Can you give me a specific example?'
sampleDialogue: A: Thanks for making time. I'd like to share something that has been on my mind.
B: Of course, go ahead.
A: I may have misread this, but I've noticed that in the last few weekly calls, the junior analysts have gone quiet. The facts are that three of them stopped contributing after being interrupted.
B: Interrupted? I don't think I interrupt people.
A: Let me put that differently. When a senior voice jumps in quickly, junior team members sometimes feel there isn't space for them. The impact is that we're losing their input.
B: I see. Can you give me a specific example?
A: Last Tuesday, Ana started to share her analysis on the Brazil contract and didn't get to finish. What I'd like going forward is that we pause a moment before responding, to give everyone space.
B: That's fair. I'll be more aware of it.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three softeners and follows the facts-impact-ask structure. Student B reacts naturally and asks at least one clarifying question.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: This role play can feel intense. Brief both students beforehand. After each round, acknowledge the difficulty and give constructive feedback on tone, not just language.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — James preparing his approach
additionalAudios.speaker: James (RP British)
additionalAudios.transcript: Right. I've been putting this off, but it's only getting worse. Let me think about how to structure this. The facts: in the last three weekly calls, at least two junior analysts stopped talking after being interrupted. The impact: we are losing their ideas, and one of them told me privately she feels her contributions don't matter. The ask: I'd like my colleague to give more space in meetings — maybe pause for three seconds before responding. I'll start with a softener: 'I'd like to share something that's been on my mind.' Keep it factual. Keep it respectful. Don't over-soften.

But James was calm, he gave me specific examples, and he wasn't attacking me as a person. He was talking about the impact on the team. I think the fact that he said 'I may have misread this' helped — it gave me space to not feel accused. I'll try to pause more in the next meeting. It's a fair point.

qAndA.question: What are the three parts of a well-structured difficult conversation?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Facts (what happened, in neutral language), impact (how it affected others, without blame), and the ask (what you would like to be different going forward).

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say 'kindness is not the same as vagueness'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because if you soften the message so much that the other person doesn't understand the problem, you haven't helped them. True kindness is being clear enough for them to act on it.

qAndA.question: How would you soften this sentence for a Czarnikow colleague: 'You always dominate the meeting and nobody else can speak'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: I've noticed that in recent meetings, there hasn't been much space for others to contribute. I wonder whether we could try pausing before responding, so everyone has a chance to share their thoughts.

qAndA.question: In your culture, is it common to give direct feedback to a senior colleague? How does it compare to the British approach in this lesson?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Open answer. Useful for discussing cultural differences. In many Brazilian workplaces, hierarchy makes direct upward feedback rare. The British approach uses softeners to enable it.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'I wonder whether' and 'I want'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'I wonder whether' is a softener — it sounds like a suggestion, not a demand. 'I want' is direct and can feel confrontational in a difficult conversation. Both can convey the same meaning, but the tone is very different.

lessons.title: Managing Up and Managing Stakeholders
lessons.objective: Influence without authority — manage senior stakeholders with structured communication.
lessons.intro:
Managing up is one of those topics nobody teaches explicitly, yet everyone is secretly judged on. It is the skill of keeping your manager well informed, well supported and well positioned to make good decisions on your behalf — without ever crossing the line into being difficult.

The core principle is respect for the other person's time and attention. Come with proposals, not just problems. Give context before details. Summarise long topics into two or three lines that a busy senior can skim between meetings.

With senior stakeholders more broadly, the game is similar. Influence without authority comes from credibility, not volume. Be reliable. Be honest when the news is bad. Make their job easier in small ways consistently, and they will return the favour in moments that matter.

grammarDeepDive.title: Conditional Type 2 for Diplomatic Suggestions
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In business English, being right is not always enough — you also need to sound respectful. The Conditional Type 2 (also called the Second Conditional) is one of the best tools for making suggestions to senior people without sounding pushy. Instead of saying 'You should do this', you say 'If I were in your position, I would do this'. The meaning is the same, but the tone is completely different.

The structure is: If + past simple, would + base verb. The past tense does not refer to the past — it creates distance and politeness. 'If we had more time, we could look at other options' is softer than 'We need more time'. This is why diplomats, consultants and senior managers use Type 2 conditionals constantly. It lets you influence a decision without challenging someone's authority.

One important detail: with the verb to be, we use were for all subjects in formal English — 'If I were you', not 'If I was you'. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) confirm that 'were' is the standard form in Type 2 conditionals, especially in professional and written contexts. In casual speech, 'was' is common, but in a business meeting, 'were' is the safer choice.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 38: Second Conditional (If + past simple, would).
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 38: If I knew... / If I were... (Second Conditional for unreal situations).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on Second Conditional with examples of polite suggestions and hypothetical advice.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I was you, I would talk to the CEO.
commonMistakes.right: If I were you, I would talk to the CEO.
commonMistakes.why: In formal English and business settings, 'were' is used for all subjects in Type 2 conditionals.

commonMistakes.wrong: If we would have more time, we could review this.
commonMistakes.right: If we had more time, we could review this.
commonMistakes.why: The if-clause takes past simple, not 'would'. 'Would' only goes in the main clause.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I were you, I will raise this at the meeting.
commonMistakes.right: If I were you, I would raise this at the meeting.
commonMistakes.why: Type 2 conditionals use 'would', not 'will'. 'Will' makes it a Type 1 conditional, which sounds less polite.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I were in your position, I would to brief the team.
commonMistakes.right: If I were in your position, I would brief the team.
commonMistakes.why: After 'would', use the base verb without 'to'. It is 'would brief', not 'would to brief'.

commonMistakes.wrong: If the CEO knew about the delay, he can adjust.
commonMistakes.right: If the CEO knew about the delay, he could adjust.
commonMistakes.why: 'Can' is too direct for a hypothetical situation. Use 'could' to maintain the polite, hypothetical tone.

rolePlays.title: Briefing the CEO Before an External Meeting
rolePlays.setup: Sophie has two minutes to brief the Czarnikow CEO before he walks into a meeting with a major Brazilian sugar buyer. There is one risk (a freight delay) and one opportunity (a volume increase). She needs to be concise and diplomatic.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Sophie. Brief the CEO on the risk and the opportunity. Use Type 2 conditionals to suggest how he might handle each topic. Keep it under 2 minutes.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the CEO. You are busy and slightly distracted. Ask one clarifying question about the freight delay and thank Sophie for the brief.
sampleDialogue: A: Good morning. I wanted to give you a very quick brief before the meeting — two points, nothing more.
B: Go ahead, Sophie. I have about two minutes.
A: First, there is a freight delay on the Santos shipment. If I were in your position, I would mention it briefly but position it as under control.
B: How long is the delay exactly?
A: Five days. The logistics team is already working on alternatives. Second, the buyer wants to increase volumes by 15 percent. If we had confirmation today, we could lock in the current price.
B: Good. Thank you, Sophie. That is exactly what I needed.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least two Type 2 conditionals ('If I were...', 'If we had...'). Student A keeps the brief concise (under 2 minutes). Student B asks a relevant clarifying question.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run it once as written, then swap roles. After each round, highlight one good use of a conditional and suggest one improvement. If the student struggles, give them the first conditional sentence as a starter.

If I were presenting this to the board, I would frame it as a known risk with a mitigation plan already in place. Second, the Brazilian buyer mentioned interest in increasing volumes. If we had a confirmed number by Friday, we could lock in pricing before the market moves. I have prepared a one-page summary — it is on your desk.

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, what is the core principle of managing up?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Respect for the other person's time and attention. Come with proposals, not just problems, and summarise long topics into two or three lines.

qAndA.question: Why does Sophie prepare a two-slide brief instead of a longer document?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because senior leaders are busy and need to skim key information between meetings. Two slides keep the message focused and actionable.

qAndA.question: Why do we use 'If I were' instead of 'If I was' in business suggestions?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because 'were' is the standard form in Type 2 conditionals for formal and professional settings. It sounds more polished and diplomatic.

qAndA.question: Why is it important to bring proposals rather than just problems to a senior manager?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because proposals show initiative and save the manager's time. They can say yes or no instead of having to think of a solution themselves. It also builds your credibility as someone who solves, not just reports.

qAndA.question: How does influence without authority work at a company like Czarnikow?
qAndA.modelAnswer: It comes from being reliable, honest and helpful consistently. When you make people's jobs easier — preparing good briefs, flagging risks early, giving honest feedback — they trust you and support your ideas in return.

lessons.title: Working Across Cultures
lessons.grammar: Advanced comparatives — far more, significantly less
lessons.objective: Navigate cultural differences in international business with nuance.
lessons.intro:
Business culture varies enormously between countries, and much of the variation is invisible until someone breaks an unwritten rule. How direct can you be in disagreement? How quickly is it acceptable to start negotiating? How important is small talk before the real conversation? Every culture answers these differently, and none of them are wrong.

The most useful attitude is curiosity over judgement. When something feels strange, assume there is a reason, and ask. In Japan, for example, silence at the table is significantly more comfortable than in Brazil. In Germany, a direct "this won't work" is far more acceptable than in the UK, where it would probably arrive as "I wonder if we might consider another angle."

Stereotypes have their limits. Every country has introverts and extroverts, direct people and diplomatic ones. Cultural awareness is a starting point, not a script. When in doubt, slow down, listen more, and trust the individual in front of you.

grammarDeepDive.title: Advanced Comparatives with Intensifiers
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In everyday English, we compare things with simple words like more and less. But in business English, especially when discussing cultures, markets and strategies, we need to be more precise. Instead of saying 'Japanese meetings are more formal', we can say 'Japanese meetings are significantly more formal'. The meaning is sharper, and the speaker sounds more confident and knowledgeable.

The main intensifiers are: far, significantly, considerably, noticeably, substantially, slightly, marginally. They go before the comparative: far more direct, significantly less common, considerably better. The word order is always intensifier + comparative — never the other way around. You cannot say 'more far direct'.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) explain that these intensifiers add degree to comparisons. Far and significantly indicate a big difference. Slightly and marginally indicate a small one. Choosing the right intensifier shows that you are thinking carefully about the size of the difference, which is exactly what cross-cultural communication requires.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 110: Comparative adjectives and adverbs with modifiers (much, far, a lot, significantly).
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 104: Much / far / a lot / slightly + comparative.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on 'far more', 'significantly', 'considerably' with usage examples in formal contexts.

examples.en: Cross-cultural training makes international negotiations substantially more effective.

commonMistakes.wrong: Japanese meetings are more far formal than Brazilian ones.
commonMistakes.right: Japanese meetings are far more formal than Brazilian ones.
commonMistakes.why: The intensifier (far) must come before the comparative (more formal), not between 'more' and the adjective.

commonMistakes.wrong: Germans are very more direct than the British.
commonMistakes.right: Germans are far more direct than the British.
commonMistakes.why: 'Very' does not combine with 'more'. Use 'far', 'much', or 'significantly' instead.

commonMistakes.wrong: The São Paulo office is significantly more informal as London.
commonMistakes.right: The São Paulo office is significantly more informal than London.
commonMistakes.why: Comparatives always use 'than', not 'as'. 'As...as' is for equal comparisons.

commonMistakes.wrong: Email response times are considerable less predictable.
commonMistakes.right: Email response times are considerably less predictable.
commonMistakes.why: Use the adverb form 'considerably' (not the adjective 'considerable') before a comparative.

commonMistakes.wrong: Trust is built significant faster face-to-face.
commonMistakes.right: Trust is built significantly faster face-to-face.
commonMistakes.why: The intensifier must be in adverb form (-ly) when modifying a comparative.

rolePlays.title: Cross-Cultural Negotiation in Tokyo
rolePlays.setup: James is meeting a Japanese sugar buyer for the first time in Tokyo. The Japanese team values formality, consensus and patience. James needs to present Czarnikow's offer while respecting the cultural context. The Japanese team will not say 'no' directly.
rolePlays.studentA: You are James. Present a sugar supply proposal politely. Respect the pace of the meeting. Use advanced comparatives to compare approaches ('Our London process is far more informal than what I understand is typical here...').
rolePlays.studentB: You are the Japanese buyer. Be polite but indirect. If you have concerns, express them with phrases like 'That is interesting, we will need to discuss internally' rather than 'no'. Ask one question about delivery timelines.
sampleDialogue: A: Thank you very much for receiving us today. I know meetings here tend to be significantly more structured than in our London office, so please guide me on the format.
B: Thank you, James. We appreciate that. Perhaps you could begin with your proposal.
A: Of course. We would like to offer a 12-month supply contract for raw sugar. The volumes are considerably larger than our previous arrangement.
B: That is interesting. The volumes are noticeably higher than we expected. We will need to discuss this internally with our team.
A: Absolutely. I understand decision-making here is far more consensus-driven, and we are happy to wait for your response.
B: Thank you. Could you tell us more about the delivery timeline?
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least two advanced comparatives (far more, significantly, considerably). Student A shows cultural sensitivity by acknowledging differences respectfully. Student B maintains an indirect communication style.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: After the first round, discuss: what did Student A do well culturally? What could they improve? Then swap roles. Emphasise that the goal is not to change who you are but to adapt your style to the audience.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — James reflects on cultural differences after a Tokyo meeting
additionalAudios.speaker: james
additionalAudios.transcript: That was a very different experience from our usual London meetings. The pace was significantly slower, which I actually found quite productive. Nobody interrupted. Silence was far more comfortable than I expected — they were thinking, not disengaging. I noticed the hierarchy was considerably more visible too. The most senior person spoke last, and everyone waited. I think we need to be substantially more patient in these negotiations than we would be in Europe.
tasks: Listen once without reading. Was James's overall impression positive or negative? (Answer: positive)
Listen again. Find four advanced comparatives James uses (significantly slower, far more comfortable, considerably more visible, substantially more patient).
Listen a third time. What surprised James most about the meeting? Write one sentence.
Pronunciation drill: repeat 'significantly slower' and 'considerably more visible' three times each.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — Sophie compares the London and São Paulo office cultures
additionalAudios.speaker: sophie
additionalAudios.transcript: Having worked with both offices, I can say the cultures are noticeably different. São Paulo is far more energetic and informal. People chat before meetings and the atmosphere is considerably warmer. London is more reserved, but that is not a bad thing — it is just different. I find that communication with Brazil needs to be slightly more personal to be effective. A quick call is far more appreciated than a formal email.
tasks: What two offices is Sophie comparing? (Answer: London and São Paulo)
According to Sophie, which office is more informal? (Answer: São Paulo)
Find three intensifiers Sophie uses with comparatives.
Do you agree with Sophie's comparison? Share your own experience in 2-3 sentences.

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, what is the most useful attitude when working across cultures?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Curiosity over judgement. When something feels strange, assume there is a reason and ask, rather than making assumptions.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say stereotypes have their limits?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because every country has different types of people — introverts and extroverts, direct and diplomatic ones. Cultural awareness is a starting point, not a complete script for how to deal with every individual.

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'far more direct' and not 'very more direct'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because 'very' does not combine with comparative forms. To intensify a comparative, we use words like 'far', 'much', 'significantly', 'considerably' or 'substantially'.

qAndA.question: How should a Czarnikow employee adapt their communication style when working with the Tokyo office versus the São Paulo office?
qAndA.modelAnswer: With Tokyo, they should be more formal, patient and indirect. Allow silence. Respect hierarchy. With São Paulo, they can be warmer, more personal and more informal. Building personal rapport first is important in Brazil.

qAndA.question: Why is cultural awareness especially important for a commodity trading company like Czarnikow?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because Czarnikow operates globally — buying sugar in Brazil, selling to buyers in Japan, Europe and the Middle East. Every deal involves cross-cultural communication, and misunderstandings can delay or lose business.

pairWork.title: Cultural comparison debate
pairWork.description: In pairs, each student picks a country they have done business with (or would like to). They take turns describing one cultural difference using an advanced comparative (e.g., 'Meetings in Germany are far more punctual than in Brazil'). The other student responds with a follow-up question or a counter-example. Continue for 4 rounds each. After both rounds, discuss: which comparison was the most surprising?

lessons.title: Data Storytelling
lessons.grammar: Describing trends — rose / fell / remained stable
lessons.objective: Turn data into clear, memorable business stories and charts.
lessons.intro:
A chart is not a story. A chart is raw material. The story is what you choose to say about it, and how you guide the audience through what matters.

Good data storytellers start with the message. They decide, before opening Excel, what they want the audience to conclude. Then they build the chart that supports that message in the cleanest, simplest way. Every colour, every axis label, every annotation serves the message or gets removed.

Numbers also need context to mean anything. "Sales grew 12 percent" sounds good until you discover the market grew 18 percent. Always provide the benchmark, the trend, or the comparison that makes the number interpretable. A number without context is noise dressed up as insight.

teacherGuide.overview: Lesson 97 teaches data storytelling — turning numbers and charts into clear, memorable business narratives. Grammar focus: trend verbs (rose, fell, remained stable, plateaued, peaked, recovered). By the end, the student should be able to describe business trends clearly and build a story around data at Czarnikow.

lessonFlow.instructions: Ask: when was the last time you presented data to someone? What was the main message? Let them describe the experience freely.
Read the intro aloud. Go through the 10 vocab words: student repeats each one and uses it in a sentence about Czarnikow data (sugar prices, freight costs, volumes).

Explain trend verbs and how to combine them with adverbs (sharply, steadily, gradually). Read the 12 examples aloud. Do the 5 gap-fills together. Review common mistakes (especially 'it raised' vs 'it rose').
Read the situation about Harry's board update. Do the Read Aloud and Describe the Trend exercises. Play Audio A once without reading, then again with the transcript.
Run the role play: presenting a data story to the board. Swap roles after the first round. Then do 2-3 of the Q&A questions orally.
Run the contextualization prompts. Student records a 60-second data story. End with the pair work exercise.

commonChallenges: Students often confuse 'rise' (intransitive — the price rose) with 'raise' (transitive — we raised the price). Drill both forms with clear examples.
Some students describe every data point instead of telling a story. Encourage them to pick the one message first, then select only the data that supports it.
Brazilian students may struggle with irregular past forms: rise/rose/risen, fall/fell/fallen. Create a quick reference card with the three forms of each trend verb.

grammarDeepDive.title: Describing Trends: Verbs, Adverbs and Narrative Structure
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When we present data in English, we use a specific set of trend verbs to describe what happened. The most important ones are: rose, fell, climbed, dropped, remained stable, plateaued, peaked, recovered, fluctuated. These verbs are intransitive — the subject does the action by itself. We say 'Sales rose', not 'Sales were risen'. The price rises; we do not rise the price (we raise it).

To make descriptions more precise, we add adverbs that describe the speed or size of the change: sharply, steadily, gradually, slightly, dramatically, significantly. The adverb usually comes after the verb: 'Costs fell sharply', 'Revenue grew steadily'. We can also use adjective + noun patterns: 'a sharp fall', 'a steady recovery'. Both structures are common in board presentations and quarterly reviews.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) cover irregular past tenses, which are essential for trend language. Rise/rose/risen, fall/fell/fallen, grow/grew/grown — these must be memorised because they appear in almost every data presentation. The key to good data storytelling is not just knowing the verbs but choosing the right verb and adverb combination to match the size and speed of the change you are describing.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 16: Past Simple of irregular verbs (rise/rose, fall/fell, grow/grew).
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 11: Past Simple (irregular verbs) and Appendix 1 (irregular verb list).
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on 'rise', 'fall', 'plateau', 'peak' with usage examples in financial and business contexts.

examples.en: Sugar prices rose sharply in Q1 due to the Brazilian harvest delay.
examples.pt: Os preços do açúcar subiram fortemente no Q1 devido ao atraso na safra brasileira.

commonMistakes.wrong: The price raised sharply in January.
commonMistakes.right: The price rose sharply in January.
commonMistakes.why: 'Raise' is transitive (we raise something). 'Rise' is intransitive (something rises by itself). Prices rise; companies raise prices.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sales were fallen by 10 percent.
commonMistakes.right: Sales fell by 10 percent.
commonMistakes.why: Trend verbs are active, not passive. Say 'Sales fell', not 'Sales were fallen'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Revenue growed steadily in Q2.
commonMistakes.right: Revenue grew steadily in Q2.
commonMistakes.why: 'Grow' is irregular: grow/grew/grown. There is no 'growed' form.

commonMistakes.wrong: Costs have been remained stable.
commonMistakes.right: Costs have remained stable.
commonMistakes.why: 'Remain' is intransitive and does not take a passive form. Use present perfect: 'have remained'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The chart shows a sharp raise in prices.
commonMistakes.right: The chart shows a sharp rise in prices.
commonMistakes.why: As a noun, 'rise' means an increase. 'Raise' as a noun means a salary increase (American English). For data trends, always use 'rise'.

rolePlays.title: Presenting a Quarterly Data Story to the Board
rolePlays.setup: Harry is presenting a three-slide quarterly update to the Czarnikow board. The data shows: sugar trading volumes rose 15% in Q1, plateaued in Q2, and recovered in Q3 after a mid-year dip. Freight costs fell sharply. One outlier month (March) needs explanation.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Harry. Present the data story in 2 minutes. Start with the main message, then walk through the trend. Explain the March outlier. Use at least four trend verbs.
rolePlays.studentB: You are a board member. Listen carefully. Ask one question about the Q2 plateau and one about the freight cost reduction.
sampleDialogue: A: Good morning, everyone. The headline is positive: trading volumes are up 15 percent year on year, and freight costs have fallen sharply.
B: Good to hear. Walk us through the detail.
A: In Q1, volumes rose strongly, driven by the Brazilian harvest. In Q2, they plateaued as we waited for new contracts. Then in Q3, volumes recovered after we signed two new supply agreements.
B: What happened in March? I noticed a spike in the chart.
A: Good question. The March outlier is explained by a one-off bulk order from a Japanese buyer. It is not part of the underlying trend.
B: And the freight costs — what drove the reduction?
A: Freight costs dropped significantly after we renegotiated our shipping contracts in April. We expect this saving to continue into next year.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least four different trend verbs (rose, plateaued, recovered, dropped, etc.). Student A explains the outlier clearly. Student B asks relevant follow-up questions.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Before starting, remind students: message first, data second. Run once, then swap roles. After each round, give feedback on verb variety and story clarity. If the student lists data points without a narrative, stop and ask: what is the one thing you want the board to remember?

In Q2, they plateaued around 21 cents as the market digested the Brazilian harvest news. Then in Q3, we saw a sharp fall to 18.5 cents after the Indian export quota was announced. Prices have since recovered to about 20 cents. The key message here is that despite the volatility, we remained profitable in every quarter because our hedging strategy worked.

Pronunciation drill: repeat 'rose steadily', 'sharp fall', and 'recovered to about 20 cents' three times each.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — Sophie summarises freight cost data for a report
additionalAudios.speaker: sophie

They started high in January at around 45 dollars per tonne, then fell gradually through Q1 and Q2 as new shipping capacity came online. By June, they had dropped to 32 dollars. In Q3, costs remained stable at around 30 to 33 dollars. The benchmark index fell by 8 percent over the same period, so we actually outperformed the market. Year on year, our freight spend is down 12 percent.

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, why is a chart not a story?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because a chart is raw material. The story is what you choose to say about it — which trend to highlight, what context to provide, and what message to deliver. Without interpretation, a chart is just data.

qAndA.question: Why does Harry remove two charts and keep only one for the board update?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because a focused presentation with one clear chart and one clear message is more powerful than multiple charts that compete for attention. Each element should serve the main message or be removed.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'rise' and 'raise' in data language?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'Rise' is intransitive — the price rises by itself. 'Raise' is transitive — someone raises the price. In data storytelling, we almost always use 'rise' because we are describing what the data did, not what someone did to it.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say 'a number without context is noise dressed up as insight'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because numbers only have meaning when compared to something — a benchmark, a previous period, a target. Saying 'sales grew 12 percent' sounds good, but if the market grew 18 percent, you actually underperformed. Context is what turns data into useful information.

qAndA.question: How can a Czarnikow analyst make a board presentation more effective using data storytelling?
qAndA.modelAnswer: By deciding the main message before building the chart, removing anything that does not support that message, providing context (benchmarks, trends, comparisons), and explaining any outliers. The board should walk away remembering one clear takeaway.

lessons.title: Leading Through Change
lessons.objective: Lead a team through organisational change with clear communication and empathy.
lessons.intro:
Most business change fails not because the idea was wrong, but because the humans involved were never brought along. The new process is explained in detail, while the emotional and practical impact on real people is treated as an afterthought. Unsurprisingly, the old habits come back within months.

Effective change leaders start by acknowledging the loss. Something is going away — a tool, a routine, a team, a status — and the people affected need to hear that loss recognised before they can embrace what comes next. Skipping that step almost always costs more time later.

They also communicate far more often than feels natural. In the absence of official updates, people invent their own versions of events, and those versions are usually worse than reality. Regular, honest communication is not reassurance theatre — it is how uncertainty is genuinely reduced.

grammarDeepDive.title: Sequencers and Discourse Markers
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Sequencers and discourse markers are words and phrases that help you organise what you say into a logical order. In business English, they are essential when you need to explain a plan, walk someone through a process, or deliver a message that has several parts. Without them, even a good message sounds like a random collection of ideas.

The most common sequencers are to start with, first of all, in the first place, secondly, on top of that, more importantly, in particular, furthermore, finally, and to sum up. Each one tells the listener where they are in the message: at the beginning, in the middle, or near the end. Think of them as road signs that keep the audience from getting lost.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) note that discourse markers do not change the grammar of a sentence — they sit at the front and connect ideas. The key is to use them naturally: one or two per paragraph is usually enough. Overloading a short email with five sequencers makes it feel robotic rather than structured.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units on linking words and discourse markers.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Appendix on connecting words and sequencing.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on 'to start with', 'furthermore', 'in particular' with usage notes.

commonMistakes.wrong: To start with the new model is better.
commonMistakes.right: To start with, the new model is better.
commonMistakes.why: Sequencers at the beginning of a sentence need a comma after them.

commonMistakes.wrong: Firstly, secondly, thirdly, fourthly, fifthly...
commonMistakes.right: First of all... On top of that... More importantly... Finally...
commonMistakes.why: Overusing numbered sequencers sounds robotic. Mix different types for a natural flow.

commonMistakes.wrong: In particular the freight team is affected.
commonMistakes.right: In particular, the freight team is affected.
commonMistakes.why: 'In particular' is a discourse marker and needs a comma when it opens a sentence.

commonMistakes.wrong: Finally I want to say more importantly we need time.
commonMistakes.right: Finally, I want to say that, more importantly, we need time.
commonMistakes.why: When stacking discourse markers, use commas to keep the sentence readable.

commonMistakes.wrong: To sum up, firstly we need training.
commonMistakes.right: To sum up, we need training first.
commonMistakes.why: 'To sum up' signals the end of a message — do not restart the sequence with 'firstly' inside a summary.

rolePlays.title: Communicating a Change to the Team
rolePlays.setup: James is announcing a new operating model to the Czarnikow sugar desk. The change affects daily workflows, reporting lines, and the tools people use. He needs to explain the 'why', acknowledge concerns, and outline next steps.
rolePlays.studentA: You are James. Use at least four sequencers to structure your message. Start by acknowledging the loss, then explain the reason, outline the phases, and end with a commitment to communicate.
rolePlays.studentB: You are a senior trader on the sugar desk. You are sceptical but open. Ask two questions: one about the timeline and one about how the team's feedback will be collected.
sampleDialogue: A: Good morning, everyone. To start with, I want to acknowledge that this change means losing some routines we all valued.
B: Thanks, James. Can I ask — what is the timeline for the first phase?
A: Of course. First of all, Phase 1 runs from January to March. On top of that, each team will have a champion to collect feedback weekly.
B: And how will our feedback actually reach the leadership team?
A: More importantly, that is exactly why we are running weekly check-ins. Finally, I promise you will hear from me every Friday with a written update.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least four different sequencers naturally. Student B asks relevant, professional questions.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run twice, swapping roles. After each round, highlight one well-used sequencer and suggest one that could replace a weaker connector.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — James announces the new operating model
additionalAudios.speaker: james
additionalAudios.transcript: Good morning, everyone. To start with, I want to be honest — this change is going to feel uncomfortable for a while. In the first place, the old model served us well for five years, and I respect that. On top of that, I know some of you were not consulted early enough last time. More importantly, this time will be different. We are rolling out in three phases, and your feedback will shape each one. Finally, I will send a written update every Friday. No silence, no surprises.

Secondly, the training sessions are all full, which is great. In particular, the freight team has been really engaged. To sum up, we are in a good place. Any questions, message me directly.

Which team has been especially engaged? (Answer: the freight team)

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, why does most business change fail?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because the people involved were never brought along. The emotional and practical impact on real people is treated as an afterthought.

qAndA.question: What should an effective change leader do before asking people to embrace the new?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Acknowledge the loss — recognise that something is going away (a tool, a routine, a team, a status) and that the people affected need to hear that recognised.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'more importantly' and 'on top of that'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'More importantly' signals that the next point matters more than the previous one. 'On top of that' simply adds another point without ranking it higher.

qAndA.question: Why does James promise to over-communicate rather than wait for questions?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because in the absence of official updates, people invent their own versions of events, and those are usually worse than reality. Regular communication reduces uncertainty.

qAndA.question: Think of a real change at your company. How would you structure a message about it using sequencers?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Open answer. The student should use at least three sequencers (e.g., 'To start with... On top of that... Finally...') and include an acknowledgement of what is being lost.

contextualization: Think of a time when a change at Czarnikow was communicated well. What made it effective?
If you had to announce a new system to the sugar desk, which sequencers would you use and why?
How does James's approach compare to how change is usually communicated in your experience?
What is one change at work you would handle differently now, after this lesson?

productionTasks.task: Present to your teacher, in 60-second announcing a change to your team. Use at least four sequencers. Include: an acknowledgement of the loss, the reason for the change, the timeline, and a promise to communicate regularly.

lessons.title: Building Long-Term Client Relationships
lessons.objective: Nurture client relationships beyond transactions, in line with Czarnikow's tradition.
lessons.intro:
Czarnikow has survived more than 160 years on one simple idea: long-term relationships. Transactions come and go; relationships, when genuinely invested in, compound over decades. The most durable client relationships rarely depend on the current contract — they depend on a quiet track record of doing what you said you would do, repeatedly.

A professional relationship is built in small moments. Answering a non-urgent email on a Friday evening because you know the client is stressed. Sharing an article you think might be useful, without expecting anything in return. Admitting quickly when something went wrong on your side, before the client discovers it elsewhere. None of these moments appear on a dashboard, but they are what clients remember five years later when a competitor calls.

A common mistake is to invest only when something is being negotiated. The best account managers stay in touch consistently, especially when nothing is on the table. That is precisely when trust is being quietly deposited, ready to be drawn on when it matters.

grammarDeepDive.title: Present Perfect for Long Relationships
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The Present Perfect is the tense you need when you want to talk about something that started in the past and is still true now. In business, this happens all the time: relationships that are still active, partnerships that are still running, clients you still work with. Whenever the past connects to the present, Present Perfect is the right choice.

The structure is straightforward: have / has + past participle. We use for to say how long something has lasted (for eight years) and since to say when it started (since 2016). Both answer the question 'how long?', but from different angles. If someone asks 'How long have you worked with that client?', you can answer either way: 'For eight years' or 'Since 2016'.

According to Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy), the key test is: is the situation still going on? If yes, use Present Perfect. If the situation ended, use Simple Past. Compare: 'I have worked at Czarnikow for ten years' (I still work there) vs 'I worked at Czarnikow for ten years' (I left). This distinction is crucial in professional contexts, because saying the wrong tense can imply a relationship has ended when it has not.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 13–15 on Present Perfect with for/since and unfinished time.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 7–8 (Present Perfect) and Unit 12 (Present Perfect vs Past Simple).
Cambridge Dictionary — entry on Present Perfect with usage notes for 'for' and 'since'.

commonMistakes.wrong: I know him since 2016.
commonMistakes.right: I have known him since 2016.
commonMistakes.why: 'Since 2016' means the situation started in the past and continues now — this requires Present Perfect, not Present Simple.

commonMistakes.wrong: We worked together for eight years. (if still working together)
commonMistakes.right: We have worked together for eight years.
commonMistakes.why: Simple Past ('worked') implies the relationship ended. Present Perfect ('have worked') means it is still ongoing.

commonMistakes.wrong: He has visited the client yesterday.
commonMistakes.right: He visited the client yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: 'Yesterday' is a finished time — use Simple Past, not Present Perfect. Present Perfect does not go with specific past times.

commonMistakes.wrong: We have been working together since eight years.
commonMistakes.right: We have been working together for eight years.
commonMistakes.why: 'Since' needs a point in time (since 2016); 'for' needs a duration (for eight years).

commonMistakes.wrong: Oliver has know the CEO for a decade.
commonMistakes.right: Oliver has known the CEO for a decade.
commonMistakes.why: After 'has/have', you must use the past participle: 'known', not 'know'.

lessons.title: Ethics, Compliance and Integrity
lessons.grammar: Modal verbs of obligation — must, shall, be expected to
lessons.objective: Discuss professional ethics and compliance with appropriate formal register.
lessons.intro:
Ethics at work are tested in small, ordinary moments far more often than in dramatic ones. A gift that feels slightly too generous. A question from a client about another client. A request to sign off on something you have not actually reviewed. These are the moments where integrity is quietly built or quietly lost.

Good companies make the right choice easier, by providing clear policies and safe channels to raise concerns. Good professionals make the right choice automatic, by deciding in advance what they will and will not do. "I don't accept gifts over £50" is much easier to say than "well, I'll think about it", because there is no thinking to do — the decision was already made.

Compliance is the legal minimum. Ethics is the private standard you hold yourself to when the legal minimum is clearly not enough. In the long run, clients can smell the difference, even when they cannot articulate it.

teacherGuide.overview: Lesson 100 of General Business Rise. Charlotte leads an annual compliance refresher using modal verbs of obligation (must, shall, be expected to). By the end, the student should distinguish between strict rules, formal/legal language, and professional norms.

lessonFlow.instructions: Ask: what is one rule at your company that everyone knows? Is it written down or just understood? Let the student talk freely.
Read the intro aloud. Go through the 10 vocab items. Student repeats each and uses it in a sentence about a real compliance situation.
Explain must vs shall vs are expected to. Read the 12 examples aloud. Do the 5 quick-practice exercises. Review the 5 common mistakes carefully.
Read the situation. Do the Read Aloud exercise. Do the Modal Choice exercise. Play Audio A, then Audio B. Check comprehension.
Run the role play twice, swapping roles. Then do 2–3 Q&A questions orally. Pay attention to whether students choose the right modal for each context.
Ask the 4 contextualisation prompts. Do the speaking production task. Finish by reading the 10 takeaway phrases aloud together.

commonChallenges: Students often use 'must' for everything. Help them see that 'are expected to' is softer (a professional norm, not a legal rule) and 'shall' is more formal/legal.
The negative 'must not' vs 'do not have to' is a classic confusion. 'Must not' = it is forbidden; 'do not have to' = it is not necessary. Drill with examples.
Some students feel uncomfortable discussing ethics in English. Use Charlotte's everyday examples (gifts, sign-offs) rather than dramatic scenarios to keep it approachable.

grammarDeepDive.title: Modal Verbs of Obligation — must, shall, be expected to
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In business English, we use modal verbs of obligation to talk about rules, duties and professional expectations. The three most important ones are must, shall, and be expected to. Each one carries a different weight, and choosing the right one tells the listener how serious the obligation is.

Must is the strongest. It means 'this is a firm rule — you have no choice'. We use it for policies, legal requirements, and zero-tolerance rules: Employees must disclose conflicts of interest. Shall appears in formal and legal documents — contracts, codes of conduct, compliance policies. It means roughly the same as 'must', but it sounds more official: The report shall be filed within seven days. Be expected to is softer. It describes a professional norm — what a good professional would do, even if it is not written in a rulebook: Managers are expected to lead by example.

Both Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) explain that understanding obligation modals is essential for professional communication. The key is register: must for hard rules, shall for legal or formal contexts, and be expected to for norms and best practice. Using the wrong one can make a suggestion sound like a command, or a legal requirement sound like a mere recommendation.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 17–19 on modal verbs of obligation and necessity.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 31–33 (must, have to, should) and modal verbs for obligation.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on 'must', 'shall', and 'be expected to' with register notes.

commonMistakes.wrong: You don't must accept gifts over £50.

commonMistakes.why: The negative of 'must' is 'must not' (forbidden). 'Don't must' does not exist in English.

commonMistakes.wrong: Employees should disclose conflicts of interest. (when it is a firm rule)
commonMistakes.right: Employees must disclose conflicts of interest.
commonMistakes.why: 'Should' is advice; 'must' is a rule. For legal and compliance requirements, use 'must'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The report must be filed within seven days. (in a legal contract)
commonMistakes.right: The report shall be filed within seven days.
commonMistakes.why: In formal legal documents, 'shall' is the standard choice, not 'must'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Managers must lead by example. (when it is a professional norm, not a rule)
commonMistakes.right: Managers are expected to lead by example.
commonMistakes.why: 'Must' sounds like a strict rule. 'Are expected to' describes a professional expectation that is not legally binding.

commonMistakes.why: 'Must not' means it is forbidden. 'Do not have to' means it is not necessary. These have opposite meanings.

rolePlays.title: Annual Compliance Refresher Session
rolePlays.setup: Charlotte is running the annual compliance refresher for the Czarnikow commercial team. She uses real, small examples — gifts, sign-offs, conflicts of interest — rather than dramatic scenarios. A team member asks about a specific grey area.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Charlotte. Present three key compliance rules using 'must', 'shall', and 'are expected to' appropriately. When the team member asks a question, answer clearly and explain the reasoning.
rolePlays.studentB: You are a trader on the commercial team. Listen to Charlotte's presentation and then ask about a specific situation: a client has invited you to a football match worth about £200. What should you do?
sampleDialogue: A: Good morning, everyone. Let's start with a quick reminder: all employees must disclose any conflict of interest in writing.
B: Charlotte, I have a question. A client has invited me to a football match. The tickets are worth about two hundred pounds.
A: Good question. Under our gift policy, you must not accept gifts worth more than fifty pounds. So you would need to politely decline.
B: What if I pay the difference myself?
A: That is a grey area. In cases like this, you are expected to speak to the compliance officer before accepting. The rule is: when in doubt, ask.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses 'must', 'shall', and 'are expected to' correctly in different contexts. Student B asks a relevant, specific question.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Encourage natural dialogue, not a lecture. After each round, check whether the student chose the right modal for each obligation type. Swap roles so both students practise being Charlotte.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Charlotte opens the compliance refresher
additionalAudios.speaker: charlotte
additionalAudios.transcript: Good morning, everyone. Welcome to the annual compliance refresher. I want to keep this practical, so let's use real examples. First: gifts. You must not accept gifts worth more than fifty pounds from any client or supplier. If someone offers you something, you are expected to politely decline and explain our policy. Second: conflicts of interest. Any conflict of interest shall be disclosed in writing within five working days. This is not optional — it is in our code of conduct. Third: whistleblowing. If you see something wrong, you must report it. All reports are treated with absolute confidentiality.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — A team member asks about a grey area
additionalAudios.speaker: james
additionalAudios.transcript: Charlotte, thanks for the refresher. I have a question about conferences. A client has offered to pay for my flights and hotel to attend an industry conference in Geneva. The total value is about two thousand pounds. I know I must not accept gifts over fifty pounds, but is a conference invitation the same as a gift? What am I expected to do here?

How much is the total value? (Answer: about two thousand pounds)
What rule does James reference? (Answer: must not accept gifts over fifty pounds)

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, where are ethics tested most often — in dramatic moments or ordinary ones?
qAndA.modelAnswer: In small, ordinary moments: a gift that feels too generous, a question about another client, a request to sign off on something you have not reviewed.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between compliance and ethics, as described in the lesson?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Compliance is the legal minimum. Ethics is the private standard you hold yourself to when the legal minimum is clearly not enough.

qAndA.question: When would you use 'shall' instead of 'must'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'Shall' is used in formal and legal contexts — contracts, codes of conduct, official policies. 'Must' is used for firm rules in everyday professional communication.

qAndA.question: Why does Charlotte use small, everyday examples in her compliance refresher instead of dramatic ones?
