lessons.title: Meetings That Move the Business
lessons.objective: Run high-stakes meetings with executive discipline and sharp facilitation.
lessons.intro:
The most expensive meetings in any organisation are the ones where nothing visibly goes wrong. Everyone turns up, speaks politely, and leaves with a warm feeling of alignment — which dissolves quietly over the following days, as each participant returns to their own interpretation of what was actually agreed.

The discipline that prevents this is unfashionable but effective. It is a clear, written pre-read circulated in advance, so the meeting can discuss, not inform. It is an explicit statement of what this particular meeting must decide, separated from what it cannot. And it is a tight close in which decisions, owners and dates are repeated aloud — not because the chair doubts the attention of the room, but because the act of saying them out loud turns implied consensus into actual commitment.

Skilled facilitators also manage the dynamics, not only the agenda. They notice who has not spoken, and create the gap for them. They interrupt the person who is drifting, gently but without apology. They pause when the air goes heavy, knowing that the most important sentence in the meeting is often the one no one wants to be the first to say.

grammarDeepDive.title: Cleft Sentences — It is… that… / What… is…
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Cleft sentences are one of the most powerful emphasis tools in formal English. They allow the speaker to take an ordinary sentence and split it into two clauses, placing maximum focus on the element that matters most. In business meetings, this is invaluable: when ten people are in the room and only one point matters, a cleft sentence forces attention onto exactly that point.

There are two main types. It-clefts use the structure It is/was + focused element + that/who + rest: 'It is the close of the meeting that decides whether anything was actually agreed.' Wh-clefts use What + clause + is/was + focused element: 'What really matters is who owns the decision afterwards.' Both achieve the same goal — emphasis — but it-clefts tend to sound more formal and wh-clefts more conversational.

In executive English, cleft sentences appear frequently in meeting summaries, board papers and strategic discussions because they force precision. Instead of a vague statement like 'several things matter', the speaker must choose which one thing to highlight. Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) both treat clefts as advanced-level structures that improve the clarity and authority of formal speech.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Unit on cleft sentences and emphasis structures.
Cambridge Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 40: It-clefts and wh-clefts for emphasis.
Cambridge Dictionary — Grammar entry on cleft sentences with business English examples.

commonMistakes.wrong: It is the close of the meeting what decides everything.
commonMistakes.right: It is the close of the meeting that decides everything.
commonMistakes.why: In it-clefts, use 'that' (or 'which/who'), never 'what'. 'What' starts wh-clefts only.

commonMistakes.wrong: What really matters are the owners and the dates.
commonMistakes.right: What really matters is the owners and the dates.
commonMistakes.why: The verb after the focused element in a wh-cleft is usually singular ('is'), even when the complement is plural.

commonMistakes.wrong: It is Oliver who chair the meeting.
commonMistakes.right: It is Oliver who chairs the meeting.
commonMistakes.why: The verb in the relative clause must agree with the focused noun — 'Oliver' is third person singular, so 'chairs'.

commonMistakes.wrong: What we need is to that everyone agrees.
commonMistakes.right: What we need is for everyone to agree.
commonMistakes.why: After 'what… is', use a noun phrase or infinitive construction, not a 'that' clause.

commonMistakes.wrong: It was the pre-read that it changed the discussion.
commonMistakes.right: It was the pre-read that changed the discussion.
commonMistakes.why: Do not repeat the subject pronoun inside the 'that' clause — the focused element already serves as the subject.

rolePlays.title: Chairing a Strategic Review Under Tension
rolePlays.setup: Oliver is chairing a strategic review meeting at Czarnikow. Two senior executives hold opposing views on a major investment in African logistics infrastructure. The room has gone quiet — the disagreement is real but no one wants to be the first to name it.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Oliver (the chair). Open the discussion, acknowledge the tension directly, create space for both sides, and close with clear decisions, owners and dates.
rolePlays.studentB: You are one of the two executives. Present your position firmly but professionally. When Oliver asks you to find common ground, offer one conditional concession.
sampleDialogue: A: Thank you, everyone. Before we continue, I want to name what is in the room. We have two clear positions on this investment, and it is important that we hear both fully before we decide.
B: Thank you, Oliver. My concern is that the capital commitment is front-loaded and the returns are uncertain for at least eighteen months.
A: Understood. What I would like us to do is separate the question of timing from the question of principle. Does anyone disagree with the strategic direction itself?
B: No — the direction is sound. It is the pace that concerns me.

A: Good. Then what we are really deciding today is the pace of deployment, not whether to proceed. Let me close with the decision: we proceed, but in two phases. Sarah owns Phase 1 delivery by Q3. We reconvene in eight weeks to review.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least two cleft sentences and closes with explicit decisions, owners and dates. Student B makes a clear conditional concession.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run it once; swap roles and run again. After each round, highlight one moment of strong facilitation and one area to sharpen.

qAndA.modelAnswer: A clear pre-read circulated in advance, an explicit statement of what the meeting must decide, and a tight close where decisions, owners and dates are repeated aloud.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between an it-cleft and a wh-cleft? Give one example of each.
qAndA.modelAnswer: An it-cleft uses 'It is/was + focus + that': 'It is the close that matters.' A wh-cleft uses 'What + clause + is + focus': 'What matters is the close.' Both add emphasis but it-clefts sound more formal.

lessons.title: Executive Writing and Communication
lessons.objective: Write at the level of expectation for a senior audience: dense, precise, economical.
lessons.intro:
Senior readers share a common habit: they read everything quickly and trust almost nothing. Their experience has taught them that most corporate prose is either too optimistic, too vague, or both. A well-written executive memo earns attention by violating those defaults — offering precision where others offer generality, and intellectual honesty where others offer reassurance.

The craft is mostly subtractive. Remove phrases that add no information. Remove qualifiers that exist to soften uncomfortable truths. Remove headings that only rename the sections below. What remains should be dense enough that every sentence rewards the thirty seconds of attention it receives from a senior reader between other meetings.

There is also a discipline of clarity about uncertainty. Great executive writers do not pretend to know more than they do — but they do not hide what they know behind hedged language either. They distinguish between what the data shows, what we believe, and what we are guessing, and label each clearly. That alone is enough to earn the ear of most senior audiences for a career.

grammarDeepDive.title: Nominal Style for Formal Prose
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Nominal style is the backbone of formal business writing. Instead of relying on verbs to carry meaning, nominal style shifts the weight to nouns and noun phrases. Compare 'We reduced operating costs' (verbal) with 'The reduction of operating costs' (nominal). The second version sounds more formal, more detached, more authoritative — exactly the register that senior readers expect in board papers, strategy memos and executive summaries.

The transformation follows a simple pattern: take the verb and turn it into its noun form. Reduce → reduction. Accelerate → acceleration. Decide → decision. Deteriorate → deterioration. The resulting noun phrase can then serve as the subject of a new, denser sentence: 'The acceleration of the commercial pipeline is now the team's primary objective.' This packs more information into fewer words, which is exactly what a busy executive wants.

The danger of nominal style is over-use. A paragraph composed entirely of noun phrases becomes impenetrable. The best executive writers use nominal style for the key ideas — the ones that need to feel weighty and permanent — and keep supporting sentences in active, verbal style for readability. Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) discusses nominalisation in the context of formal register, while Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) covers it under word formation and advanced sentence structure.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Sections on nominalisation and formal register.
Cambridge Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Units on word formation and noun phrases in formal writing.
Cambridge Dictionary — Usage notes on nominal style and academic/business register.

commonMistakes.wrong: The costs were reduced by the team in a significant manner.
commonMistakes.right: The reduction of costs was significant.
commonMistakes.why: Avoid weak passive + adverbial phrase. Nominalise the verb and let the noun carry the weight.

commonMistakes.wrong: The acceleration of the pipeline was done by us.
commonMistakes.right: The acceleration of the pipeline required cross-desk coordination.
commonMistakes.why: 'Was done by us' is a weak passive. Replace with a stronger verb that adds real information.

commonMistakes.wrong: There was a decision to restructure the team.
commonMistakes.right: The decision to restructure the team followed a quarter of underperformance.
commonMistakes.why: Avoid empty 'there was' constructions. Make the nominal phrase the subject and add meaningful context.

commonMistakes.wrong: The reduction of the operating costs and the acceleration of the commercial pipeline and the resilience of the supply chain.
commonMistakes.right: Three factors converged: cost reduction, pipeline acceleration, and supply-chain resilience.
commonMistakes.why: Stacking too many nominals kills readability. Use a framing sentence and a list.

commonMistakes.wrong: We did the assessment of the credit.
commonMistakes.right: The assessment of credit exposure was completed last Friday.
commonMistakes.why: 'Did the assessment' is verbal disguised as nominal. Commit fully to the nominal style or stay verbal.

rolePlays.title: Editing a Strategy Paper for the Board
rolePlays.setup: Charlotte has drafted a five-page strategy paper on Czarnikow's sugar sourcing in West Africa. James, the board sponsor, has asked her to cut it to two pages before the board meets on Thursday. They are reviewing the draft together.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Charlotte. Present one paragraph of your draft and explain why you think it is already tight enough.
rolePlays.studentB: You are James. Identify two sentences that add no information and suggest how to compress the paragraph using nominal style.
sampleDialogue: A: James, here is the opening paragraph. I think it sets the context well — the market has shifted, sourcing options have changed, and the team has been working on alternatives.

B: Charlotte, the first two sentences are context the board already knows. What if we start with the third sentence — 'The shift towards sustainable sourcing in West Africa has opened three new supply corridors' — and let that carry the argument?
A: Fair point. And I can nominalise the team's work: 'The identification of three new corridors by the sourcing team now offers the board a genuine choice.'
B: Better. Dense, precise, and it respects their time. Every sentence earns its place.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least two nominal constructions. Student B identifies specific sentences to cut and explains why. Both maintain a professional, collaborative tone.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run once with current roles; swap and run again. Encourage the 'editor' to be specific — not 'this is too long' but 'this sentence adds no information because…'.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Charlotte reads her edited paragraph
additionalAudios.speaker: charlotte
additionalAudios.transcript: The shift towards sustainable sourcing in West Africa has opened three new supply corridors for Czarnikow. The identification of these corridors by the sourcing team, combined with the reduction of logistics costs through the new Abidjan hub, now offers the board a genuine strategic choice. The recommendation is to proceed with corridor two, which offers the strongest combination of volume reliability and margin protection. The risk — and it is a real one — is that corridor two depends on a single port facility that has no proven track record above fifty thousand tonnes per quarter.
tasks: Listen once without reading. What is Charlotte's recommendation? (Answer: proceed with corridor two)
Listen again. Count the number of nominal phrases Charlotte uses. (Expected: at least 5)
Listen a third time. Find the sentence where Charlotte labels a risk. Why does she say 'and it is a real one'?
Rewrite one of Charlotte's nominal phrases in verbal style. Which version is better for a board paper? Why?

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — James gives feedback on density
additionalAudios.speaker: james
additionalAudios.transcript: Charlotte, this is much tighter. Two observations. First, the opening sentence does real work — it tells the board something new. Good. Second, the risk sentence is honest, which is exactly what this audience needs. One small edit: 'the combination of volume reliability and margin protection' could be compressed to 'the reliability-margin balance'. Every word you save buys the board another second of attention.
tasks: What two things does James praise? (Answer: the opening sentence tells the board something new; the risk sentence is honest)
What edit does James suggest? (Answer: compress 'combination of volume reliability and margin protection' to 'reliability-margin balance')
Why does James say 'every word you save buys the board another second of attention'? Do you agree?
Find one nominal phrase in James's feedback and rewrite it in verbal style.

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, what do senior readers share as a common habit?
qAndA.modelAnswer: They read everything quickly and trust almost nothing. Their experience has taught them that most corporate prose is either too optimistic, too vague, or both.

qAndA.question: What three categories should executive writers distinguish between when writing about uncertainty?
qAndA.modelAnswer: What the data shows, what we believe, and what we are guessing. Each should be labelled clearly.

qAndA.question: What is nominal style and when should you use it?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Nominal style shifts meaning from verbs to nouns: 'reduce' becomes 'the reduction of'. It is used in formal writing — board papers, strategy memos, executive summaries — to create density and authority.

qAndA.question: Why does the intro say the craft of executive writing is 'mostly subtractive'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because the biggest improvement in executive writing comes from removing what does not add information — unnecessary qualifiers, vague phrases, headings that rename sections. What remains is denser and more respected.

qAndA.question: The intro says great executive writers 'do not hide what they know behind hedged language.' How does this differ from epistemic modesty?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Epistemic modesty means honestly labelling what you do not know. Hedged language used defensively means softening what you do know to avoid accountability. The first is a virtue; the second is a waste of the reader's time.

contextualization: Find a real email or memo you wrote recently at Czarnikow. Identify one sentence that could be compressed using nominal style. Read both versions aloud — which sounds more executive?
Think about the last board paper or strategy document you read. Was it too long? What would you cut? Describe your edits in 30 seconds in English.
Write one sentence in nominal style about a real Czarnikow project you are involved in. Then write the same idea in verbal style. Which is better for your audience?

Describe in English: what is the difference between a qualifier that is honest ('we estimate') and one that is defensive ('it could potentially be argued that')? Give one example of each from your work.

lessons.title: Strategic Calls and Executive Presence
lessons.objective: Run executive calls with composure, pace and deliberate presence.
lessons.intro:
Executive presence on a call is a learned discipline, not a personality trait. It shows in small signals: the speed at which someone speaks in contested moments, the length of the pause before they answer a hostile question, the choice to wait ten more seconds before typing an immediate response in the chat.

At the most senior level, calls tend to be shorter, sharper and more consequential than regular meetings. A single well-placed sentence can shift a quarter's priorities. A single careless phrase can take weeks to recover from. Experienced executives prepare for difficult calls in advance — not the content, which they already know, but the stance: where they will hold ground, where they will genuinely concede, and what they want the others to walk away thinking about.

Language carries unusual weight in this register. Passive constructions, conditional forms and diplomatic hedging are used surgically, not defensively. "That would be a difficult position to defend at board level" communicates the same message as "I disagree", but leaves the other person with an exit and the speaker with their credibility intact.

vocab.example: In sugar trading, executive presence often decides the outcome of a trade desk.
The trader had to hold ground the sugar contract under pressure.
The team will concede the harvest report before the client call.
Czarnikow's analyst team highlighted the role of stance in every deal.
In sugar trading, diplomatic hedging often decides the outcome of a trade desk.
We reviewed composure before finalising the cargo.
Czarnikow's freight deal highlighted the role of contested moment in every deal.
The trader had to signal the cargo under pressure.
Her feedback on the harvest report was calibrated and well received.
The team discussed with gravity during the risk committee review.

teacherGuide.overview: Apex-level lesson on executive presence during strategic calls. Grammar focus: advanced discourse signalling. By the end, the student should be able to navigate a contested executive call with composure, using discourse markers to control tone and direction.

lessonFlow.instructions: Ask: have you ever been on a call where someone said something careless and it took weeks to recover? What happened? Let the student describe it freely.
Read the intro aloud together. Go through the 10 vocab items. The student uses each in a sentence about a real or imagined executive call at Czarnikow.

Explain advanced discourse signalling — markers that shift tone, concede ground, or redirect without losing authority. Read the 12 examples aloud. Do the 5 quick-practice gap-fills. Review common mistakes, especially overusing 'with all due respect'.
Read the situation. Do the Read Aloud and the 10-item discourse marker exercise. Play Audio A once without transcript, then with. Check answers.
Run the role play — a contested call between two offices. Swap roles after the first round. Highlight moments where discourse markers were used well or missed. Then do 2–3 Q&A questions orally.
Ask the 4 contextualisation prompts. Do the speaking production task. Finish by reading the 10 takeaway phrases aloud together.

commonChallenges: Students often use discourse markers mechanically ('with all due respect' before every sentence). Teach variety — cycle through different markers and explain when each fits.
Some students confuse 'executive presence' with 'speaking loudly'. Emphasise that presence comes from pace, pause and deliberate word choice, not volume.
The concept of 'pre-deciding non-negotiables' is new to some students. Use a concrete Czarnikow example (e.g., payment terms on a large contract) to make it tangible.

grammarDeepDive.title: Advanced Discourse Signalling
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Discourse markers are the invisible architecture of executive conversation. They signal to the listener what is about to happen: a shift in position, a concession, a challenge, or a reinforcement. Without them, senior conversation sounds abrupt or clumsy. With them, even strong disagreement can land with precision and professionalism.

At the apex level, discourse markers are not filler — they are strategic. 'That said' signals a shift: I have acknowledged your point, and now I am about to qualify it. 'In all candour' signals honesty: what follows is uncomfortably direct. 'If I may' signals a polite interruption. 'With the greatest respect' signals disagreement without personal attack. Each marker sets the listener's expectation before the main message arrives, giving them time to receive it without defensiveness.

The skill is in matching the marker to the moment. Overuse of any single marker — especially 'with all due respect', which has become a cliche for 'I disagree' — erodes credibility. The best executives vary their markers naturally, the way a skilled writer varies sentence length. Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) covers discourse markers under spoken grammar and linking devices, while Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) discusses them in the context of formal and semi-formal conversation.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Sections on discourse markers, linking devices, and spoken grammar.
Cambridge Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Units on discourse markers in formal and semi-formal contexts.
Cambridge Dictionary — Entries on discourse markers with usage notes for formal business English.

commonMistakes.wrong: With all due respect, you are completely wrong.
commonMistakes.right: With the greatest respect, I see the situation differently.
commonMistakes.why: 'With all due respect' followed by a blunt attack sounds sarcastic. Use a softer marker and a diplomatic alternative.

commonMistakes.wrong: That said, that said, I also think we should consider...
commonMistakes.right: That said, I also think we should consider...
commonMistakes.why: Repeating a discourse marker weakens it. Use each marker once, then vary.

commonMistakes.wrong: In all candour, maybe the numbers might possibly not quite support this.
commonMistakes.right: In all candour, the numbers do not support this.
commonMistakes.why: 'In all candour' promises directness. If you hedge immediately after, the marker loses its power.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I may, I completely disagree with everything you said.
commonMistakes.right: If I may, I would like to challenge one specific point.
commonMistakes.why: 'If I may' signals politeness. Following it with a blanket rejection is contradictory.

commonMistakes.wrong: To be fair, I am right and they are wrong.
commonMistakes.right: To be fair, both sides have valid reasons.
commonMistakes.why: 'To be fair' signals balance. Using it to claim victory defeats the purpose of the marker.

rolePlays.title: A Contested Call Between Two Offices
rolePlays.setup: Emily is mediating a call between the London sugar desk and the São Paulo office. London wants to reduce the credit line to a Brazilian counterparty; São Paulo argues the relationship is critical and the risk is manageable. Emily has pre-decided that the credit line will be reduced, but she wants both sides to feel heard.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Emily. Open the call, acknowledge both positions using discourse markers, steer the conversation towards the decision you have already made, and close with a clear outcome.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the São Paulo desk head. Present your case firmly, using at least two discourse markers to soften your disagreement with London's position.
sampleDialogue: A: Thank you both for joining. I know this is a sensitive topic, and I want both sides to feel they have been heard. Let me start by saying — in all candour — that the credit committee has concerns.

B: Emily, if I may — I understand the concern, but the relationship with this counterparty is worth more than the headline number suggests. That said, I accept that the exposure needs tighter monitoring.
A: I take your point, and I appreciate the honesty. With the greatest respect to both sides, here is what I propose: we reduce the line by thirty per cent, with a formal review in sixty days.
B: That notwithstanding, I would ask that we protect the Q4 shipments already in the pipeline.
A: Agreed. The reduction applies to new exposure only. Sophie will circulate the revised terms by end of day.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three different discourse markers and closes with a clear decision. Student B uses at least two discourse markers and makes one conditional concession.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run once, then swap roles. After each round, identify the most effective discourse marker each student used and explain why it worked in that moment.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Emily opens a contested call
additionalAudios.speaker: emily
additionalAudios.transcript: Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for making time at short notice. I know there are strong views on both sides, and I want to make sure we have an honest conversation today. In all candour, the credit committee has flagged this exposure as a concern. That said, I also recognise the commercial value of the relationship. What I would like us to do is separate the risk question from the relationship question, and address each on its own merits. London, would you like to go first?
tasks: Listen once without reading. What does Emily ask the group to separate? (Answer: the risk question from the relationship question)
Listen again with the transcript. Identify all discourse markers Emily uses.
Why does Emily say 'in all candour' before mentioning the credit committee's concern? What tone does it set?
Pronunciation drill: repeat Emily's opening three sentences. Focus on the pace — slow and deliberate, not rushed.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — The São Paulo desk pushes back
additionalAudios.speaker: oliver
additionalAudios.transcript: Emily, if I may — the São Paulo desk has worked with this counterparty for seven years. To be perfectly fair, the risk has always been managed within limits. On the other hand, I accept that the current exposure is higher than usual. What I would propose is a phased reduction, not a cliff edge. That preserves the relationship and addresses the committee's concern at the same time.
tasks: How many discourse markers does the São Paulo desk head use? (Answer: 3 — 'if I may', 'to be perfectly fair', 'on the other hand')
What compromise does he propose? (Answer: a phased reduction, not a cliff edge)
Why does he say 'to be perfectly fair' before defending his position? What is the strategic effect?
Rewrite his proposal without any discourse markers. Compare: which version is more persuasive in an executive call?

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, what three things do experienced executives prepare before a difficult call?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Where they will hold ground, where they will genuinely concede, and what they want the others to walk away thinking about.

qAndA.question: What does the intro mean by 'passive constructions and diplomatic hedging are used surgically, not defensively'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: It means that at senior level, indirect language is used deliberately and precisely to achieve a specific effect — not to avoid saying something uncomfortable, but to say it in a way that preserves the other person's dignity and the speaker's credibility.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'that said' and 'that notwithstanding'? When would you use each?
qAndA.modelAnswer: 'That said' is slightly more conversational and is used after acknowledging a point to introduce a qualification. 'That notwithstanding' is more formal and is used after accepting a point to introduce a stronger counterargument or condition.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say 'a hedged sentence can be stronger than a blunt one'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because a hedged sentence like 'that would be a difficult position to defend at board level' communicates disagreement while leaving the other person an exit. A blunt 'I disagree' forces confrontation. The hedged version is stronger because it achieves the goal — changing the other person's mind — without triggering defensiveness.

qAndA.question: Emily has pre-decided the outcome of the call. Is it ethical to let both sides 'feel heard' when the decision is already made?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Yes, if the pre-decision is based on sound analysis and the conversation could genuinely change it if new information emerges. The process of hearing both sides validates the decision, surfaces any missing information, and ensures the losing side feels respected — which matters for long-term relationships.

contextualization: Think of a recent call at Czarnikow where someone disagreed with you. Replay the moment in English, but this time use a discourse marker to soften your response. Say it aloud.

Pre-decide your non-negotiables for an upcoming Czarnikow discussion. State them aloud in English: 'I will not move on…' and 'I am willing to concede on…'
Practise three different discourse markers in response to the same challenge: 'Your timeline is unrealistic.' Say each version aloud and notice how the tone changes.

productionTasks.task: Present to your teacher, in 60-second of yourself responding to a hostile question on an executive call. pairWork.title: Diplomatic disagreement drill

lessons.title: Board-Level Presentations
lessons.objective: Present to board-level audiences with rigour, concision and authority.
lessons.intro:
Presenting to a board is not the same activity as presenting to a team, however similar the slides may look. A board audience has, collectively, hundreds of years of business experience; seen dozens of similar stories before; and developed a near-infallible sense for when a presenter is overclaiming, hiding something, or simply out of their depth.

The mistake many senior presenters make is to treat board time as if it were classroom time — walking the audience through what they already know, before arriving at the actual question. Board members almost always want to start where the presenter wants to finish. State the recommendation in the first two minutes. Explain the reasoning, compactly, across the next eight. Leave generous room for questions, which is where the real conversation happens.

Rarely is a board won over by enthusiasm; still more rarely by defensiveness. What tends to earn their trust is the presenter's willingness to name the uncomfortable facts themselves, before any board member can do so. A presenter who opens with "There are three things that might worry you, and I would like to address each directly" instantly changes the dynamic in the room.

teacherGuide.overview: Apex-level lesson on board-level presentations at Czarnikow. Grammar focus: inversion for emphasis. By the end, the student should be able to present to a board with authority, using inverted structures to control emphasis and front-running difficult questions.

lessonFlow.instructions: Ask: have you ever presented to a very senior audience? What was the hardest part? If not, what do you imagine would be hardest? Let the student reflect freely.
Read the intro aloud together. Go through the 10 vocab items. The student uses each in a sentence about presenting at Czarnikow.

Explain inversion for emphasis — rarely, only, not only, never, seldom, hardly. Read the 12 examples aloud. Do the 5 quick-practice inversions. Review common mistakes, especially forgetting to invert the auxiliary.
Read the situation. Do the Read Aloud and the 10-item inversion exercise. Play Audio A once without transcript, then with. Check answers.
Run the role play: a board presentation followed by tough questions. Swap roles. After each round, note one moment where inversion was used effectively. Then do 2–3 Q&A questions.
Ask the 4 contextualisation prompts. Do the speaking production task. Finish by reading the 10 takeaway phrases aloud together.

commonChallenges: Inversion feels unnatural to most students at first. Drill the pattern 'Rarely + auxiliary + subject + main verb' several times before expecting fluent production.
Students often want to walk the board through context before the recommendation. Train them to state the recommendation first, then support it — the opposite of their instinct.
Some students confuse 'front-running difficult questions' with 'being negative'. Explain that owning the risks builds credibility; ignoring them destroys it.

grammarDeepDive.title: Inversion for Emphasis
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Inversion is one of the most striking emphasis tools in English. In normal word order, the subject comes before the auxiliary verb: 'We have rarely faced this.' In inverted order, the auxiliary moves before the subject: 'Rarely have we faced this.' The effect is immediate — the sentence sounds more formal, more dramatic, and more authoritative. In a boardroom, this is exactly the register that commands attention.

Inversion is triggered by certain negative or restrictive adverbs placed at the beginning of a sentence: rarely, seldom, never, only, not only, hardly, no sooner, at no point, under no circumstances. When any of these opens the sentence, the auxiliary verb must come before the subject. If there is no auxiliary, do/does/did is added: 'Only by owning the risks does the presenter earn the board's trust.'

The power of inversion in presentations is that it allows the speaker to front-load the emphasis. Instead of burying the key idea at the end of a sentence, inversion places it at the very beginning — where a board member's attention is at its sharpest. Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) covers inversion under emphasis and word order, while Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) discusses it in the context of formal written and spoken English.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Units on inversion, emphasis, and formal word order.
Cambridge Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 41: Inversion after negative adverbs.
Cambridge Dictionary — Grammar entry on inversion with examples of formal and emphatic usage.

rolePlays.title: Presenting a Capital Allocation Recommendation to the Board
rolePlays.setup: James is presenting a recommendation to allocate capital to a new West African logistics corridor. The board is sceptical — they have seen similar proposals fail. James decides to open with the three things he expects to be challenged on.
rolePlays.studentA: You are James. Open with your recommendation (not background). Name the three risks upfront. Use at least two inverted sentences for emphasis. Close with a clear ask.
rolePlays.studentB: You are a board member. Ask two tough questions — one about the downside scenario and one about the timeline. Challenge James on specifics, not generalities.
sampleDialogue: A: Thank you, Chair. My recommendation is that we allocate forty million to the new Abidjan corridor, in two phases. Before I explain the reasoning, I want to name the three things that should concern you. First, the port facility has never handled volume above fifty thousand tonnes. Second, the local regulatory environment is uncertain. Third, the return profile depends on sugar prices holding above sixteen cents.
B: James, what happens if prices drop below sixteen cents in the first year?

A: If prices fall below sixteen cents, the corridor remains operationally viable but the margin drops below our hurdle rate. Rarely have we committed capital to a project with this level of price sensitivity — I want to be honest about that.
B: And the timeline? You said two phases, but the board has seen phased commitments slip before.

A: That is exactly why I am recommending a hard gate between Phase 1 and Phase 2. Only after Phase 1 delivers on three specific KPIs do we commit to Phase 2. The gate protects the board's optionality.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A states the recommendation in the first 30 seconds, names risks before being asked, and uses at least two inverted structures. Student B asks specific, challenging questions.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run once; swap roles. After each round, note whether the presenter front-ran the tough questions or waited to be challenged. The first is the target behaviour.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — James opens a board presentation
additionalAudios.speaker: james
additionalAudios.transcript: Thank you, Chair. My recommendation is that we proceed with the Abidjan corridor investment, phased over two years. I want to start with the three things that might worry you. First, the port has never handled this volume. Second, the regulatory landscape is still developing. Third, our return model is price-sensitive below sixteen cents. Rarely have we brought a case to this board with so many open variables — and I would not bring it unless I believed the opportunity justified them. Not only does this corridor open a new supply route; it also reduces our concentration risk in Brazil by twenty per cent.

Listen again. Find the two inverted sentences James uses. Write them down.
Why does James name the three risks before the board asks? What effect does this have on his credibility?
Pronunciation drill: repeat James's first three sentences. Focus on sounding authoritative but calm.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — A board member challenges the timeline
additionalAudios.speaker: charlotte
additionalAudios.transcript: James, I appreciate the honesty about the risks. My concern is the timeline. Seldom have we seen phased commitments delivered on schedule in frontier markets. What gives you confidence that Phase 1 will hit its KPIs? And if it does not, at what point do we write this off? I would rather hear an uncomfortable answer now than discover a problem in Q4.

qAndA.question: According to the lesson, what mistake do many senior presenters make when presenting to a board?
qAndA.modelAnswer: They treat board time like classroom time — walking the audience through what they already know before arriving at the actual question. Board members want to start where the presenter wants to finish.

qAndA.question: What does James do in the first two minutes of his presentation, and why?
qAndA.modelAnswer: He states his recommendation and names the three risks upfront. This front-runs the board's likely challenges and earns credibility by showing he is not hiding anything.

qAndA.question: Explain the grammatical structure of 'Rarely have we faced a decision this big.' Why does 'have' come before 'we'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: This is subject-auxiliary inversion triggered by the negative adverb 'rarely' at the beginning of the sentence. When a negative or restrictive adverb opens the sentence, the auxiliary verb must precede the subject for emphasis.

qAndA.question: The intro says 'a board has, collectively, hundreds of years of business experience.' How should this change the way you prepare a presentation?
qAndA.modelAnswer: You should assume the board already knows the context and background. Spend your time on the recommendation, the reasoning, and the risks — not on educating them. Show respect for their experience by being concise and honest.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say 'enthusiasm rarely wins a board'? What does win them?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because board members are experienced enough to be sceptical of enthusiasm without substance. What wins them is rigour — clear reasoning, honest risk assessment, and the willingness to name uncomfortable facts before being asked.

lessons.title: High-Stakes Negotiation
lessons.grammar: Subjunctive — were I to, should it, had we
lessons.objective: Navigate high-stakes negotiations with strategic patience and sophisticated language.
lessons.intro:
High-stakes negotiation is, above all, a test of emotional self-regulation. The commercial stakes, the political stakes and sometimes the personal stakes combine to produce a pressure that lesser negotiators cannot quite think clearly through. The edge belongs to whoever can remain thoughtful when everyone else, including themselves, is being pulled by urgency.

Experienced negotiators prepare for three different worlds before a significant meeting: the best realistic outcome, the worst acceptable one, and the walk-away point beyond which no deal is better than the deal on offer. Knowing those three in advance makes it far easier to decide, in the room, whether a difficult concession moves them towards or away from acceptable. Those who negotiate without that clarity end up conceding in the direction of the other side's energy, rather than their own interests.

Language in these moments is surgical. "Were we to accept those terms, we would need a corresponding shift on payment" carries more precision than "we want a better deal". Conditional and subjunctive forms create cognitive room to trade without publicly committing. They are the quiet tools of people who close complicated deals.

grammarDeepDive.title: Subjunctive and Inverted Conditionals — Were I to, Should It, Had We
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The subjunctive mood and its inverted conditional forms are among the most sophisticated structures in English. They allow the speaker to explore hypothetical scenarios with precision and formality — exactly what is needed in high-stakes negotiation, where every word carries commercial weight. Instead of the everyday 'If we accepted those terms…', the inverted form 'Were we to accept those terms…' sounds more deliberate, more measured, and more powerful.

There are three main patterns. Were + subject + to + verb replaces 'If + subject + past tense' for present/future hypotheticals: 'Were I to accept, I would need…' Should + subject + verb replaces 'If + subject + present tense' for formal conditionals about possible future events: 'Should the price hold, the picture changes.' Had + subject + past participle replaces 'If + subject + had + past participle' for past hypotheticals: 'Had we known earlier, the strategy would have been different.'

In negotiation, these forms serve a specific strategic purpose: they allow the speaker to propose, counter-propose and explore trade-offs without publicly committing to any position. 'Were we to extend the contract by two years, we would need a corresponding improvement in margins' is not a commitment — it is an exploration. That cognitive room is what makes complex deals possible. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy) classify these as advanced conditional forms used primarily in formal, written, or highly educated spoken English.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar — Advanced (John Eastwood) — Units on conditionals, subjunctive mood, and formal inversion.
Cambridge Grammar in Use — Advanced (Raymond Murphy) — Units 38–39: Conditionals with inversion (were, had, should).
Cambridge Dictionary — Grammar entry on subjunctive mood and inverted conditionals with formal usage examples.

commonMistakes.wrong: Was I to accept those terms, I would need a concession.
commonMistakes.right: Were I to accept those terms, I would need a concession.
commonMistakes.why: The subjunctive always uses 'were', never 'was', regardless of the subject — even with 'I'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Were we to accept those terms, we will need a concession.
commonMistakes.right: Were we to accept those terms, we would need a concession.
commonMistakes.why: The result clause of a hypothetical condition uses 'would', not 'will'. 'Will' implies certainty; 'would' maintains the hypothetical.

commonMistakes.wrong: Should the price will hold above sixteen cents...
commonMistakes.right: Should the price hold above sixteen cents...
commonMistakes.why: After 'should' in an inverted conditional, use the bare infinitive. No 'will' is needed — 'should' already carries the conditional meaning.

commonMistakes.wrong: Had we knew about this earlier, the strategy would be different.
commonMistakes.right: Had we known about this earlier, the strategy would have been different.
commonMistakes.why: After 'had', use the past participle ('known'), not the simple past ('knew'). The result clause needs 'would have been', not 'would be'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Were we accepting those terms, we would need changes.
commonMistakes.right: Were we to accept those terms, we would need changes.
commonMistakes.why: The subjunctive inversion uses 'were + to + base verb', not 'were + -ing'. The -ing form sounds like a description of an ongoing action, not a hypothesis.

rolePlays.title: Negotiating a Five-Year Sugar Contract
rolePlays.setup: Oliver is negotiating a five-year commercial contract worth several hundred million with a major Brazilian sugar producer. Czarnikow wants volume certainty; the producer wants price protection. Oliver has pre-decided his walk-away point: no deal is better than a deal with payment terms longer than 90 days.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Oliver (Czarnikow). Open by anchoring on a five-year commitment with quarterly pricing reviews. Use subjunctive forms to explore trade-offs without committing. Remain the calmest person in the room.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the Brazilian producer's head of commercial. Push for annual pricing with a floor. Make one conditional concession on volume in exchange for payment terms.
sampleDialogue: A: Thank you for making time today. I would like to start by exploring a structure. Were we to commit to a five-year volume guarantee, would you be open to quarterly pricing reviews linked to the market?
B: Oliver, five years is attractive. But quarterly pricing is too much volatility for our planning. Were we to accept quarterly reviews, we would need a price floor at fifteen cents.

A: I understand the need for predictability. Should both sides agree on volume first, I believe the pricing conversation becomes much simpler. Had we locked in volume at the levels we discussed in March, we would already be ahead.
B: Fair point. Were I to propose annual pricing with a two-cent band, would that give you enough flexibility?
A: Possibly. But I must be direct: were the payment terms to exceed ninety days, the structure would not work for us regardless of price. That is a firm boundary.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three subjunctive/inverted conditionals and maintains calm, measured language throughout. Student B uses at least two and makes one conditional concession. Neither commits to a final position — the conversation remains exploratory.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: This is the most important exercise of the lesson. Run it twice with swapped roles. After each round, highlight moments where subjunctive forms successfully created 'cognitive room' to trade. Note any moments where a student accidentally committed instead of explored.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Oliver opens a negotiation
additionalAudios.speaker: oliver
additionalAudios.transcript: Thank you for sitting down with us today. I want to be transparent about what I am hoping to explore. Were Czarnikow to commit to a five-year volume guarantee — and I am talking about a real commitment, not a soft letter of intent — would your side be prepared to discuss quarterly pricing linked to the NY11 index? I ask because, had we been having this conversation a year ago, the market was in a very different place. Should the reference price continue to hold above sixteen cents, I believe there is a structure here that works for both sides.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — The counterparty makes a conditional offer
additionalAudios.speaker: charlotte
additionalAudios.transcript: Oliver, I appreciate the directness. Were we to agree to quarterly pricing — and I am not saying we will — we would need two things. First, a price floor at fifteen cents. Second, payment terms of a hundred and twenty days. Had the market been more stable, I might be more flexible on the floor. But given where we are, those are the conditions under which we can make this work. Should your side find those terms unworkable, I would rather know now than in round three.
tasks: What two conditions does the counterparty name? (Answer: a price floor at fifteen cents and payment terms of 120 days)
Find the inverted conditional the counterparty uses. How does it maintain optionality?
The counterparty says 'I would rather know now than in round three.' What does this signal about their approach?
If you were Oliver, would you accept, reject, or counter-propose? Practise your response in 20 seconds using one subjunctive form.

qAndA.question: What three scenarios does the intro say experienced negotiators prepare for before a significant meeting?
qAndA.modelAnswer: The best realistic outcome, the worst acceptable one, and the walk-away point beyond which no deal is better than the deal on offer.

qAndA.question: Why does the intro say that conditional and subjunctive forms 'create cognitive room'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because they allow the speaker to propose and explore trade-offs without publicly committing to any position. 'Were we to accept…' is an exploration, not a commitment. This lets both sides test ideas without losing face.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'If we accept those terms' and 'Were we to accept those terms'?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Both express a condition, but 'were we to accept' is more formal, more hypothetical, and more deliberate. It signals that the speaker is exploring, not offering. In negotiation, this distinction matters — it preserves optionality.

qAndA.question: Oliver is 'deliberately the calmest person in the room.' Why is self-regulation an advantage in negotiation?
qAndA.modelAnswer: Because negotiation under pressure pulls people towards emotional decisions — conceding to relieve tension, or escalating to release frustration. The person who can remain calm thinks more clearly, reads the room better, and makes strategic rather than reactive choices.

qAndA.question: The intro says 'no deal is better than the deal on offer' beyond the walk-away point. When might this not be true?
qAndA.modelAnswer: When the relationship is more valuable than the specific deal — for example, with a long-term strategic partner like a key origin supplier. In those cases, the walk-away point may be lower because preserving the relationship has its own commercial value.

pairWork.title: Offer and counter-offer drill
pairWork.description: One student makes a conditional offer using a subjunctive form ('Were we to commit to X, we would need Y'). lessons.title: Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
lessons.grammar: Hedged modality — it is conceivable that, one might reasonably expect
lessons.objective: Discuss strategic decisions under uncertainty with epistemic care.
lessons.intro:
Strategic decisions are rarely made with clean data. Most of the time, the executive is choosing between imperfect options, on the basis of partial information, while the environment continues to change underneath them. The honest response is not to pretend otherwise, but to make better decisions despite the fog.

There are a few tools that help. One is to separate the quality of the decision from the quality of the outcome. A well-reasoned decision can still end badly, and a reckless one can still end well; confusing the two systematically erodes the judgement of any leadership team. Another is to build explicit plans for being wrong — what would we do differently, how quickly would we notice, what would it cost to reverse?

Perhaps most importantly, mature decision-makers cultivate the habit of distinguishing three very different things: what the data shows, what they believe on the basis of experience, and what they are frankly guessing. Each of those has its place in a decision, but conflating them quietly is how boards end up confident about things they should be cautious about.

items.q: How do you communicate a forecast you are not fully confident in?
items.a: I present it as a working hypothesis, noting that the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive and that one might reasonably expect the picture to shift.

items.q: How do you make a high-stakes call when the data is thin?
items.a: On balance, I favour the more reversible option, since it would be premature to commit irreversibly on evidence this incomplete.

items.q: How do you guard against overconfidence in your own judgement?
items.a: I discipline myself to state explicitly what I know and what I am merely inferring, conceding that it may well be that I am wrong.

items.q: How do you frame uncertainty to a board without sounding indecisive?
items.a: I distinguish the decision from the certainty behind it, recommending a course while candidly marking the confidence as moderate rather than high.

items.q: What role does reversibility play in your decisions?
items.a: Where a decision is reversible, I act quickly; where it is not, I err firmly on the side of caution and gather further evidence.

items.q: How do you respond when pressed for a definitive answer you cannot give?
items.a: I resist the pressure to overclaim, offering my best judgement on the available evidence while declining to dress an inference up as a fact.

grammarDeepDive.title: Hedged Modality — The Language of Responsible Uncertainty
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Hedged modality is the grammar of intellectual honesty. In business English, it refers to the set of structures and phrases that allow a speaker to express a view while simultaneously marking the degree of certainty behind it. At the apex level, this is not about being vague — it is about being precise about what you know and what you are guessing.

The core structures fall into three groups. First, epistemic modal verbs: might, could, may, would — each signals a different shade of possibility. Second, impersonal hedging constructions: it is conceivable that, one might reasonably expect, on balance we would argue, the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Third, qualifying adverbs and phrases: arguably, in all likelihood, to a reasonable degree, on the balance of probabilities. Together, these allow the speaker to position every claim on a spectrum from near-certainty to frank speculation.

In practice, hedged modality is what separates confident senior communication from reckless assertion. A board member who says 'the market will turn' is making a promise; one who says 'one might reasonably expect a turn, given the current signals' is making an informed judgement. Both Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's Cambridge Grammar in Use treat modal verbs as expressions of probability, not just politeness. At this level, the student should be able to select the right hedge for the right degree of uncertainty — and know why the choice matters.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 42–46 on modal verbs for possibility, probability and deduction.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 29–32 on may, might, could, must for degrees of certainty.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on hedging language, epistemic modality and discourse markers of uncertainty.

commonMistakes.wrong: The market will definitely turn next quarter.
commonMistakes.right: One might reasonably expect the market to turn next quarter.
commonMistakes.note: Absolute certainty about future markets is almost never warranted. Hedge the claim.

commonMistakes.wrong: Maybe the price goes up.
commonMistakes.right: It is conceivable that the price appreciates over the medium term.
commonMistakes.note: 'Maybe' is too casual for senior business prose. Use a structured hedge.

commonMistakes.wrong: I think probably it could perhaps be possible.
commonMistakes.right: On balance, we would argue this is likely.
commonMistakes.note: Stacking multiple hedges weakens the sentence. Choose one clear hedge and commit to it.

commonMistakes.wrong: The evidence proves we are right.
commonMistakes.right: The evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive, but it supports our position.
commonMistakes.note: 'Proves' is almost never appropriate in business uncertainty. Use 'suggests' or 'supports'.

commonMistakes.wrong: We are not sure but we think so.
commonMistakes.right: In all likelihood, this is the case, though we would want to stress-test the assumption.
commonMistakes.note: Vague hedging undermines credibility. Be specific about your degree of confidence.

rolePlays.title: Pre-Mortem on a Major Trading Decision
rolePlays.setup: Czarnikow is considering a large forward purchase of raw sugar from a new Brazilian supplier. The price is attractive but the supplier has no track record with Czarnikow. Sophie has called a pre-mortem: the team must assume the decision has already failed and work backwards to identify what went wrong.
roles: Risk manager (identifies what could go wrong)
rolePlays.instructions: Run the pre-mortem for 5 minutes. Sophie opens by saying: 'Let us assume we made this purchase and it went badly. What happened?' Each participant must use at least two hedged modality phrases.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Sophie presents the pre-mortem findings
additionalAudios.speaker: sophie
additionalAudios.transcript: Good morning. I want to share the results of our pre-mortem on the Brazilian supplier decision. We identified three credible failure scenarios. First, it is conceivable that delivery timelines slip by four to six weeks, given the supplier's limited logistics infrastructure. Second, one might reasonably expect quality variance in the first two shipments, as the supplier adjusts to our specifications. Third, on the balance of probabilities, the exchange rate moves against us if the real weakens further. None of these is fatal individually, but together they could erode the margin advantage that made the deal attractive in the first place. Our recommendation: proceed, but build in contractual protections for each scenario.
additionalAudios.task: Listen once without reading. How many failure scenarios did the pre-mortem identify? Listen again and write down the hedging phrase used for each scenario.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — A board member challenges the recommendation
additionalAudios.speaker: oliver
additionalAudios.transcript: Thank you, Sophie. I appreciate the rigour. But let me push back on one point. You say it is conceivable that delivery slips by four to six weeks. Conceivable is doing a lot of work in that sentence. What does the evidence actually suggest? Is this a five per cent risk or a fifty per cent risk? Because if it is the latter, we are not hedging our language — we are hedging our decision, and those are very different things. I would like to see the probability estimate before we proceed.
additionalAudios.task: Listen once. What distinction does Oliver draw between hedging language and hedging a decision? Listen again and identify which hedging phrase Oliver questions.

qAndA.q: What is the difference between the quality of a decision and the quality of an outcome?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A good decision follows a sound process with available evidence; a good outcome is what actually happens. They can diverge — a well-reasoned decision can still produce a poor outcome, and vice versa.

qAndA.q: Why does the lesson recommend separating data, belief, and guess?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because conflating them leads to false confidence. Data is evidence, belief is informed judgement, and guess is speculation. Each has its place, but the team must know which is which.

qAndA.q: What is the purpose of a pre-mortem, and how does it differ from a post-mortem?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A pre-mortem is done before the decision: the team imagines the decision has failed and works backwards. A post-mortem analyses what went wrong after the fact. The pre-mortem surfaces risks while there is still time to act.

qAndA.q: Why might hedging language actually strengthen rather than weaken a recommendation?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because it signals intellectual honesty. A recommendation that acknowledges uncertainty is more credible than one that pretends certainty exists. Decision-makers trust advisers who are precise about what they do and do not know.

qAndA.q: Describe a situation at Czarnikow where sunk cost bias could lead to a poor decision.
qAndA.sampleAnswer: If Czarnikow has invested heavily in a supplier relationship that is underperforming, sunk cost bias might push the team to continue rather than switch. The past investment is irrecoverable and should not drive future choices.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Complex Problems
lessons.grammar: Logical connectors of cause and consequence
lessons.objective: Structure complex problem diagnosis with analytical precision.
lessons.intro:
A certain class of business problem resists simple diagnosis. The symptoms are visible and uncomfortable, but the underlying causes are distributed across several functions, partially hidden by organisational politics, and frequently mis-described by the people closest to them. These are the problems that mediocre analysis merely rearranges, rather than solves.

Serious diagnosis begins with a deliberate pause. Before any explanation is entertained, the investigator collects the facts in neutral language — what happened, when, and how that compares to what was expected. That simple discipline prevents the most common failure: choosing an explanation first, and then fitting the evidence around it.

Only then can the real work begin: generating multiple plausible explanations, stress-testing each against the evidence, and resisting the comfortable pull of the one that is politically convenient. The best diagnosticians are often those willing to conclude, patiently, that the real cause is something nobody wanted to hear.

grammarDeepDive.title: Logical Connectors of Cause and Consequence
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In senior business English, the ability to connect cause and consequence with precision is essential. Logical connectors allow the speaker or writer to build chains of reasoning — showing not just what happened, but why it happened and what followed. At the apex level, the goal is not merely to use these connectors, but to select the right one for the right logical relationship.

The main connectors fall into several categories. Direct consequence: consequently, as a result, therefore, accordingly. Indirect or cascading consequence: which in turn, in turn, this in turn produced. Cause or reason: owing to, on account of, given that, in light of. Partial explanation: this goes some way towards explaining, this accounts in part for. Each carries a slightly different weight and formality, and the best analytical prose uses them with deliberate variety.

Both Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's Cambridge Grammar in Use cover causal connectors, but at this level the student should go beyond textbook usage. The goal is to build sentences that mirror the structure of the analysis itself: layered, precise, and honest about which links in the chain are strong and which are tentative. A sentence like 'The supplier change affected lead times, which in turn drove a shift in mix, and this goes some way towards explaining the margin compression' is not just grammatically correct — it is analytically useful.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 245–250 on linking words for cause, reason and result.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 112–115 on although, in spite of, because, so, therefore.
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on discourse markers, logical connectors and academic linking words.

examples.en: The supplier change affected lead times, which in turn drove a shift in the product mix.
examples.pt: A mudança de fornecedor afetou os prazos de entrega, o que por sua vez provocou uma mudança no mix de produtos.

examples.en: Consequently, the margin fell by 200 basis points in Q3.
examples.pt: Consequentemente, a margem caiu 200 pontos-base no terceiro trimestre.

examples.en: Owing to the complexity of the root cause, the investigation took six weeks.

examples.en: This goes some way towards explaining the gap between forecast and actual.
examples.pt: Isso explica em parte a diferença entre o previsto e o realizado.

examples.en: As a result of the misdiagnosis, the team spent three months fixing the wrong problem.
examples.pt: Como resultado do diagnóstico equivocado, a equipe passou três meses resolvendo o problema errado.

examples.en: The price spike was symptomatic of a deeper structural issue in the supply chain.
examples.pt: O pico de preço era sintomático de uma questão estrutural mais profunda na cadeia de fornecimento.

examples.en: Harry ruled out the obvious explanation and, in turn, discovered a process failure nobody had documented.
examples.pt: Harry descartou a explicação óbvia e, por sua vez, descobriu uma falha de processo que ninguém havia documentado.

examples.en: On account of confirmation bias, the commercial team had dismissed the operational data.
examples.pt: Por conta do viés de confirmação, a equipe comercial havia descartado os dados operacionais.

examples.en: The distributed nature of the cause meant that no single team could see the whole picture.
examples.pt: A natureza distribuída da causa significava que nenhuma equipe sozinha conseguia ver o quadro completo.

examples.en: Accordingly, the steering committee requested a first-principles review.
examples.pt: Portanto, o comitê diretor solicitou uma revisão a partir de princípios fundamentais.

examples.en: The failure to decompose the problem led, predictably, to a solution that addressed only the surface.
examples.pt: A falha em decompor o problema levou, previsivelmente, a uma solução que abordava apenas a superfície.

examples.en: Given that three functions were involved, a single-team diagnosis was structurally insufficient.
examples.pt: Dado que três funções estavam envolvidas, um diagnóstico de uma única equipe era estruturalmente insuficiente.

commonMistakes.wrong: The costs went up, so consequently therefore margins fell.
commonMistakes.right: The costs went up; consequently, margins fell.
commonMistakes.note: Do not stack multiple connectors. Choose one and use it cleanly.

commonMistakes.wrong: Owing to costs went up, margins fell.
commonMistakes.right: Owing to the increase in costs, margins fell.
commonMistakes.note: 'Owing to' takes a noun phrase, not a clause. Use 'owing to the fact that' if a clause is needed.

commonMistakes.wrong: The problem was because of the supplier.
commonMistakes.right: The problem was attributable to the supplier change.
commonMistakes.note: 'Was because of' is informal. In analytical prose, use 'was attributable to' or 'arose from'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Which in turn it caused a delay.
commonMistakes.right: Which in turn caused a delay.
commonMistakes.note: After 'which in turn', do not add an extra subject pronoun. The 'which' is already the subject.

commonMistakes.wrong: As a result of, the team changed the process.
commonMistakes.right: As a result, the team changed the process.
commonMistakes.note: 'As a result of' needs a noun phrase after it. Without one, use 'As a result' (no 'of').

rolePlays.title: Investigating the Margin Drop
rolePlays.setup: Czarnikow's Q3 margins have dropped unexpectedly. The commercial team blames rising costs, the finance team blames product mix, and operations says neither explanation is correct. Harry has been asked to lead a cross-functional diagnostic session.
rolePlays.instructions: Harry opens by collecting facts in neutral language. Each participant must use at least two cause-and-consequence connectors. Harry should challenge each explanation with evidence-based questions before proposing a hypothesis tree.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Harry presents the diagnostic framework
additionalAudios.speaker: harry
additionalAudios.transcript: Right. Before we discuss explanations, let me share what we actually know. Margins fell by 200 basis points in Q3. Costs rose by 8 per cent, which in turn compressed the spread on three key products. However, this goes only some way towards explaining the full drop. Owing to a shift in product mix — we sold more low-margin refined sugar and less high-margin raw — the overall margin was further diluted. But here is the part nobody has mentioned: the pricing model was updated in July, and consequently, the comparison with Q2 is not like-for-like. My recommendation is that we treat each of these as a separate hypothesis and test them against the data before choosing an explanation.
additionalAudios.task: Listen once without reading. How many separate causes does Harry identify? Listen again and write down every cause-and-consequence connector he uses.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — The commercial lead pushes back
additionalAudios.speaker: sophie
additionalAudios.transcript: Harry, I hear what you are saying, but I think you are overcomplicating this. Costs went up. As a result, margins went down. That is the story. The mix shift is marginal, and the pricing model change is a technicality. We should be talking to suppliers, not building hypothesis trees. Owing to the urgency of the situation, I would prefer we act now and diagnose later.
additionalAudios.task: Listen once. What is Sophie's main argument against Harry's approach? Listen again and identify the cause-and-consequence connectors she uses. Do you agree with her reasoning? Why or why not?

qAndA.q: Why does the lesson recommend collecting facts before generating explanations?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because choosing an explanation first creates confirmation bias — you fit the evidence around the explanation rather than letting the evidence guide you to the right cause.

qAndA.q: What does the lesson mean by 'distributed causes'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: It means the root cause is spread across several functions or factors, rather than sitting in one place. No single team can see the whole picture, which makes diagnosis harder.

qAndA.q: Explain the difference between 'consequently' and 'which in turn' in analytical writing.
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'Consequently' marks a direct result. 'Which in turn' marks a cascading or indirect result — one thing leads to another, which then leads to a third. 'Which in turn' shows the chain more explicitly.

qAndA.q: Why might a politically convenient explanation be dangerous in a diagnostic process?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because it stops the investigation too early. If the explanation is comfortable for powerful stakeholders, there is less pressure to dig deeper — even if the real cause is something more uncomfortable or systemic.

qAndA.q: Describe a situation at Czarnikow where confirmation bias could compromise a diagnosis.
qAndA.sampleAnswer: If the trading desk believes a margin drop is caused by costs alone, they may only look at cost data and ignore mix or pricing changes. Confirmation bias means they find evidence for what they already believe and dismiss evidence that contradicts it.

contextualization: Think about a recent problem at Czarnikow that took longer to diagnose than expected. In three sentences, describe the symptoms, the initial explanation, and the real cause.
Describe a situation where confirmation bias affected a decision at work. How did the team eventually see past it?
If Harry asked you to build a hypothesis tree for the biggest challenge your team faces right now, what would the top three branches be?
Think of a time when the politically convenient explanation was different from the correct one. What happened when the truth emerged?

productionTasks.task: Present to your teacher, in 60-second in which you present a structured diagnosis of a problem at Czarnikow (real or invented). Include: neutral facts first, then two plausible hypotheses connected with cause-and-consequence connectors, then a recommendation for which to investigate first.
productionTasks.successCriteria: Facts are presented before explanations. At least three cause-and-consequence connectors are used naturally. Two hypotheses are articulated clearly.

pairWork.title: Hypothesis tree challenge
pairWork.instructions: One student describes a business problem (real or invented). The other builds a hypothesis tree aloud, generating at least three plausible causes and connecting them with logical connectors. After 3 minutes, swap roles. Both students should resist the urge to jump to solutions.

lessons.title: Leading Complex Programmes
lessons.grammar: Complex time expressions — by the time, no sooner had
lessons.objective: Lead multi-workstream programmes with senior stakeholder management.
lessons.intro:
Large programmes fail quietly. They almost never die in a single, dramatic moment; instead, they leak time, goodwill and credibility over months, long before anyone is willing to say out loud that the original plan is no longer viable. The best programme leaders treat that slow erosion as the real risk, and organise everything else around spotting and acting on it early.

By the time a traditional red-amber-green report turns red, several earlier signals have usually been missed. Good leaders build informal listening systems to supplement the formal one: weekly quiet conversations with key workstream leads, direct sampling of end users, pointed questions in one-to-ones with the sponsor. These are not substitutes for governance — they are the texture that gives the governance meaning.

No sooner had the original scope been agreed than it began, of course, to change. Skilled programme leaders do not resist that reality; they design for it. They build in regular, scheduled moments of honest renegotiation, where scope, budget, timeline and quality can all be revisited. A programme that never renegotiates is not disciplined — it is in denial.

lessonFlow.instructions: Ask: have you ever been part of a project or programme that failed quietly? What were the early signs? Let the student tell the story.
Read the intro aloud. Work through the 10 vocab items. Student uses each in a sentence about a Czarnikow programme or project.
Present complex time expressions. Read the 12 examples. Do the 5 quick practice exercises. Review the 5 common mistakes, paying special attention to inversion after 'no sooner'.
Read Oliver's situation. Do the Read Aloud and Complex Time exercises. Play Audio A once without transcript, then again with it.
Run the quarterly renegotiation role play. Swap roles after the first round. Then discuss 3 Q&A questions orally.
Ask the 4 contextualisation prompts. Do the speaking production task. Read the 10 takeaway phrases aloud together.

commonChallenges: Inversion after 'no sooner' is consistently difficult. Drill it: 'No sooner had we agreed than...' Repeat several times until the word order feels natural.
Students confuse 'by the time' (= before that moment) with 'until' (= up to that moment). Use a timeline on the board to clarify.
The concept of 'informal listening systems' may be unfamiliar. Give concrete examples: a five-minute corridor chat, a direct question in a one-to-one.

items.q: How do you defend against scope creep?

grammarDeepDive.title: Complex Time Expressions — By the Time, No Sooner Had
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Complex time expressions allow the speaker to describe sequences of events with precision and elegance. In senior business English, they are particularly useful for programme management, where timing, sequencing and the relationship between events are central to every conversation. The two key structures in this lesson — by the time and no sooner … than — each serve a distinct purpose.

By the time emphasises that something has already happened (or will have happened) before a reference point. It pairs naturally with the Past Perfect (by the time we noticed, the damage had been done) or the Present Perfect (by the time the report turns red, several signals have been missed). The effect is to highlight a gap — between when something should have been noticed and when it actually was. This makes it ideal for discussing programme risks and missed signals.

No sooner … than describes two events in rapid succession, often with an ironic or rueful tone: no sooner had we agreed the scope than it began to change. It requires subject-auxiliary inversion after no sooner — the same inversion used in formal written English after negative adverbs. Both Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's Cambridge Grammar in Use classify this as an advanced structure that appears frequently in formal reports, board papers and senior presentations. Mastering it gives the speaker a compact, elegant way to convey that events moved faster than planned.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 51–54 on Past Perfect, time clauses and complex sequencing.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 15–16 (Past Perfect) and Unit 112 (no sooner, hardly, scarcely).
Cambridge Dictionary — entries on 'by the time', 'no sooner … than', and inversion after negative adverbs.

commonMistakes.right: By the time we notice, the damage will have been done.
commonMistakes.note: After 'by the time', use Present Simple (not future) in the time clause, and Future Perfect in the main clause.

commonMistakes.wrong: No sooner had we agreed when the scope changed.
commonMistakes.right: No sooner had we agreed than the scope changed.
commonMistakes.note: 'No sooner' pairs with 'than', not 'when'. This is a fixed collocation.

commonMistakes.wrong: By the time the meeting, three issues had appeared.
commonMistakes.right: By the time of the meeting, three issues had appeared.
commonMistakes.note: 'By the time' needs a clause or 'by the time of' + noun phrase. Do not leave it incomplete.

commonMistakes.wrong: No sooner the budget was approved than changes started.
commonMistakes.right: No sooner had the budget been approved than changes started.
commonMistakes.note: Inversion and Past Perfect are both required: 'had the budget been approved'.
