grammarDeepDive.title: Passive voice — is sent, is received
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In trade finance, we often describe processes where the action is more important than who does it. 'The payment is sent through SWIFT' focuses on the payment, not on the person who clicked the button. This is the passive voice, and it is extremely common in banking and international trade. At Czarnikow, you will hear it every day: 'The money was received this morning', 'The documents are sent by courier', 'The fee is charged by the correspondent bank.'

The passive is formed with be + past participle: is sent, was received, are charged, will be transferred. In the present, use is/are + past participle. In the past, use was/were + past participle. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and English Grammar in Use (Murphy) recommend the passive for formal and professional contexts, especially in finance and reporting.

Why does finance love the passive? Because it sounds objective, professional and process-focused. Instead of saying 'We sent the money yesterday', a banker says 'The money was sent yesterday.' The focus shifts to the money and the action, making the language more neutral. The Cambridge Dictionary notes that the passive is especially frequent in written business English, reports, and process descriptions — exactly the kind of language used at Czarnikow every day.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 22: The passive (1) — be + past participle.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 42: Passive (1) — is done / was done.
Cambridge Dictionary — grammar section on passive voice with business usage examples.

qAndA.question: What is SWIFT and what does it do?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: SWIFT is a global messaging network used by banks to send payment instructions. It is not a bank itself — it carries the messages between banks.

qAndA.question: How long does a typical wire transfer take?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A typical wire transfer takes one to three business days, depending on the countries and banks involved.

qAndA.question: Why is the passive voice common in banking language?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because in banking, the action and the process matter more than who performs them. 'The payment was sent' sounds more professional and objective than 'John sent the payment'.

qAndA.question: Why do wire transfers sometimes pass through a correspondent bank?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because the sender's bank and the receiver's bank may not have a direct relationship. The correspondent bank acts as a middle link to move the funds.

qAndA.question: Why is SWIFT still the standard despite being slower than newer systems?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because SWIFT is trusted, secure and used by thousands of banks worldwide. It has a long track record. Newer systems are faster but not yet as widely adopted.

lessons.title: Currencies and Why Rates Move
lessons.objective: Understand the basic idea of currency exchange and why it matters.
lessons.intro:
Every country has a currency. When you buy or sell in another country, you have to change one currency into another. This is called currency exchange, or FX.

The problem is that rates move every second. Today the pound is strong; tomorrow it may be weaker. A small change in the rate can turn a profit into a loss.

For this reason, companies that trade across borders pay very close attention to FX. A little knowledge here protects a lot of margin.

grammarDeepDive.title: Comparatives — stronger, weaker, more volatile
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In trade and finance, we constantly compare: Is the pound stronger or weaker today? Is this deal more profitable than the last one? Comparatives are essential for describing market movements, and at Czarnikow, you will use them every day. The exchange rate is higher today. The margin is smaller this month. The real is weaker than last quarter.

The rules are clear: for short adjectives (one syllable), add -er: strong → stronger, weak → weaker, cheap → cheaper. For longer adjectives (two or more syllables), use more: volatile → more volatile, profitable → more profitable. After the comparative, use than: The pound is stronger than the euro. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and English Grammar in Use (Murphy) present this as one of the fundamental structures of English — simple to learn, but easy to get wrong under pressure.

In FX discussions, comparatives help you be precise and professional. Instead of saying 'The dollar is bad today', say 'The dollar is weaker today than yesterday.' This gives your colleague exact information. The Cambridge Dictionary notes that comparatives are among the most frequently tested structures in business English exams, and for good reason — they appear in every market report, every financial briefing, and every FX conversation at companies like Czarnikow.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 44: Comparatives — -er / more.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 104: Comparatives (1) — cheaper, more expensive, etc.
Cambridge Dictionary — grammar section on comparatives with business and finance examples.

commonMistakes.wrong: The pound is more strong today.
commonMistakes.right: The pound is stronger today.
commonMistakes.why: Short adjectives (one syllable) take '-er', not 'more'. 'Strong' → 'stronger'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The rate is more lower this week.
commonMistakes.right: The rate is lower this week.
commonMistakes.why: Do not use 'more' with an adjective that already has '-er'. Just say 'lower'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The dollar is weaker that the euro.
commonMistakes.right: The dollar is weaker than the euro.
commonMistakes.why: After a comparative, use 'than' — not 'that'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Our margin is more small this month.
commonMistakes.right: Our margin is smaller this month.
commonMistakes.why: 'Small' is a short adjective — add '-er': 'smaller', not 'more small'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The real is volatiler than the euro.
commonMistakes.right: The real is more volatile than the euro.
commonMistakes.why: Longer adjectives (3+ syllables) use 'more', not '-er'. 'More volatile', not 'volatiler'.

qAndA.question: What is currency exchange (FX)?

qAndA.question: Why do exchange rates matter for companies like Czarnikow?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because Czarnikow trades across borders. A small change in the exchange rate can make a deal more or less profitable — it can turn a profit into a loss.

qAndA.question: How do we form comparatives in English?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: For short adjectives (one syllable), we add '-er': stronger, weaker. For longer adjectives, we use 'more': more volatile, more profitable. We use 'than' to compare.

qAndA.question: Why can a 2% move in the exchange rate change the result of a deal?

qAndA.question: How can Czarnikow protect itself from FX risk?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: By monitoring rates closely, converting at the right time, and using financial tools like forward contracts to lock in rates in advance.

lessons.title: Agreeing Payment Terms
lessons.objective: Negotiate simple payment terms with a customer or supplier.
lessons.intro:
Payment terms tell you when and how the money moves. They are part of almost every business deal, and they are always open to negotiation.

Common terms are net 30 (pay within 30 days), 50% upfront (pay half before, half after) or COD (pay on delivery). Each one has a different balance of risk for the buyer and the seller.

A good negotiator asks for what they want, but also listens. Payment terms are a conversation, not a fight.

In sugar trading, counter-offer often decides the outcome of a ethanol shipment.

grammarDeepDive.title: Would + if for soft negotiation
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In business English, especially in trade and finance, being direct is not always the best approach. When you negotiate payment terms, you want the other side to say yes — and soft language helps. The word would is the key. Instead of 'We need 50% upfront', say 'Would 50% upfront work for you?'. The meaning is the same, but the tone is completely different. At Czarnikow, where long-term relationships matter, this makes a real difference.

The structure is simple: would + base verb for statements (We would be happy to…) and would + subject + base verb for questions (Would you consider…?). When combined with if, you create a soft conditional proposal: We would extend the terms if you could pay a deposit. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood, Unit 38) and Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy, Unit 36) classify this as the 'polite conditional' — a core tool for professional negotiation.

Note the difference between a direct demand and a softened proposal. 'Pay before we ship' sounds like an order. 'Would you be comfortable with payment before shipment?' sounds like a conversation. In international trade, where cultures, expectations and legal systems differ, soft negotiation language builds trust and keeps deals moving forward. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that would is the single most important modal for politeness in professional English.

Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 36: Would / would you like / I'd like.

lessons.title: Cross-Border Sales: The Basics
lessons.objective: Understand the typical steps and extra costs in a cross-border deal.
lessons.intro:
A cross-border transaction is any deal where the buyer and the seller are in different countries. It looks like a normal sale, but many small extras appear along the way.

You will pay for shipping. You will pay customs. You will lose a little in the currency exchange. There may be a small bank fee. None of these are huge, but together they change the price.

The lesson is simple: always check the real cost of a cross-border deal, not just the invoice price.

grammarDeepDive.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In trade and finance, you talk about money, costs, fees and goods every day. Some of these words are countable — you can put a number in front of them (three fees, two invoices). Others are uncountable — they have no plural form and you cannot count them directly (money, shipping, information). This distinction matters because it changes the grammar: a lot of money (not many money), but many fees (not a lot of fees — though this is also possible).

The practical rule at Czarnikow is straightforward. If you can say 'one __, two __s', it is countable. If that sounds wrong, it is uncountable. Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood, Unit 85) explains that uncountable nouns often refer to substances, materials, abstract ideas or mass concepts — exactly the language of trade: money, equipment, cargo, shipping, insurance. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy, Unit 69) adds that some words change meaning: paper (uncountable: material) vs a paper (countable: document).

In cross-border transactions, getting this right affects how you write emails, reports and contracts. You would never write 'the shippings cost €200' — you write 'the shipping costs €200'. Likewise, 'we have received all the necessary informations' is wrong; it should be 'all the necessary information'. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary marks each noun as [C] or [U], which is a quick reference for any trade professional writing in English.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 85: Countable and uncountable nouns.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 69: Countable and uncountable nouns (1).
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — noun entries marked [C] countable or [U] uncountable.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between the invoice price and the landed cost?

qAndA.question: What are the four extra costs Emily explains in the lesson?

qAndA.question: Why do we say 'a lot of money' but 'many fees'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because 'money' is uncountable — we cannot say 'one money, two moneys'. 'Fees' is countable, so we use 'many'. With uncountable nouns, we use 'a lot of', 'much' or 'how much'.

qAndA.question: Why should Czarnikow always show the landed cost to clients, not just the invoice price?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because it builds trust and avoids surprises. If the client knows the real cost from the start, they can plan their budget and will not complain later.

qAndA.question: How could a company reduce the extras in a cross-border deal?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: By negotiating lower shipping rates, using banks with lower fees, timing the exchange rate carefully, or finding suppliers in countries with lower customs duties.

lessons.title: Risk in International Trade
lessons.objective: Recognise the main types of risk in international trade.
lessons.intro:
International trade comes with more risks than selling at home. The goods travel further. The buyer is harder to check. The law may be different. And the money may move more slowly.

We usually talk about three main risks: the commercial risk (the buyer does not pay), the country risk (something goes wrong in the country), and the currency risk (the exchange rate moves against you).

The good news is simple: for each risk, there is a tool. The first step is just to see the risk clearly.

grammarDeepDive.title: First conditional — if + will
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The first conditional is the grammar of real risk. In trade and finance, we use it every day to talk about what will happen if something goes wrong — or right. The structure is simple: if + present simple in one clause, will + base verb in the other. At Czarnikow, you might say 'If the buyer defaults, we will lose the margin' or 'If we hedge the currency, we will protect the profit'. These are not hypothetical — they are real possibilities.

Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood, Unit 144) explains that the first conditional is for 'things that are possible or likely in the future'. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy, Unit 25) adds that the if clause uses the present simple (not will), even though we are talking about the future. This is the single most common mistake: 'If the buyer will not pay' is wrong; 'If the buyer does not pay' is correct.

In risk management, the first conditional lets you map causes to consequences clearly. 'If the government changes the import rules, our licence will expire.' 'If the real weakens, our costs will increase.' Each sentence is a mini risk assessment. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that first conditionals are 'the standard form for discussing business contingencies' — exactly what Sophie does in this lesson when she presents her risk map.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 144: First conditional — if + will.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 25: If I do… / If I don't… (first conditional).
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entry on 'if' with usage notes on conditional structures.

commonMistakes.why: The result clause needs 'will + base verb'. Also, 'loose' means not tight; 'lose' means to not have any more.

rolePlays.setup: It is Monday morning at Czarnikow's London office. Sophie is presenting a simple risk map for a new sugar deal in a developing market. The team needs to understand the three main risks and what will happen if they are not managed.

qAndA.question: What are the three main risks in international trade?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Commercial risk (the buyer does not pay), country risk (something goes wrong in the destination country), and currency risk (the exchange rate moves against you).

qAndA.question: What does Sophie recommend for each type of risk?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Insurance for commercial risk, market diversification for country risk, and hedging for currency risk.

qAndA.question: Why do we use present simple in the 'if' clause, not 'will'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because the first conditional describes real future possibilities. The 'if' clause sets the condition (present simple), and the 'will' clause shows the result. Using 'will' in both clauses is a grammar error.

qAndA.question: Which of the three risks is hardest for Czarnikow to control, and why?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Country risk, because it depends on governments and political events that Czarnikow cannot influence. Commercial and currency risks have clearer tools (insurance, hedging).

qAndA.question: Why is 'seeing the risk clearly' described as 'half the work'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because once you identify and understand a risk, you can choose the right tool to manage it. If you do not see the risk, you cannot prepare for it, and surprises cost more than planned responses.

lessons.title: Fraud and Simple Due Diligence
lessons.objective: Know the basic steps to check a new business partner.
lessons.intro:
Every year, businesses lose money to fraud. The most common problem is simple: a seller ships goods to a buyer who never really existed, or who never planned to pay.

This is where due diligence comes in. Before you do business with a new partner, you should check who they are. Look up the company. Ask for references. Run a basic background check. Visit them, if you can.

A few quiet questions at the start save a lot of pain at the end.

grammarDeepDive.title: Should for advice
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In compliance and due diligence, you need to tell people what is sensible to do — without sounding like you are giving an order. That is exactly what should does. When Charlotte says 'You should check the company before the first order', she is giving advice, not an instruction. The structure is simple: should + base verb (no to). At Czarnikow, where compliance is part of everyday work, should is one of the most useful words in the language.

Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood, Unit 34) explains that should is used for recommendations and opinions about what is right or sensible. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy, Unit 33) adds that should is softer than must: 'You must check the watchlist' (rule) vs 'You should also ask for references' (good idea). In compliance, this distinction matters — some checks are legal requirements (must), while others are best practices (should).

The negative form is should not (or shouldn't): 'You should not send payment without verifying the company first.' Questions use inversion: 'Should we ask for references?' The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that should is 'the standard modal for professional advice in British English' — exactly the tone Charlotte uses when training new analysts at Czarnikow.

qAndA.question: What are the three basic due diligence checks Charlotte describes?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Look up the company on the trade register, ask for at least two references, and run a basic background check online.

qAndA.question: Why is a prepaid email address considered a red flag?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because legitimate companies usually have their own domain email (e.g. @company.com). A free or prepaid email (e.g. @gmail.com) suggests the contact may not represent a real company.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'should' and 'must' in a compliance context?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'Should' is for advice and best practices — things that are sensible to do. 'Must' is for legal requirements and rules — things that are obligatory. For example: 'You must check the sanctions list' (legal obligation) vs 'You should also ask for references' (good practice).

qAndA.question: What would you do if a new supplier had no red flags but also no online presence at all?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: I would ask for more documentation, request a video call to see their facilities, and contact their references directly. No online presence is not necessarily a red flag, but it means extra caution is needed.

qAndA.question: Why does Charlotte say due diligence 'saves ten months of problems'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because if you do not check a partner properly, you might ship goods to someone who never pays, which leads to months of chasing payments, legal action and potential losses. Ten minutes of checks prevents all of that.

lessons.title: Sanctions: The Rules We Must Follow
lessons.objective: Understand what sanctions are and why they must be respected.
lessons.intro:
Sanctions are rules that stop companies from doing business with certain countries, people or products. They are set by governments and international bodies for political or legal reasons.

The rules can be strict. You cannot sell certain products to a country on the list. You must not send money to certain names. The fines are very big, and the damage to the company's name can be even bigger.

The safe answer is simple: if you are not sure, ask — and always check the list first.

grammarDeepDive.title: Cannot / must not for prohibition
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In compliance and sanctions, precision matters — not just in law, but in language. English has two main ways to express prohibition: cannot and must not. Both mean 'it is not allowed', but the tone is slightly different. Cannot focuses on ability or permission: 'You cannot sell this product to that country' means the rules do not permit it. Must not focuses on obligation or duty: 'We must not send payment to this name' means it is our responsibility not to do it. At Czarnikow, both forms appear in compliance guidelines every day.

Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood, Unit 26) explains that cannot is used for external rules and restrictions, while must not carries a stronger sense of personal duty or legal obligation. Cambridge Grammar in Use (Murphy, Unit 31) adds that in formal business writing, must not is often preferred because it sounds more serious. In spoken English, cannot (or can't) is more common and slightly less formal.

The key difference from don't have to (which means 'it is not necessary') is crucial in compliance. 'You must not ship to an embargoed country' (prohibition) is completely different from 'You don't have to ship today' (no obligation). Getting this wrong in a sanctions context could have serious legal consequences. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary flags this distinction as 'essential for professional and legal English'.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 26: Cannot and must not — prohibition and negative obligation.
Cambridge Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 31: Must / must not / don't have to.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on 'cannot' and 'must not' with usage notes on prohibition.

commonMistakes.wrong: You don't can sell to that country.
commonMistakes.right: You cannot sell to that country.
commonMistakes.why: Modal verbs (can, must, should) do not use 'do' for negatives. The negative of 'can' is 'cannot' or 'can't'.

commonMistakes.wrong: We can not ship the goods. (when meaning prohibition)
commonMistakes.right: We cannot ship the goods.
commonMistakes.why: 'Cannot' (one word) means prohibition. 'Can not' (two words) is ambiguous and should be avoided.

commonMistakes.wrong: You must not to send payment.
commonMistakes.right: You must not send payment.
commonMistakes.why: 'Must not' is followed by the base verb — no 'to'.

commonMistakes.wrong: We don't have to ship to that country. (when meaning prohibition)
commonMistakes.right: We must not ship to that country.
commonMistakes.why: 'Don't have to' means 'it is not necessary' — not the same as prohibition. For prohibition, use 'must not' or 'cannot'.

commonMistakes.wrong: You not can export without a licence.
commonMistakes.right: You cannot export without a licence.
commonMistakes.why: 'Not' goes between the modal and the base verb. The correct form is 'cannot' (one word).

qAndA.question: What are sanctions and who sets them?

lessons.title: Contracts: The Words That Matter
lessons.objective: Understand the most important parts of a business contract.
lessons.intro:
A contract is just a promise on paper. It says who does what, when, and for how much. In international trade, contracts are especially important because the two sides often speak different languages and follow different laws.

Every contract has the same basic parts: the names of the two sides, the product or service, the price, the payment terms, the delivery and what happens if something goes wrong.

You do not need to write contracts from memory. You only need to read them carefully before you sign.

takeaways: Every contract has the same basic parts: parties, product, price, delivery and governing law.
Read every clause carefully before you sign.

You do not need to write contracts — but you must be able to read them.

grammarDeepDive.title: Shall / will in contractual language
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In everyday English, shall and will are almost the same. But in contracts and legal documents, they have very different meanings. Shall is the word of obligation: when a contract says 'The Seller shall deliver', it means the seller must deliver — it is a legal duty, not a choice. Will, by contrast, is often used for predictions or statements of fact, not obligations.

This distinction matters enormously at Czarnikow, where contracts govern every trade. When you read 'The Buyer shall pay within 60 days', you know it is a binding obligation. If the buyer does not pay, that is a breach of contract. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and English Grammar in Use (Murphy) note that shall has largely disappeared from spoken English but remains alive and essential in legal and contractual writing. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary confirms this formal, obligatory use.

A useful rule of thumb: in a contract, replace shall with must in your head to check the meaning. If it makes sense with must, you are reading an obligation. If not, the clause may be descriptive or informational. Practice reading contract clauses aloud, stressing shall each time, so the word becomes natural and carries the weight it deserves.

English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 21: will/shall — obligations in formal writing.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entry on 'shall' with legal usage notes.

lessons.title: Working Capital: Money You Need Every Day
lessons.objective: Understand what working capital is and why it matters.
lessons.intro:
Working capital is the money a company needs to run its daily business. It pays the salaries, buys the materials and covers the bills while the company waits to get paid.

The idea is simple: there is money coming in from customers, and money going out to suppliers, staff and tax. Working capital is the gap between the two — and how you manage it is often the difference between a healthy company and a stressed one.

Good trade companies watch their working capital every week.

grammarDeepDive.title: There is / there are
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In English, we use there is and there are to say that something exists or to introduce new information. There is goes with singular and uncountable nouns: 'There is a payment due Friday', 'There is enough cash'. There are goes with plural nouns: 'There are three invoices open', 'There are two suppliers waiting'. This structure is one of the most common in business English because we constantly describe what exists in accounts, warehouses and reports.

At Czarnikow, treasury and finance teams use there is / there are every day when reporting on working capital. A typical weekly update might say: 'There are five receivables past due and there is a payable of EUR 200,000 due next week.' Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and English Grammar in Use (Murphy) treat this as a foundational structure. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that in informal speech, some people use there's even with plurals, but in professional writing you should always match the verb to the noun.

To form questions, simply invert: Is there enough cash? Are there any invoices due? For negatives: There is no inventory left. There are no payments pending. Practice by describing the financial position of a department using five there is / there are sentences — it builds fluency fast.

lessons.title: Cash Flow: Money In and Money Out
lessons.objective: Understand the basic idea of cash flow and why it is critical in trade.
lessons.intro:
Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of a company. Money comes in when customers pay. Money goes out when bills arrive. A healthy company always has enough cash when the bills arrive.

In international business, cash flow is harder. Payments from abroad can be slow. A client in another country may take sixty or ninety days. In the meantime, you still have to pay suppliers and staff.

Many good companies fail not because they are unprofitable, but because they run out of cash.

grammarDeepDive.title: Present continuous for ongoing situations
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The present continuous tense (am/is/are + verb-ing) describes what is happening right now or around this period. In business, it is essential for talking about current trends, temporary situations and ongoing processes. At Czarnikow, you might hear: 'We are waiting for a payment from Brazil' or 'The cash position is improving this month.' These are not permanent facts — they are happening now and may change.

The present continuous is different from the simple present. Compare: 'We receive payments every month' (routine, simple present) vs 'We are receiving fewer payments this month' (temporary, present continuous). Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and English Grammar in Use (Murphy) emphasise this distinction. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary also notes that the continuous form often carries a sense of something being in progress or not yet complete — perfect for describing cash flow, which is always moving.

To form it: subject + am/is/are + verb-ing. For questions: Is the money coming in? Are we waiting for payment? For negatives: The inflows are not arriving on time. We are not paying early this month. A useful exercise: describe what is happening with your company's cash flow right now using five present continuous sentences.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 3: Present Continuous — actions in progress and temporary situations.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 1: Present Continuous — I am doing.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on present continuous for trends and temporary states.

qAndA.question: What is cash flow?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of a company. Inflows are money coming in from customers; outflows are money going out to suppliers, staff and expenses.

qAndA.question: Why can a profitable company still run out of cash?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because profit is calculated on paper, but cash depends on timing. If customers pay late and suppliers want money early, there is a gap even when the company is profitable.

qAndA.question: When do we use the present continuous instead of the simple present?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: We use the present continuous for things happening right now or in a temporary period (e.g. 'We are waiting for a payment'). The simple present is for routines and permanent facts.

qAndA.question: What does the phrase 'Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact' mean?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Profit depends on accounting choices and assumptions — it can be calculated different ways. But cash is real: either you have the money in the bank or you do not.

qAndA.question: How should Czarnikow manage the risk of late international payments?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: By planning ahead, keeping a cash reserve, chasing receivables early, and using tools like letters of credit to guarantee payment timing.

lessons.objective: Understand the opportunities and challenges of trading with emerging markets.
lessons.intro:
Emerging markets — places like Brazil, India or Indonesia — are some of the fastest-growing economies in the world. For many trade companies, they are the most exciting partners of the next ten years.

But business there is not always easy. The currency can move a lot. Banks may be less experienced. Laws may change quickly. And payments sometimes take longer than expected.

The trick is to go in with open eyes: real opportunity, real risks, and a careful plan. People who have worked these markets for years know: patience pays.

grammarDeepDive.title: Present Perfect for experience
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
The present perfect tense (have/has + past participle) is one of the most useful tenses in business English. We use it to talk about experiences and achievements that connect the past to the present. When James says 'I have worked in Brazil for fifteen years', he means he started in the past and the experience is still relevant now. This is different from the past simple ('I worked in Brazil in 2010'), which is finished and over.

At Czarnikow, the present perfect is essential for talking about market experience, client relationships and trade history. 'We have expanded into four new markets since 2020' tells you the expansion is still relevant. 'She has never visited Indonesia' means up to this moment. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and English Grammar in Use (Murphy) classify this as the 'experience' use of the present perfect. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that it is particularly common with ever, never, already, yet, for and since.

Key signals: use for with a duration (for ten years), since with a starting point (since 2015), ever in questions (Have you ever traded with India?), and never for negative experience (We have never had a problem). Practice by listing five things you have done in your career using the present perfect — it builds confidence and fluency.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 14: Present Perfect — experience and result.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 7: Present Perfect (I have done).
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — usage notes on present perfect with ever/never/for/since.

qAndA.question: What are emerging markets and why are they important for trade companies?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Emerging markets are fast-growing economies like Brazil, India and Indonesia. They are important because they offer huge opportunities for trade and growth.

qAndA.question: What are the main risks of trading with emerging markets?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Currency volatility, less experienced banks, laws that change quickly, and payments that can take longer than expected.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'I worked in Brazil' and 'I have worked in Brazil'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'I worked in Brazil' means a finished experience in the past. 'I have worked in Brazil' means the experience is still relevant to the present — maybe I still work there or the experience still matters.

qAndA.question: Why does James say 'patience pays' in emerging markets?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because things take longer — payments, relationships, legal processes. Companies that rush often fail, but those that invest time and build trust succeed in the long run.

qAndA.question: How can a strong local partner reduce risk in an emerging market?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A local partner knows the language, the laws, the banks and the culture. They can navigate problems faster and build trust with clients and suppliers that a foreign company cannot build alone.

lessons.objective: Learn simple phrases to negotiate politely with international partners.
lessons.intro:
Negotiation across cultures is different from negotiation at home. What sounds direct in one country may sound rude in another. What sounds polite in one may sound weak in another.

The safe rule: stay polite and clear. Use soft language — Could we, Would you, Is it possible. Ask questions before you make demands. Give time to think.

Most international deals are not won by the loudest voice. They are won by the side that listens well and keeps its promises.

grammarDeepDive.title: Could / would for polite requests
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In international business, how you say something is often as important as what you say. Could and would are the two most powerful words for making polite requests in English. Compare: 'Give me a better price' (direct, potentially rude) vs 'Could we discuss a better price?' (polite, professional). The meaning is the same, but the tone is completely different. In cross-cultural negotiation, this difference can make or break a deal.

At Czarnikow, where teams negotiate with partners in Brazil, India, Indonesia and beyond, soft language is not optional — it is essential. 'Would you consider a longer payment term?' opens a conversation. 'I want longer payment terms' shuts one down. Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and English Grammar in Use (Murphy) classify could and would as modal verbs used for politeness, possibility and hypothetical situations. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary specifically notes their use in formal and business contexts.

The patterns are simple: Could we + verb? (Could we review the terms?), Would you + verb? (Would you accept a deposit?), and Is it possible to + verb? (Is it possible to extend the deadline?). After could and would, always use the bare infinitive — no to. Practice converting five direct requests into polite ones — it will transform your negotiation style.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 40: could/would — requests and offers.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 35: would/could — polite requests and suggestions.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entry on 'could' and 'would' with politeness usage notes.

qAndA.question: Why is polite language important in international negotiation?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because what sounds normal in one culture may sound rude in another. Polite language keeps the conversation open and builds trust between the two sides.

qAndA.question: What are the three soft language patterns taught in this lesson?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Could we + verb, Would you + verb, and Is it possible to + verb. These are the safest ways to make requests in cross-cultural negotiations.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'Can you give me a better price?' and 'Could we discuss a better price?'
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'Can you give me' sounds like a direct demand. 'Could we discuss' is softer and invites conversation. In formal negotiations, 'could' is much more professional.

qAndA.question: Why does James say 'the loudest voice rarely wins'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because in international business, aggressive negotiation often pushes the other side away. The side that listens, understands, and stays patient usually gets a better deal and a longer relationship.

qAndA.question: How can listening help you win a negotiation?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: By listening, you understand what the other side really wants, what they can be flexible on, and where their limits are. This information helps you make better offers and find compromises.

lessons.title: Running an Import and Export Operation
lessons.grammar: Present simple vs present continuous in operations
lessons.objective: Coordinate a live import/export operation using intermediate business English.
lessons.intro:
Running an import or export operation means turning a single deal into a repeatable process. You have dozens of shipments in motion — some leaving the factory, some at sea, some clearing customs, some being invoiced. Each one has a story, and each one needs attention at a different moment.

The people who do this well share one habit: they separate the routine from the exception. Ninety per cent of shipments follow a standard path. They deserve a standard process, not endless emails. The remaining ten per cent, the exceptions, deserve real thinking.

A good trade operator spends most of the day protecting the exceptions from interrupting the routine, and most of the week making sure the routine actually holds.

grammarDeepDive.title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous in Operations
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In operations, you constantly switch between describing what you always do and what is happening right now. The Present Simple covers routines, schedules and general facts: We ship forty containers a week. The warehouse closes at six. The Present Continuous covers actions in progress at the moment of speaking: We are dealing with a backlog this morning. James is leading the review right now.

The signal words help: always, usually, every Monday, normally point to the Simple; right now, this week, at the moment, today point to the Continuous. Both Eastwood (Oxford Practice Grammar) and Murphy (English Grammar in Use) emphasise that confusing the two tenses is one of the most common errors for intermediate learners — and in a business context it can change meaning. Saying 'We ship on Wednesday' means it is the regular day; saying 'We are shipping on Wednesday' means this specific week is different.

At Czarnikow, operations reviews are full of these contrasts. A board of forty shipments will have routine ones (Simple) and exceptions being handled now (Continuous). Mastering this distinction lets you report status clearly and make decisions faster. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that native speakers switch tense mid-sentence without thinking — your goal is to reach that same fluency.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 3: Present Simple and Present Continuous — form, use and contrast.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 1–4: Present Simple and Present Continuous, including stative verbs.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on 'ship', 'clear', 'handle' with tense usage notes.

rolePlays.title: Monday Morning Operations Review
rolePlays.setup: It is Monday morning at Czarnikow's London office. James is leading the weekly operations review. There are forty live shipments on the board. Thirty-six are routine. Four are exceptions that need immediate attention: one container is stuck in Santos, one is missing documents, one has a port congestion issue in Rotterdam, and one client is requesting an urgent expedite.
rolePlays.studentA: You are James. Walk through the board: describe what normally happens (Present Simple) and what is happening this week (Present Continuous). Flag the four exceptions.
rolePlays.studentB: You are a colleague. Ask questions: 'Are we shipping on time this week?', 'What is happening with the Santos container?', 'Do we normally have this many exceptions?'
sampleDialogue: A: Good morning. We have forty shipments in motion this week. Thirty-six follow the standard path — they ship, they clear, they arrive. Nothing unusual.
B: What about the other four?
A: Right. One container is sitting in Santos because of a dock strike. We are waiting for it to clear. Another one is missing the certificate of origin, so we are chasing the supplier right now.
B: Do we normally have four exceptions in one week?
A: No, we usually deal with one or two. This week is busier because of the strikes.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three Present Simple and three Present Continuous forms correctly. Student B asks at least two questions mixing tenses.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run it once, then swap roles. Focus on whether the student naturally chooses Simple for routines and Continuous for current exceptions. Do not interrupt during the role play — note errors and review afterwards.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between a routine shipment and an exception, according to the lesson?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A routine shipment follows the standard path without problems. An exception is a shipment that has an issue — like missing documents or port congestion — and needs special attention.

qAndA.question: Why does James separate routine cases from exceptions on the Monday board?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because routine cases deserve a standard process, and exceptions deserve real thinking. Separating them protects the team's attention for what matters most.

qAndA.question: When do you use the Present Simple and when do you use the Present Continuous in operations reporting?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: The Present Simple is for habitual actions and schedules — things that always happen. The Present Continuous is for actions happening right now or this week — things that are in progress at the moment.

qAndA.question: Why is visibility the first priority in operations management?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because you cannot manage what you cannot see. If you do not know where each shipment is, you cannot separate the routine from the exceptions and you will waste time reacting instead of planning.

qAndA.question: What happens when a team treats every shipment as an exception?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: The team loses focus and wastes energy on things that should be routine. The real exceptions do not get enough attention, and the whole operation slows down.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Incoterms
lessons.objective: Select the right Incoterm for a given deal and justify it in English.
lessons.intro:
Choosing an Incoterm is not just paperwork — it is a risk decision dressed up as three letters. The difference between FOB and CIF is not academic; it changes who pays insurance, who bears the risk of the sea, and who has to handle a claim if something goes wrong.

Experienced buyers often prefer terms that give them control: CIF or DDP, where the seller handles most of the journey. Experienced sellers usually prefer EXW or FOB, where their responsibility ends early. Neither is right in every case.

The best way to choose is to ask yourself: if something went wrong on this leg, who would be best placed to fix it? That answer usually points you to the correct Incoterm.

grammarDeepDive.title: Second Conditional — would + if (Hypothetical Trade Decisions)
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In trade, you constantly evaluate hypothetical scenarios: If we shipped FOB, who would handle the insurance? If the buyer chose DDP, would the seller bear all the risk? The Second Conditional is the grammar structure that powers these conversations. It uses if + past simple in the condition clause and would + base verb in the result clause.

Eastwood (Oxford Practice Grammar) points out that the past tense in the 'if' clause does not refer to past time — it signals unreality or hypothesis. Murphy (English Grammar in Use) adds that 'were' can replace 'was' in formal contexts: If the shipment were lost, who would pay? This is especially common in trade negotiations and legal discussions at Czarnikow.

The Second Conditional is essential in Incoterms discussions because you are always comparing options that have not happened yet. Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that 'would' can also be softened with 'might' or 'could' for less certain outcomes: If we changed to CIF, the buyer might save on logistics. Mastering this structure lets you sound professional and precise when advising colleagues on trade terms.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 38: Second Conditional — if + past simple, would + verb.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 38: If I did… I would… (Second Conditional).
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entry on 'would' with conditional usage notes.

rolePlays.title: Choosing the Incoterm for the Vietnam–Rotterdam Coffee Route
rolePlays.setup: Harry is advising a colleague on which Incoterm to use for a new coffee route from Vietnam to Rotterdam. The seller has strong freight relationships in Asia but no presence in Europe. The buyer has a warehouse in Rotterdam but no shipping contacts in Vietnam. They need to decide between FOB, CIF, and DDP.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Harry. Analyse the strengths of each party and recommend an Incoterm. Use at least three second conditional sentences: 'If we used FOB, the buyer would…'
rolePlays.studentB: You are the colleague. Challenge Harry's recommendation: 'But if the shipment were delayed, who would bear the cost?' Ask at least two hypothetical questions.
sampleDialogue: A: I would recommend CIF for this route. If we used CIF, Czarnikow would handle the freight from Vietnam, which is our strength.
B: But if the shipment were delayed in transit, who would bear the extra cost?
A: Under CIF, the risk transfers at the ship's rail, so the buyer would bear it after loading. But if we offered insurance, the buyer would be covered.
B: And if we used DDP instead?
A: If we used DDP, we would carry all the risk — including European customs. That would not be ideal because we have no local agent in Rotterdam.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least three correct second conditional forms. Student B asks at least two hypothetical questions with 'if + past simple'.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run it once, swap roles. Focus on natural use of 'would' and 'if + past simple'. Note if the student defaults to 'will' and correct gently after the role play.

That is fine if they have a good freight forwarder there — but they do not. If we used CIF, we would handle the freight and insurance, which plays to our strengths. And if we offered DDP, we would carry everything, door to door. That is the most expensive option, and I would not recommend it unless the margin is very high.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say an Incoterm is 'a risk decision dressed up as three letters'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because the three-letter code determines who pays, who bears the risk, and who handles problems at each stage of the journey. It looks simple but has major financial consequences.

qAndA.question: What is the key question Harry recommends asking when choosing an Incoterm?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: If something went wrong on this leg, who would be best placed to fix it? The answer points to the correct Incoterm.

qAndA.question: How do you form the second conditional, and why is it useful in Incoterms discussions?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: You use 'if + past simple' for the condition and 'would + base verb' for the result. It is useful because Incoterm choices are hypothetical — you are comparing options that have not happened yet.

qAndA.question: Why might a buyer prefer CIF even though the seller controls the freight?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because under CIF the buyer gets insurance included and does not need to arrange freight — which is convenient if the buyer has no shipping contacts in the origin country.

qAndA.question: When would DDP be the wrong choice for a seller?

lessons.title: Managing Global Supply Chains
lessons.objective: Discuss supply chain issues with suppliers and colleagues at an operational level.
lessons.intro:
A global supply chain looks tidy on a slide, but up close it is a long rope of relationships: the farmer, the mill, the trucker, the port, the ship, the freight forwarder, the warehouse, the customer. When one link slows down, the whole rope feels it — and the people on the other end want answers.

Managing the chain well means two things. First, visibility: you need to know, in close to real time, where each shipment is. Second, quick judgement: when a problem appears, you have to decide fast whether to wait, expedite, re-route, or tell the customer. The chain does not pause for hesitation.

The managers who earn trust are the ones who share bad news early and clearly.

commonChallenges: Students often put 'because' at the start of a sentence but forget to add the main clause. Remind them: 'Because X, Y' or 'Y because X' — both need two clauses.

The difference between 'so' (result) and 'because' (reason) causes confusion when translating from Portuguese. Drill: 'The port is congested, SO we re-route' vs 'We re-route BECAUSE the port is congested'.
Students sometimes use 'although' and 'but' in the same sentence. Explain: use one or the other, never both together.

grammarDeepDive.title: Linking Words — because, so, although (Supply Chain Communication)
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Clear communication in supply chain management depends on showing the reason, the result, and the contrast between events. Three linking words do most of this work: because introduces the reason (The shipment is delayed because of port congestion), so introduces the result (The port is congested, so we are re-routing), and although introduces a contrast or surprise (Although the delay looks bad, the customer is calm).

Eastwood (Oxford Practice Grammar) notes that these three connectors cover most of the logical linking a business professional needs at intermediate level. Murphy (English Grammar in Use) adds that although can appear at the start or in the middle of a sentence, but a comma is needed when it starts the sentence. At Czarnikow, these words appear constantly in operational updates, client calls, and email chains.

The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary distinguishes between although (formal) and though (informal). In business writing and client communication at Czarnikow, although is preferred. Mastering these three connectors means your supply chain updates will be logical, professional, and easy to follow — whether you are talking to a colleague or calming a client whose container is stuck.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 46: Linking words — because, so, although, and others.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 112–113: Although/though/even though, and because/so/therefore.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on 'because', 'so', 'although' with usage notes and formality levels.

commonMistakes.wrong: Because the port is congested. We are re-routing.
commonMistakes.right: Because the port is congested, we are re-routing.
commonMistakes.why: 'Because' needs a main clause to complete the sentence — do not put a full stop after the reason.

commonMistakes.wrong: Although the delay is bad, but the customer is calm.
commonMistakes.right: Although the delay is bad, the customer is calm.
commonMistakes.why: Do not use 'although' and 'but' together — choose one connector.

commonMistakes.wrong: The shipment delayed so port congestion.
commonMistakes.right: The shipment is delayed because of port congestion.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'because of' + noun or 'because' + clause for reasons, not 'so'.

commonMistakes.wrong: We re-routing because the bottleneck.
commonMistakes.right: We are re-routing because of the bottleneck.
commonMistakes.why: Do not forget 'are' in the continuous and 'of' after 'because' when followed by a noun.

commonMistakes.wrong: Although we warned the client, so they were calm.
commonMistakes.right: Although we warned the client, they were calm.
commonMistakes.why: 'Although' already introduces the contrast — adding 'so' creates a contradiction.

rolePlays.title: Client Call — Container Stuck at Port
rolePlays.setup: Oliver is on a call with a Czarnikow client whose sugar container has been stuck at a congested port in Santos for four days. The client wants answers: why is it stuck, what is being done, and when will it arrive. Oliver needs to explain the situation clearly using linking words.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Oliver. Explain the situation: the port is congested because of a labour dispute, so you are considering re-routing through Paranaguá. Although it will cost more, the container would arrive only three days late. Use at least three linking words (because, so, although).
rolePlays.studentB: You are the client. Ask questions: 'Why is it stuck?', 'So what are you doing about it?', 'Although it costs more, will you cover the difference?' Push for clear answers.
sampleDialogue: A: Good morning. I am calling about your container. It is currently held in Santos because of a labour dispute at the port.
B: So what is the plan?
A: We are looking at re-routing through Paranaguá, so the delay would be reduced to about three days.
B: Although the delay is shorter, will it cost more?
A: Yes, re-routing is slightly more expensive, although the difference is small. We will cover the extra cost because we want to protect the delivery date.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least one 'because', one 'so', and one 'although' correctly. Student B asks at least two clear follow-up questions.
rolePlays.teacherNotes: Run it once, then swap. Focus on natural use of linking words. After the role play, review any sentences where the student used the wrong connector.

additionalAudios.title: Audio A — Oliver updates the team on a disruption
additionalAudios.speaker: oliver
additionalAudios.transcript: Right, so here is the situation. The Santos port has been congested for four days because of a labour dispute. We have three containers stuck there. Although the dispute may end soon, we cannot afford to wait, so we are looking at re-routing through Paranaguá. The extra cost is about eight per cent, although the client has not been told yet. I want to call them today because bad news is always better early.

Listen again. Why is Santos congested? (Answer: a labour dispute)
Find one use each of 'because', 'so', and 'although' in the transcript.
Pronunciation drill: repeat 'Bad news is always better early' three times with emphasis on 'early'.

additionalAudios.title: Audio B — The client responds
additionalAudios.speaker: sophie
additionalAudios.transcript: Oliver, thank you for calling early. Although I am not happy about the delay, I appreciate the transparency. So, if you re-route through Paranaguá, when would the container arrive? I need a date because my warehouse team is waiting. And although the extra cost concerns me, I understand these things happen in global shipping.
tasks: What does the client appreciate? (Answer: the transparency / being told early)
What does the client need? (Answer: a specific arrival date)
Identify the two uses of 'although' and explain what contrast each one introduces.
Repeat the client's first sentence with the same calm, professional tone.

qAndA.question: What does the lesson mean by 'a long rope of relationships'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: It means a supply chain is a connected series of partners — farmer, mill, trucker, port, ship, forwarder, warehouse, customer. When one link has a problem, all the others feel the impact, like pulling on a rope.

qAndA.question: What are the two key skills for managing a global supply chain, according to the lesson?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Visibility — knowing where each shipment is in real time — and quick judgement — deciding fast whether to wait, expedite, re-route, or inform the customer.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'because', 'so', and 'although'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'Because' gives the reason for something. 'So' gives the result. 'Although' introduces a contrast — something that is surprising or opposite to what you might expect.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say 'share bad news early'? What happens if you wait?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Sharing bad news early protects trust because the client can adjust their plans. If you wait, the client loses trust, the problem gets bigger, and you lose credibility even if you eventually fix it.

qAndA.question: When should a supply chain manager choose to re-route instead of waiting?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: When the cost of waiting — lost trust, missed deadlines, client penalties — is greater than the cost of re-routing. Quick judgement means comparing both options and acting before the window closes.

pairWork.title: Disruption Relay
pairWork.instructions: In pairs, Student A describes a supply chain problem using 'because' ('The shipment is late because...'). Student B continues with a result using 'so' ('...so we are...'). Then Student A adds a contrast using 'although' ('Although..., we...'). Build three complete disruption stories this way, then swap who starts. Each story should be about a different Czarnikow scenario.

lessons.title: Customs Clearance in Practice
lessons.grammar: Passive voice with modals — must be, can be
lessons.objective: Handle a customs clearance process and talk about it professionally.
lessons.intro:
Customs clearance turns a shipment on paper into goods you can actually sell. It is a small, technical job that feels boring until it goes wrong — and then it is the only thing anyone can talk about for days.

In practice, clearance depends on three things: the right documents, the right classification, and the right values. If any of these is wrong, the shipment can be held, fined, or sent back. Experienced trade teams check every document twice: commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin, and sometimes sanitary or safety certificates.

Customs officers are not the enemy. They are paid to look for problems, and you are paid to make sure they do not find any in your paperwork.

grammarDeepDive.title: Passive Voice with Modals — must be, can be, will be (Customs Processes)
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Customs clearance is full of processes where the action matters more than the person doing it. That is why the passive voice with modals is so natural in this context: The HS code must be checked. The shipment can be released. The documents will be reviewed. The focus is on what happens to the shipment, not on who does it.

Eastwood (Oxford Practice Grammar) explains that the structure is straightforward: modal + be + past participle. The modal carries the meaning — must for obligation, can for possibility, will for future certainty. Murphy (English Grammar in Use) adds that this structure is especially common in formal and professional writing, which is exactly the register used in customs documentation and trade communication.

At Czarnikow, customs clearance involves dozens of steps that are described in the passive: documents must be filed, codes must be verified, goods can be inspected, shipments will be released. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that the passive with modals is one of the most tested structures at B1–B2 level because it combines two grammar points. Mastering it means you can describe any process step clearly and professionally.

English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 43: Passive (be done / been done / being done) with modal verbs.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on 'release', 'file', 'classify' showing passive usage in professional contexts.

qAndA.question: How do you form the passive voice with a modal verb?

lessons.title: Using Letters of Credit Effectively
lessons.objective: Use a letter of credit in practice and spot the most common errors.
lessons.intro:
A letter of credit only works if it is used with discipline. The bank does not pay for the deal. It pays for the documents that match the LC. One small difference between the two — a wrong date, a spelling mistake, a missing stamp — and the bank refuses.

In practice, this means the letter of credit and the shipping documents must be prepared by people who read the text word by word. It also means that the LC itself must be checked the moment it arrives: impossible dates, documents you cannot provide, or conditions you cannot meet should be negotiated out before you ship.

Used well, an LC is one of the safest tools in trade. Used carelessly, it is a trap the seller builds for themselves.

grammarDeepDive.title: Relative Clauses — which, that, whose (Letters of Credit)
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
When you describe the terms of a letter of credit, you often need to add information about a specific document, clause, or person. Relative clauses let you do this in one smooth sentence instead of two choppy ones: The LC has a clause that cannot be met is clearer than The LC has a clause. The clause cannot be met.

Eastwood (Oxford Practice Grammar) distinguishes two types: defining clauses (with that) identify which thing you mean — The documents that match the LC will be paid. Non-defining clauses (with which, set off by commas) add extra information — The LC, which was issued yesterday, has three errors. Murphy (English Grammar in Use) adds that whose is used for possession and works for both people and things: the buyer whose signature is missing, the clause whose deadline is impossible.

In LC work at Czarnikow, precision matters more than in almost any other area. A relative clause that incorrectly identifies a document or condition can change the meaning of a sentence — and in trade finance, meaning is money. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that relative clauses are among the structures most associated with professional-level English, making them essential for anyone working with banks, legal documents, and international contracts.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Units 68–70: Relative clauses with who, which, that, whose — defining and non-defining.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 92–96: Relative clauses — who/which/that/whose, defining vs non-defining.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on 'which', 'that', 'whose' with grammar notes on relative clause usage.

rolePlays.title: Reviewing an LC That Just Arrived
rolePlays.setup: Sophie is reviewing a letter of credit that has just arrived at Czarnikow for a sugar export to the Middle East. She has spotted three problems: a shipping date that is impossible to meet, a clause that requires a document Czarnikow cannot provide, and a beneficiary name that has a spelling error. She is discussing these with a colleague before requesting amendments.
rolePlays.studentA: You are Sophie. Describe each problem using relative clauses: 'The shipping date, which is set for next Friday, is impossible because...', 'There is a clause that requires...', 'The beneficiary name, whose spelling is wrong, must be...' Recommend amendments for all three.
rolePlays.studentB: You are the colleague. Ask clarifying questions: 'Which clause is the problem?', 'Whose name is wrong?', 'Is there a deadline by which the amendments must be filed?'
sampleDialogue: A: I have just reviewed the LC, which arrived this morning. There are three issues. First, the shipping date, which is set for next Friday, is impossible — we need at least ten days.
B: Which clause is the second problem?
A: There is a clause that requires a phytosanitary certificate from the port of origin. We cannot provide that because our certificate comes from the Ministry of Agriculture.
B: And whose name is wrong?
A: The beneficiary name, whose spelling shows 'Czarnikow Ltd' instead of 'Czarnikow Group Ltd', must be corrected or the bank will reject the presentation.
rolePlays.successCriteria: Student A uses at least one 'which' (non-defining), one 'that' (defining), and one 'whose' correctly. Student B asks at least two clarifying questions using relative pronouns.

qAndA.question: What does the lesson mean by 'the bank pays for documents, not for deals'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: It means the bank does not care about the underlying trade. It only checks whether the documents presented match the terms of the LC exactly. If they match, it pays. If they do not, it refuses — even if the goods were delivered perfectly.

qAndA.question: Why must the LC be checked the moment it arrives?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because it may contain impossible dates, documents you cannot provide, or conditions you cannot meet. These must be negotiated and amended before you ship, not discovered after.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between a defining relative clause (with 'that') and a non-defining one (with 'which')?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A defining clause with 'that' identifies which specific thing you mean — it is essential to the sentence. A non-defining clause with 'which' adds extra information that could be removed without changing the core meaning. Non-defining clauses use commas.

qAndA.question: Why does the lesson say 'an LC is a trap the seller builds for themselves' when used carelessly?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because the seller prepares the documents. If the documents do not match the LC exactly, the bank refuses payment — and it is the seller's fault for not checking. The seller creates the discrepancy by not being careful enough.

qAndA.question: When should you request an LC amendment instead of trying to comply with the original terms?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: When the original terms contain impossible dates, require documents you cannot provide, or have conditions that do not match the real logistics of the deal. An amendment is cheaper and safer than a discrepancy.

lessons.title: Bank Guarantees That Protect You
lessons.grammar: Modal verbs of obligation — must, have to, should
lessons.objective: Discuss and negotiate bank guarantees for real projects.
lessons.intro:
Bank guarantees come in several flavours, each with a different job. A bid bond protects a buyer while suppliers are competing for a contract. A performance guarantee protects them once the contract is signed. An advance payment guarantee protects a buyer who has paid money up front. A warranty bond protects them after delivery.

Choosing the right one matters. Asking for the wrong guarantee, or for a larger amount than the project deserves, can push a supplier away — or make the deal more expensive for everyone.

The best approach is to think about the moment of risk. What could go wrong, and when? The answer points you straight to the type of guarantee you actually need, and the right size for it.

grammarDeepDive.title: Modal Verbs of Obligation — must, have to, should
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In trade finance, precision matters — and so does the language you use to express rules, requirements and recommendations. Must expresses a strong internal obligation or a rule you believe in: The guarantee must cover the full project period. Have to expresses an external requirement — something imposed by a contract, a regulation or a counterparty: We have to submit the bond before the tender deadline. Should is softer — it gives advice or a recommendation: You should ask for 10%, not 50%.

In practice, must and have to are often interchangeable in business English, but there is a subtle difference. When a Czarnikow trader says 'We must hedge this exposure', it sounds like a personal conviction. When they say 'We have to hedge this exposure', it sounds like a policy or a compliance rule. Both Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's English Grammar in Use emphasise this distinction, and the Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary provides clear usage notes for each modal.

In the negative, the difference is sharper: mustn't means 'it is forbidden' (You mustn't call the guarantee without evidence), while don't have to means 'it is not necessary' (You don't have to use a counter-guarantee for every deal). Getting this wrong in a negotiation can change the meaning entirely, so practise both forms carefully.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 18: Must, have to, should — obligation and advice.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Units 31–33: Must, have to, should, and their negative forms.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on 'must', 'have to', and 'should' with usage notes.

lessons.title: Documentary Collections in Practice
lessons.objective: Run a documentary collection and discuss it confidently.
lessons.intro:
In practice, a documentary collection is a simpler animal than a letter of credit, but it asks more from the two sides. The bank sends the documents, but it does not guarantee payment. That means the seller still needs to know, before shipping, that the buyer will pay when the documents arrive.

Many teams who are used to LCs find collections refreshing: less paperwork, fewer fees, faster cycles. But those same teams also learn that collections punish carelessness. A buyer who quietly decides not to pay can leave the seller with goods stuck at the destination port, with all the costs of shipping back or selling at a discount.

Collections work beautifully with trusted partners — and poorly with anyone else.

grammarDeepDive.title: Used to / Be used to
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
In trade finance, processes change over time — and we need language to talk about past habits and current familiarity. Used to + infinitive describes something that happened regularly in the past but no longer happens: We used to send all collections by post; now we use SWIFT. It only exists in the past tense. There is no present form of 'used to' in this sense.

Be used to + noun/-ing describes something you are accustomed to — familiar and comfortable with: Emily is used to handling documentary collections for French buyers. This form works in any tense: I am used to it, I was used to it, I will get used to it. Both Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's English Grammar in Use dedicate full units to this distinction because it causes persistent errors even at advanced levels.

A third related form is get used to + noun/-ing, which describes the process of becoming accustomed: The new analyst is getting used to filling in collection instructions. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that 'get used to' implies effort or time, while 'be used to' implies the process is already complete. In a Czarnikow context, you might say: We got used to electronic collections quickly — now we are used to them.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 52: Used to do and be used to doing.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 18: Used to (do) and Unit 60: Be/get used to.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on 'used to', 'be used to' and 'get used to' with usage notes.

qAndA.question: What is the role of the remitting bank in a documentary collection?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: The remitting bank acts on behalf of the exporter. It sends the documents and collection instructions to the collecting bank in the buyer's country.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between a sight draft and a time draft?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A sight draft requires immediate payment upon presentation. A time draft allows the buyer to pay at a future date after accepting the documents.

qAndA.question: What is the difference between 'used to + infinitive' and 'be used to + -ing'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'Used to + infinitive' describes a past habit that no longer exists. 'Be used to + -ing' means you are familiar and comfortable with something now.

qAndA.question: Why are documentary collections cheaper but riskier than letters of credit?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: Because in a collection the banks do not guarantee payment — they only handle documents. If the buyer refuses to pay, the exporter has limited recourse.

qAndA.question: When should Czarnikow use a documentary collection instead of a letter of credit?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: When the buyer is a trusted, long-term partner with a good payment history. For new or risky counterparties, a letter of credit is safer.

lessons.title: Structuring Trade Credit
lessons.grammar: Linking words — however, therefore, in addition
lessons.objective: Design and explain trade credit terms for a real customer.
lessons.intro:
Structuring trade credit means deciding not just how long but also how much and on what conditions. A good structure protects the seller without scaring the buyer away. It also tells the buyer, without saying it directly, how much the seller trusts them.

A typical structure might look like this: a credit limit of €100,000, with net 60 terms and a small early payment discount of 2% if paid within 10 days. If the buyer exceeds the limit, shipments stop until the balance comes down. Simple rules, simple to enforce.

The mistake many sellers make is to grant terms too generously at the start and then struggle to pull them back later. Credit, once given, is painful to take away.

grammarDeepDive.title: Linking Words — however, therefore, in addition
grammarDeepDive.explanation:
Clear business communication depends on showing how ideas connect. Three linking words are essential for trade finance professionals at Czarnikow: however (contrast), therefore (result/consequence), and in addition (adding information). These words signal to the listener or reader exactly how your next point relates to the previous one.

However introduces a contrast or an unexpected turn: The customer has a strong history; however, their market is volatile. Therefore introduces a logical consequence: Exposure is rising; therefore, we must tighten the terms. In addition adds a supporting point: We offer Net 30; in addition, we provide an early payment discount. Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's English Grammar in Use both classify these as 'discourse markers' or 'conjunctive adverbs' — words that connect sentences rather than clauses.

In formal business English, these words typically appear at the start of a new sentence or after a semicolon. The Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary notes that 'however' is significantly more formal than 'but', which is why it dominates in reports, proposals and credit memos at Czarnikow. Mastering these three connectors will immediately make your writing and speaking sound more structured and professional.
references: Oxford Practice Grammar (John Eastwood) — Unit 46: Linking words — however, therefore, moreover, in addition.
English Grammar in Use (Raymond Murphy) — Unit 111: Although, though, even though, in spite of, and linking adverbs.
Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary — entries on 'however', 'therefore' and 'in addition' with register notes.

qAndA.question: What is a credit limit and why does it matter?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: A credit limit is the maximum amount a customer can owe at any time. It protects Czarnikow from excessive exposure if the customer fails to pay.

qAndA.question: What are Net 30 and Net 60 terms?

qAndA.question: When do you use 'however' and when do you use 'but'?
qAndA.sampleAnswer: 'However' is more formal and is used in business writing, presentations and reports. 'But' is informal and better for casual conversation.

qAndA.question: Why should Czarnikow structure credit around a customer's cash flow rather than their order ambitions?

qAndA.question: What are the risks of not enforcing a credit policy?

lessons.title: International Payments: Speed, Cost and Risk
lessons.objective: Choose the right international payment method for a given situation.
lessons.intro:
Every international payment is a trade-off between three things: speed, cost and risk. A SWIFT wire is reliable and global but takes one to three days and costs money. A correspondent banking chain is cheap but slower and less transparent. A fintech rail can be faster and cheaper, but may be less widely accepted.

The right choice depends on what you need. For a small, urgent payment to a known supplier, speed matters most. For a large, high-value payment, certainty matters most. For routine payments to many suppliers, cost and ease of reconciliation usually win.

The best treasury teams do not use one method for everything. They match the method to the situation, and they review the choice as new options appear.
